sources.title: Ruben Hassid: Why taste is the edge when AI output is average
sources.originalTitle: Ruben Hassid: Why Taste Is the Only Skill Left
sources.summary: Ruben explains how he grew a large AI audience by testing tools for himself and sharing only what works. His thesis: AI output is average and commoditized, so taste and a unique vision are what stay valuable. He also argues for building on the side of a job, ignoring money early, and learning AI by playing with one task.

principles.text: Teach what you tested for yourself: publish only when it works and isn't obvious.
principles.quote: I'm still testing stuff to help myself as and as soon as is it is very useful and not obvious something I can actually teach you that is new then it's worth an article or a post.

principles.text: Don't chase money early; escape velocity comes from doing something else exceptionally well.
principles.quote: the more you forget about making money, the more money you make.

principles.text: Build the new thing on top of a job; if you can't handle both, you likely couldn't handle it alone.
principles.quote: you have a job and you do it on top of it and if you cannot handle it then you could probably not handle it just that and trying to make money anyway

principles.text: Generic AI output is average, so your edge is a unique vision and taste.
principles.quote: You really need to ask yourself what is so unique about my vision on doing something.

principles.text: Encode your taste, opinions and boundaries into a reusable file that steers any AI like you.
principles.quote: we created something that is like a genie in a bottle of most of my opinion, most of my tastes.

principles.text: Beat AI decision paralysis: pick one thing, treat it as a game, go deep on it.
principles.quote: pick one thing, do it as a as a game. Go down the rabbit hole. You don't have to master everything.

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid built a viral LinkedIn system: be useful, not personal
sources.originalTitle: Ruben Hassid: The System Behind Viral LinkedIn Content
sources.summary: Ruben explains his content philosophy: optimize for usefulness over personal story, write for a distracted reader on a bus, and post consistently without expecting ROI. He also covers using AI to be "greater, not lazier" through taste and volume, and how EasyGen and his own team's growth became its best marketing.

principles.text: Be useful, not personal: no one cares about your story, so solve a problem for the reader.
principles.quote: always tell my team, now I have a team, be useful, not personal. I am obsessed about being useful.

principles.text: Write for a distracted reader: get them the context and a payoff within seconds, with no long intros.
principles.quote: if within 15 seconds he's not already giving getting something, I'm probably not respecting him. So, no long introduction. I go straight to the point.

principles.text: Every post should leave the reader able to do something better; skip posts that add nothing.
principles.quote: If a post doesn't bring anything, why am I even sharing it? I'm not trying to fill up a calendar of stuff.

principles.text: Use AI to be greater, not lazier: taste and experience plus huge volume of generations beat one-click output.
principles.quote: Am I using it to be lazier or to be greater?

principles.text: Post consistently and don't expect ROI; opportunities come from being useful every day.
principles.quote: If your motivation is to be useful every day on social media, crazy stuff's going to happen because people start to um to see it.

principles.text: Prove the product by using it yourself and with your team; employees who grew with it became top affiliates.
principles.quote: My two biggest affiliates by far are my employees.

sources.title: Master AI before it masters you: Ruben Hassid on taste, free content and being the IKEA manual
sources.originalTitle: The #1 AI Teacher Explains Who Survives AI and Who Doesn't | Ruben Hassid - Author of “How to AI”
sources.outlet: Scott D. Clary - Success Story Podcast and Ruben Hassid
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid explains how he grew the How to AI newsletter by publishing free, tested, step-by-step guidance. He argues AI lifts the average rather than everyone, so human taste and judgment remain the edge. He also covers how to get hesitant people started with simple, concrete tools.

principles.text: Real AI understanding comes only from using tools long enough, not from talking about them.
principles.quote: هم فقط الأشخاص الذين جربوه، وجربوه لفترة كافية. هذا كل شيء. معظم الناس يحبون الحديث عنه.

principles.text: AI raises the average, so your edge is what AI can't supply: taste, judgment, spotting flaws.
principles.quote: الناس لا يفهمون أن الذكاء الاصطناعي لا يجعلنا جميعاً أفضل. هذه ليست الطريقة الصحيحة لتأطير الأمر. إنه يجعل المستوى المتوسط أفضل بكثير.

principles.text: Build content like an IKEA manual: only the steps a beginner needs to reach the goal.
principles.quote: وكما قلت، وأستمر في شرح ذلك لفريقي، نحن نبني كتيب تعليمات "إيكيا".

principles.text: Consensus dilutes ideas; keep teams small with a single decision-maker.
principles.quote: أقول لفريقي دائماً: " الإجماع يقتل الإبداع" ، لذا أبني فريقي ليكون فرقاً صغيرة جداً وشخص واحد فقط هو من يتخذ القرار.

principles.text: Give content away free; the small fraction who value it will find their way to paying.
principles.quote: إذا لم أضع قيوداً، فإن القلة، أي 10 آلاف أو 20 ألف شخص ممن سيدفعون لي في النهاية سيجدون طريقهم إلي، لأنني كنت مفيداً جداً للجميع

principles.text: With AI, supply rich context and know your destination first, then evaluate the output yourself.
principles.quote: قدم سياقاً كافياً، واعرف وجهتك، وطبق التقييم بعد ذلك.

sources.title: How Ruben wrote a 26-page thesis in 54 minutes with Consensus, Sci-Hub and ChatGPT
sources.originalTitle: How ChatGPT will write your (entire) thesis in under 40 minutes.
sources.summary: Ruben chains three tools to produce a cited, 7,500-word academic paper in under an hour: Consensus to find papers, Sci-Hub to get the PDFs, ChatGPT to draft section by section. The workflow shows a repeatable pattern: structured prompts, one section at a time, quotes restricted to uploaded sources, and the full outline re-pasted to keep context.

principles.text: Chain specialized tools: one finds sources, one fetches them, the LLM synthesizes.
principles.quote: سأطلب فقط من "شات جي بي تي" استخلاص الجواهر من كل تلك الأوراق ومعرفة ما يمكننا فعله بكل هذا.

principles.text: Structure prompts as role, context, task, then step-by-step chain-of-thought.
principles.quote: سأبدأ بدور ChatGPT، والسياقات، وما هي المهمة، ثم عملية خطوة بخطوة تسمى "توجيه سلسلة الأفكار".

principles.text: LLMs can't hit exact word counts, so ask for a bigger number than you need and accept the undershoot.
principles.quote: وهو أنك إذا طلبت 500 كلمة تحديداً، فلن يفعل ذلك.

principles.text: Ground the model in your own sources: extract quotes first, forbid invented studies.
principles.quote: لا يمكنك استخدام أي ملف PDF آخر أو اختراع أي دراسة.

principles.text: In long multi-step chats, keep re-pasting the full outline so the model doesn't lose the plan.
principles.quote: من المهم جدًا الاستمرار في توضيح ما يحدث وما هو جدول المحتويات بالكامل، حتى يعرف ChatGPT ما يجب عليه فعله، وما لا يجب عليه فعله.

principles.text: A workflow that works manually can become a product: wrap the tool chain in a SaaS.
principles.quote: إنه جزء يمكنني بناء برنامج (SaaS) يصنع الأوراق البحثية.

sources.title: How to prompt ChatGPT like an intern manager: few-shot, chain-of-thought, and EasyGen's LinkedIn growth
sources.originalTitle: ChatGPT Prompts and Techniques with Ruben Hassid
sources.summary: Ruben explains why generic ChatGPT prompts give generic output: LLMs are next-word predictors, so you must supply examples (few-shot) and steps (chain-of-thought) and treat the model like a precise but literal intern. He also covers using AI for brainstorming volume rather than education, and how EasyGen helped two employees hit 1M LinkedIn views in 25 days.

principles.text: Zero-shot prompts produce generic output; give examples (few-shot) of your own best work first.
principles.quote: Zero-shot means that you give it zero example before you get the results, okay? But few-shot prompting means that you give multiple examples before you get the output.

principles.text: LLMs are glorified next-word predictors, so default output is generic by design; prompt for the twist you want.
principles.quote: It's going to be as generic as possible, as dull as possible. But but it's not even a problem. It is trained that way. It is meant to be that way.

principles.text: Use chain-of-thought: spell out the steps you would take and have the AI wait for your approval between them.
principles.quote: So, you are the one doing the steps. It's called chain-of-thoughts.

principles.text: Treat the LLM as a tireless but literal intern; anything you think is obvious must be stated.
principles.quote: everything that you think is obvious is not to an intern. It's totally not to an LLM.

principles.text: Use AI to generate a thousand options, then you select the best; it is not a one-button perfect answer.
principles.quote: No, you press one button and you get a thousand solutions and then you select the best one.

principles.text: Make content about the audience going from A to B, not about you.
principles.quote: It's not about me when I'm making a post. It's about you who's listening. I need to help you go from A to B.

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid built a 78M-view LinkedIn audience: one platform, one persona, educational content
sources.originalTitle: AMA Session: Ruben Hassid – Founder at RubenHassid ai
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid explains how he grew from a music label to a top LinkedIn creator by focusing on a single platform and persona. He covers reverse-engineering what works, killing the ego, setting realistic expectations, and building problem-first rather than AI-first.

principles.text: Don't repurpose everywhere. Pick one platform and hammer it until you hit millions of views before expanding.
principles.quote: running more than one social media at high level is nearly impossible by by yourself I've I've seen very few people doing it you always have a team

principles.text: Write for one specific persona, and expect the persona to differ by platform.
principles.quote: when I'm creating Contents I keep writing for one person it's a known trick but I keep writing for one person

principles.text: Treat content like a startup product: use the fast feedback loop and track impressions as the core metric.
principles.quote: I take content and social media just like I would take like a product of a startup um you need to have feedback as fast as possible you need to Pivot with it

principles.text: Kill your ego: keep content purely educational rather than about your personal story.
principles.quote: if you look at my contents 99% of it uh it's just purely educational and I'm outside of it

principles.text: Before posting, spend days or weeks reverse-engineering what top creators in your niche do.
principles.quote: reverse engineer what's working and there's a high chance you're at least on the right path

principles.text: Posting is only a third of the game; the rest is commenting, DMs and networking on the platform.
principles.quote: content is a third and two third is commenting DM and the rest

sources.title: Ruben Hassid on growing on LinkedIn with AI: taste, volume, and one mission
sources.originalTitle: How to Use AI to Grow on LinkedIn FAST (Algorithm Update)
sources.summary: Ruben explains how he grew to 400K+ LinkedIn followers and built EasyGen, a bootstrapped post generator. AI rewards taste and volume (generate many, curate the best), not one-shot prompts. His LinkedIn playbook: one tight problem, many solutions, double down on winners, and engage.

principles.text: AI replaces mediocrity, not people. Taste, experience and high standards, multiplied by volume, are the edge.
principles.quote: mediocrity is going to be replaced very fast it's already happening if most of your job is writing OK articles you're going to be replaced really fast

principles.text: Never one-shot AI output. Generate many variations, then use your taste to select and patchwork the best parts.
principles.quote: by the time you try to find a topic I wrote and generated 30 posts on the same topic more or less

principles.text: Use AI to be greater, not lazier: do more and better work instead of finishing the day after one quick generation.
principles.quote: I'm using AI to be greater not to be lazier the idea is I can do more

principles.text: Start LinkedIn with one tight problem (your mission), then cover it with many solutions and repeat yourself often.
principles.quote: one problem to solve and the the the simpler the problem the easier for you um and then many solutions

principles.text: Run a 30-day test of formats and angles, then double down on the best five winners; don't retry the losers.
principles.quote: you analyze the best five and the worst five and you do the best five 30 times the next months

principles.text: Engagement matters as much as posting, especially early. You can't want a community and never talk to anyone in it.
principles.quote: engaging it's just as important it's not way more important in the beginning

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid built a multi-million LinkedIn AI education business as a solo creator
sources.originalTitle: De zéro à millionnaire grâce à l'IA ?
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid explains how he went from a failed music label to a $3-4M/year business by writing "IKEA instructions" for AI tools on LinkedIn. He covers sponsorship terms, riding platform pushes, content-first positioning, the human edge against AI, and handling haters and burnout. (Interview in French; quotes translated.)

principles.text: Be useful by writing step-by-step how-tos; give instructions anyone can follow rather than selling yourself.
principles.quote: I often say that I'm kind of writing the IKEA instructions for AI tools. (translated from French)

principles.text: Turn audience demand into content: log every question from comments and DMs, then answer the most requested for free.
principles.quote: I look at all the comments, all the private messages, and I look at where people ask me for things the most. (translated from French)

principles.text: Sponsored content works when you keep creative control and only back tools you believe are best. Integrity builds audience trust.
principles.quote: If I don't like your tool, if I think there's a better tool to do that, to do the task, I'm not going to promote it. (translated from French)

principles.text: Structure creator deals around guaranteed reach: commit to a minimum number of views and post more if it's missed.
principles.quote: There's a minimum number of views I'll deliver. And if I don't hit that minimum, I commit to doing more posts on it. (translated from French)

principles.text: When a platform pushes a new format, ride it hard but briefly. What works stops working once the push ends.
principles.quote: Something that works stops working after a while. (translated from French)

principles.text: Price sponsorships on the buyer's value: ask whether LinkedIn is a major channel and whether those users have high LTV before quoting.
principles.quote: Are you sure that your LTV, the value of your users, is very high when people come from LinkedIn, and is LinkedIn a big channel for you? (translated from French)

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid prompts ChatGPT like a team of creatives: layered prompts, human editing, free-first growth
sources.originalTitle: How AI Is Prompting A Thinking Revolution: Talking GPT-4 With Jason, Garrett And Ruben Hassid
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid explains how he went from joking with ChatGPT in Berlin to building an AI audience, and how he prompts it. He treats the model as a team of creatives you direct in layers (outline first, then iterate), feeds it your own data, and keeps a human editing the output. He grew by giving content away free before monetizing.

principles.text: Treat a generative AI like a team of creatives you manage: give a brief, not a vague one-line request.
principles.quote: you really need to understand for any generative AI it's like a team of people

principles.text: Prompt in layers: ideate titles, build a table of contents, then write section by section, critiquing each step.
principles.quote: prompting you don't prompt once yeah you prompt with layers of prompts and then you see what it does and then you prompt it more

principles.text: Feed the model your own data and ask it to transform it; don't use it as a judgment machine like Google.
principles.quote: what it's best at is to give it data and it gives back something really smart like a summary an outline a strategy

principles.text: Don't trust the model for facts or sources; it answers even when wrong, so supply the sources yourself.
principles.quote: GPT is one hell of a liar be careful

principles.text: Always qualify the output with a human touch; AI raises the average, so spend saved time making work better, not working less.
principles.quote: it's not the time to be lazier it's the time to do 10 times more

principles.text: Grow first, monetize later: give valuable content away free to build an audience, then add premium offers.
principles.quote: I have two hammers one for monetization and one for growth which one should I hit first and I just kept hammering a growth at all costs everything is free

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid built EasyGen and 120M LinkedIn views: content, founder branding and talking before building
sources.originalTitle: GitHub Start Up Wednesday with EasyGen.io
sources.summary: Ruben explains why he built EasyGen as a ghostwriter-style tool for his own team, and how founders should do personal branding by educating rather than sharing their life story. He also covers using employees' brands as a growth channel, LinkedIn micro-testing and language focus, and talking to people before building.

principles.text: Technical products lose without distribution; great founders invest in marketing and sharing early.
principles.quote: second time founder focus on marketing because they understand that if you build even the the best tool on the planet there's a high chance no one will care if you're not good enough at sharing it

principles.text: Personal branding means being relatable, not telling your life story; educate your audience instead.
principles.quote: you don't have to show about your life story to do that usually just educate me on that matter like tell me some of the learnings that you've discovered

principles.text: Make most of your content about the problem and journey your audience is in, not your product.
principles.quote: you can make your entire content 80% of your content about how hard it is to abandon a bad routine and how positive it is to embrace one good routine doesn't have to be about the the tool itself

principles.text: Turn employees into content channels with a small daily time investment and a simple, repeatable content workflow.
principles.quote: even if it's like 30 minutes to an hour a day that they invest in their brand it is positive to me it is positive to them

principles.text: Pick one language on LinkedIn because the algorithm micro-tests posts on small audiences and a mismatched audience scrolls away.
principles.quote: the best way is to focus on one language it's already hard enough and just double down on it

principles.text: Talk about the solution to real people before and while you build, and stay obsessed with the people you help, not the product.
principles.quote: before starting to build something as fast as possible talk about the solution as fast as possible to other people that's the best way to start

sources.title: Prompting ChatGPT like a human: Persona, Context, Mission and tree of thought
sources.originalTitle: ChatGPT Prompting Strategies for Beginners to 10X Your Results | AI Expert Ruben Hassid
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid explains how to prompt ChatGPT by treating it like an intern: give a Persona, Context and Mission, and keep the decisions yourself. He also covers token limits, custom instructions, common mistakes, and how he builds LinkedIn content with AI as a helper rather than a replacement.

principles.text: Prompt an AI like you'd brief a human intern: give context, examples and a clear mission, or expect weak output.
principles.quote: the answer is just as good as the prompt

principles.text: Structure prompts as Persona, then Context, then Mission, and make each as specific as possible.
principles.quote: that's Persona context Mission

principles.text: The biggest prompting mistake is not knowing what you want and expecting the AI to know it for you.
principles.quote: not knowing what you want and expecting the AI to know what you want

principles.text: Use AI to brainstorm options and keep the judgment call yourself (tree of thought): pick one branch, then brainstorm again.
principles.quote: you're not asking Chad GPT to select anything you're like Bren storm and I'm gonna pick it one of the answer

principles.text: Phrase instructions affirmatively (say 'stop asking questions' rather than 'don't ask questions') and call out repeated mistakes until it adapts.
principles.quote: always prefer affirmative sentences so avoid at all costs don't do that prefer stop doing that

principles.text: Manage tokens: keep brainstorming chats concise, or front-load a big prompt when you know exactly what you want; custom instructions sit outside the token limit.
principles.quote: this is out of the tokens limits so yeah whatever how long is the conversation CAD GPT will always remember the custom instruction

sources.title: How EasyGen drives ~18% of revenue via affiliates, led by employees and customers
sources.originalTitle: How EasyGen Generates 18% of Its Revenue Through Affiliate Marketing
sources.summary: Ruben explains how EasyGen, a bootstrapped LinkedIn post generator, gets about 18% of its roughly $50K MRR from affiliates, with most of it coming from four people. He covers turning employees into affiliates, coupon-based tracking, community building around one problem, and refusing automation and VC money.

principles.text: Concentrate affiliate bets on a few people, and make some of them your team: they get equity-like upside on top of salary.
principles.quote: 80% of that money it's just four people and out of those four people two of them are my employees so I'm paying them affiliate deals through re food

principles.text: Use coupon codes instead of links to track affiliates: buyers can see the discount applied, so it feels sturdier.
principles.quote: if they click on the link they're afraid it's not working if you use a coupon you can see on stripe the you know like the numbers

principles.text: Be the heaviest user of your own product; affiliates credible with it are your best sellers, so recruit from customers first.
principles.quote: I made sure that I'm the most prominent user of e gen no one used EAS gen more than me and I think it's a good thing as a Founder to be the guy who used the product the most

principles.text: Build community with realistic expectations: aim for about one engaged person a day by solving one specific problem.
principles.quote: you should aim at 1,000 people over three years 1,000 people over three years is 300 people per year that's 10 people per month

principles.text: Never automate posting: platforms hunt bot-like behavior, so keep a human on the platform.
principles.quote: if you behave like a bot well it turns out that social media have insanely big teams and their only sole purpose is to find people who behave like Bots

principles.text: Stay bootstrapped to keep ownership, speed and fun over a bigger but VC-constrained outcome.
principles.quote: I'd rather have a business that is making 100K a month um where I own 80% of the company and have a lot of fun doing it than one that is making 10 Millions a month

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid trains Claude on his best LinkedIn posts to write new ones
sources.summary: Ruben walks through scraping a profile's LinkedIn posts cheaply via Apify, having Claude analyze them into a report and SOP, then turning that into a reusable /skill that generates new posts from proven patterns. He also shows how to clone the recipe of a single viral post, and is candid about the limits: AI mirrors rather than creates, and only works if past posts were good.

principles.text: Train AI on your own best posts, not generic internet advice, so output reflects what actually worked for you.
principles.quote: And this is optimized only from MY best posts, nothing from the internet _(which is probably outdated anyway)._

principles.text: Never automate from your own LinkedIn account; extract public posts through a third-party tool instead.
principles.quote: It’s important not to do it from your account (_never do any automation_).

principles.text: Turn the analysis into a reusable skill so you stop re-pasting the same prompt and context.
principles.quote: You want to create a skill inside Claude to not copy & paste the same prompt and the same context, over and over again.

principles.text: Capture the recipe of a single ultra-viral post (format, hook, caption cadence) as a skill to repeat it.
principles.quote: Just create a Claude skill to capture the “recipe” of that post for any new post.

principles.text: Don't repeat one viral recipe endlessly; audiences tire of the same format.
principles.quote: It’s not because burgers are tasty that you want to eat burgers every day.

principles.text: AI is great at digesting context but not creative; pair it with your own human pattern-matching.
principles.quote: But it’s awesome when you can combine its capacity to digest a lot of context (like 400+ posts) + your human ability to do pattern-matching.

sources.title: Stop prompting Claude: files-as-prompts with Cowork + Obsidian as a "Second Brain"
sources.originalTitle: Prompting is the worst way to use Claude.
sources.summary: Ruben argues that one-line prompts give average, generic output because Claude lacks context. His fix is Claude Cowork pointed at a folder of text files (style, rules, goals) that act as a permanent prompt. He pairs it with Obsidian so non-developers can read, search and edit those files, and adds Skills for repeated tasks.

principles.text: Bad AI output usually comes from missing context, not a bad model; don't blame the tool.
principles.quote: You didn’t give Claude enough context. You didn’t explain your tone, your audience, your rules. Everything.

principles.text: Replace retyped prompts with saved files Claude reads every session: the files are the prompt, forever.
principles.quote: Claude reads them automatically before every session. **The files are the prompt. Forever.**

principles.text: Fix a recurring Claude annoyance once in your context file instead of re-correcting it in every chat.
principles.quote: You prompted Claude once, and it remembers forever. Literally your Second Brain.

principles.text: Pick tools by friction for non-technical users: free, local, clean, and they never alter your files.
principles.quote: I picked it because everything else failed at least one of my criteria.

principles.text: Turn tasks you repeat weekly into Skills (one file per task) callable with a slash command.
principles.quote: You say it once, fine. You say it 30 times, that’s not so efficient.

principles.text: Distribution runs on shares; make the content free and ask readers to pass it to someone helpful to them.
principles.quote: This newsletter mostly grows because of your shares. And I keep hitting 1,000+ shares. It’s my north star.

sources.title: Prompt Maker: let a free GPT turn one-line bad prompts into usable ones
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid argues you can skip learning prompt engineering by running a rough one-liner through his free "Prompt Maker" GPT, then pasting the output into a fresh chat. He shows the two-step workflow with LinkedIn hooks and newsletter ideation, and ends with a simple newsletter growth ask.

principles.text: Output quality is capped by input quality, so fix the prompt first.
principles.quote: You know ChatGPT is as good as the input ( = the prompt).

principles.text: Don't aim for a perfect prompt; a decent start from a terrible one-liner is the practical win.
principles.quote:
Is it the best prompt possible for such task? No.

Is it a fantastic start from a one-liner terrible prompt? The best you could have.

principles.text: Use a two-step workflow: generate a better prompt, then run it in a fresh chat with your own content.
principles.quote: From your bad prompt → to the Prompt Maker → to a better prompt to copy.

principles.text: Fence off your own input with delimiters so the model knows what is data versus instruction.
principles.quote: /// what I’m about to share ///

principles.text: Run the same prompt across different models to get different twists, and pick the strongest for the task.
principles.quote: You want a different twist? Select another model to write (GPT-4.5 is also good).

principles.text: Ask readers to forward the newsletter; a 1% forward rate on a large list adds meaningful free growth.
principles.quote: If 1% of you forward this email to a colleague, that’s an extra 4,000 people to keep this newsletter free forever!

sources.title: Your prompt sucks: prepare a reference, blueprint and success brief before you prompt
sources.summary: Ruben argues that asking ChatGPT to write your prompt gives vague results, because prompting is thinking, not typing. His method: find a reference and convert it to markdown, reverse-engineer it into a short blueprint, write a 4-question success brief, then stack all three into one prompt and keep chatting to steer toward the result.

principles.text: Prompting is thinking, not typing: prepare before you write a single word.
principles.quote: Most people think prompting = typing. But prompting = thinking.

principles.text: Asking AI to write your prompt fails: vague descriptions, no definition of success, everything in one shot.
principles.quote: You give _**vague**_ descriptions.

principles.text: Match effort to stakes: quick lookups need no complex prompt, serious tasks need a specific method.
principles.quote: You do NOT need to use a complex prompt for this.

principles.text: Start from a concrete reference converted to markdown, then reverse-engineer it into a short blueprint.
principles.quote: Analyze this reference so you can recreate something similar later.

principles.text: Write a success brief with four answers: output type and length, recipient reaction, what it must not sound like, and what success means.
principles.quote: Does NOT sound like**: \[What to avoid — generic AI, too casual, too legal, jargon-heavy?\]

principles.text: Treat AI as a conversation: correct errors immediately, keep messages short, steer toward convergence, and reset a bloated chat.
principles.quote: Steer aggressively toward convergence

sources.title: The 7 Deadly Sins of Prompting: briefs, not wishes, and the R-E-X prompt
sources.summary: Ruben argues most ChatGPT prompts fail because they are wishes rather than briefs. He lists seven common prompting mistakes with before/after fixes and offers the R-E-X framework (Role, Examples, Expectations). Iterating in short steps beats writing one long prompt.

principles.text: Prompts fail when they are wishes. Write a brief: good inputs produce good outputs.
principles.quote: Most (ChatGPT) prompts fail because they’re wishes, not briefs.

principles.text: Give the model context: role, task scope and constraints. Otherwise it guesses and errors multiply.
principles.quote: the model guesses your job, audience, and constraints. Guessing multiplies errors.

principles.text: Turn questions into jobs with deliverables; define success and acceptance tests up front.
principles.quote: Asking questions is level 1. Give it directives.

principles.text: Split big asks into steps and chain outputs, instead of one giant request.
principles.quote: One giant ask hides failures and creates spaghetti outputs.

principles.text: Iteration beats length: prompt quicker, not longer. It's a chat, so have a chat with it.
principles.quote: Iteration beats length: prompt quicker, not longer.

principles.text: Use R-E-X: define a Role, paste Examples to imitate, and set Expectations (format, length, tone, rubric).
principles.quote: The R-E-X prompt is to define a role, give examples & set expectations in your (ChatGPT, or other AI) prompt.

sources.title: Prompt Engineering 101: five research-backed rules for asking AI better questions
sources.summary: Ruben Hassid summarizes recent academic papers on prompting modern LLMs. Key lessons: keep questions neutral, drop "step by step", verify every AI-cited source, limit prompts to about 3 rules, and give a clear goal instead of examples. The final "One Prompt" template is paywalled.

principles.text: Keep prompts neutral: avoid tag questions and yes/no framing that bias the AI toward agreeing with you.
principles.quote: Just like when you ask a friend, don’t make them answer the way you want them to answer. Keep it neutral. Avoid yes/no questions.

principles.text: Skip "step by step" instructions; a short role ("as a reliability engineer") added to your question beat chain-of-thought.
principles.quote: The most famous “Let’s think step by step” LOST to asking normally.

principles.text: Never trust AI-cited sources on confidence; open and verify every link, since even expert reviewers miss hallucinated citations.
principles.quote: If professional reviewers can’t catch AI-hallucinated papers, you won’t either. You must open every link:

principles.text: Limit a single prompt to about 3 rules; split extra requirements into a second pass that checks them one at a time.
principles.quote: 12 of the 15 models can’t reliably hold more than 3 rules.

principles.text: State a clear goal and context rather than pasting examples, which can hurt modern models; let the AI ask for missing data.
principles.quote: Specifying a goal is the ultimate key to a good prompt.

principles.text: Prompt advice expires quickly as models change, so re-check techniques against recent research instead of trusting old tips.
principles.quote: AI changes so fast that techniques from before don’t work anymore.

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid deslops AI writing with the "Use ASD-STE100" prompt
sources.originalTitle: How to deslop Claude in 2 words.
sources.summary: Ruben shares a two-word prompt, "Use ASD-STE100", that forces Claude into simplified technical English and removes typical AI slop patterns. He notes it fits instructions and clear explanations but fails for creative writing and LinkedIn posts. Most of the essay (prompt, research workflow) is paywalled.

principles.text: A two-word prompt, 'Use ASD-STE100', removes most AI slop by forcing clear, direct simplified English.
principles.quote: But you can fix it in 2 words for 80% of your chats.

principles.text: Leverage an existing standard the model already knows instead of describing style rules from scratch.
principles.quote: AI knows enough about the ASD-STE100 to reply with simplified English.

principles.text: Package a proven prompt into a reusable Claude skill so the style is applied rigorously and repeatably.
principles.quote: And I built a skill to get Claude to truly talk like ASD-STE100 instructions.

principles.text: Don't apply the deslop trick everywhere: it is too cold for creative writing and LinkedIn posts.
principles.quote: It's really bad for creative writing. Not a fun poem to read.

principles.text: Research before writing any piece of text so the output never sounds like AI, even unintentionally.
principles.quote: Never sounding like an AI (even when you didn't intend to).

sources.title: How to stop hitting Claude usage limits: 23 token-saving habits
sources.originalTitle: How to stop hitting Claude usage limits.
sources.summary: Ruben explains that Claude re-reads the whole conversation on every message, so cost compounds as chats grow. He lists 23 habits, from converting files and planning in Chat to editing instead of following up, to cut token waste and hit limits about once a month.

principles.text: Every message makes Claude re-read the whole conversation, so long chats get expensive; every habit is about avoiding wasted tokens.
principles.quote: You send one message, and Claude re-reads your entire conversation from the top. Every previous message. Every previous answer. All of it.

principles.text: Do the thinking in the cheap product and the building in the expensive one: plan in Chat, then build the file in Cowork.
principles.quote: You do the thinking in the cheap product. You do the building in the expensive one.

principles.text: Edit your original message instead of sending corrections, so the old exchange is replaced rather than stacked in history.
principles.quote: Every time you send “No, I meant...” or “Actually, change X to Y,” you’re adding to the conversation history. The edit button avoids this entirely.

principles.text: Batch several tasks into one message to pay for one context reload instead of several, and often get better answers.
principles.quote: Three separate prompts = three full context reloads. One prompt with three tasks = one reload.

principles.text: Summarize and restart a fresh session every 15-20 messages, since most tokens in long sessions go to re-reading history.
principles.quote: One developer tracked his usage and found 98.5% of tokens were spent re-reading history. Only 1.5% went toward the actual output.

principles.text: Match model and product to the task: use Sonnet or Haiku for simple work and save Opus with extended thinking for deep work.
principles.quote: Opus + Extended thinking is your heavy machinery. Don’t use heavy machinery to move a chair.

sources.title: Stop using your own Claude at work: a safety guide to personal AI at the office
sources.originalTitle: Stop using your own Claude at work.
sources.summary: Ruben explains how employees who use personal ChatGPT or Claude accounts at work can cut their legal and career risk. He covers switching off model training, anonymizing data, using temporary chats and avoiding connectors, then points readers to his paid tiers and consulting.

principles.text: Switch off model training on any personal AI account, because the defaults let providers train on your chats.
principles.quote: On the personal plans (the free or paid AI you signed up for yourself), the AI company is allowed to train on your chats by default.

principles.text: Use a simple gut-check before pasting anything work-related into an AI.
principles.quote: Before you paste, ask: “Would I be fine if this exact text showed up in the company-wide channel, with my name on it?”

principles.text: Anonymize before you paste: swap names for roles, use fake values of similar size, and paste only the excerpt you need.
principles.quote: Anonymizing means stripping the identifying details out before you paste, so the AI helps you without ever seeing the ‘secret’.

principles.text: Run work tasks in temporary or incognito chats so nothing is saved to history or used for training.
principles.quote: a temporary chat doesn’t save to your history and isn’t used for training. Close it, and it’s gone.

principles.text: Never connect work accounts to a personal AI, and keep connectors to the narrowest access you can.
principles.quote: Never connect your work accounts to your personal AI.

principles.text: The best fix is for the company to pay for the right AI and train its team on it.
principles.quote: Get your company to pay for the best AI. And train your team on it.

sources.title: How to set up Claude Cowork: Skills + Projects, no folders, and token-saving habits
sources.summary: Ruben reverses his earlier advice to build Cowork around folders and files. He now recommends only Skills for repeatable capabilities and Projects for specific contexts, with minimal settings, voice dictation, and tactics to cut token costs. He also covers shared team projects and onboarding new hires with Claude.

principles.text: Replace folders and files with Skills and Projects; folders leak context and files are unmaintainable.
principles.quote: **Folders are leaking**. Even if I told my Cowork to “_never check my output folder_,” Claude would sometimes do it. And it poisons my context with outdated outputs.

principles.text: Skill vs Project test: if you can teach it to someone, it's a Skill; if it's a specific context, it's a Project.
principles.quote: It’s a skill you can teach someone → **Skill**.

principles.text: Don't over-instruct the AI. Too much context makes it repeat the same answers and kills creativity.
principles.quote: Once you give too much context to Claude, it falls into the same answers every single time. No more creativity.

principles.text: Use the AskUserQuestion trick: have Claude interview you with a form so your prompt gets enough context.
principles.quote: Claude will keep interviewing you until you’ve given so much context it’s impossible to fail.

principles.text: Speak your prompts with a dictation tool; you give far more context and think more naturally.
principles.quote: we end up giving much more context when we talk (_we are yappers by nature_), rather than with a lazy typed prompt.

principles.text: Save tokens by editing or restarting a prompt instead of sending follow-ups, since each message re-reads full history.
principles.quote: Every time you send a message, Claude re-reads the entire conversation history.

sources.title: How to get your first 10,000 LinkedIn followers: one mission, one profile, consistent good posts
sources.summary: Ruben argues that LinkedIn growth comes from writing good, targeted posts around one clear mission, not from pods, automations or AI comment spam. He covers profile setup (headline, featured link, experience section) and a Mission + Solution + Angle + Format post framework. The essay is paywalled, so the step-by-step 0 to 10,000 plan is not visible.

principles.text: Pick one problem to solve and nothing else; if it can't be said in one sentence, it's too broad.
principles.quote: That's it. Solve one problem. And one ONLY.

principles.text: A mission you can't state in one sentence signals a lack of focus.
principles.quote: If you can’t explain it within one sentence, you need help.

principles.text: Win with good posts (targeted, helpful, consistent, improving), not shortcuts like pods, cold automations or AI comments.
principles.quote: Good is targeted. Good is helpful. Good is consistent and gets better.

principles.text: Each post is one solution to the mission, built from solution, angle and format.
principles.quote: Post = one (of the many) solutions to the one problem.

principles.text: Make your headline your mission with a cheeky, clear twist.
principles.quote: Your mission is your headline, with a twist.

principles.text: Keep the featured section to one link and no description to cut friction and lift conversions.
principles.quote: Less clicks = More conversions.

sources.title: Why Ruben Hassid quit ChatGPT for Claude Cowork: instruction-following, files, no memory
sources.summary: Ruben explains why he stopped using ChatGPT for a month and moved his AI work to Claude Cowork. He gives four reasons (follows long instructions, avoids infinite loops, no memory overfitting, creates real files) and five non-technical use cases. The core lesson: control the full context yourself and think in workflows, not tools.

principles.text: Output quality depends on how much context you can give, so pick an AI that actually follows long instructions.
principles.quote: The quality of your output depends on how much context you can give. If the AI ignores your context, you’re stuck with generic results. Forever.

principles.text: Upload a detailed voice profile and rules so AI output sounds like you, not like AI imitating you.
principles.quote: With Claude Cowork, I upload my voice profile. Over 2,000 words describing how I write, what I hate, phrases I never use, structures I prefer.

principles.text: Persistent memory causes overfitting; start fresh and supply context explicitly for each task.
principles.quote: I decide what matters. Not some algorithm guessing based on a conversation I don’t even remember having.

principles.text: Keep a markdown file about yourself and upload it at the start of conversations instead of re-introducing yourself.
principles.quote: Create a markdown file with everything about you, and upload it to any AI at the start of every conversation (when necessary).

principles.text: When a session goes off track, have the AI interview you with forms to reset direction without losing context.
principles.quote: Claude Cowork is the one prompting me.

principles.text: Think in terms of how things can be done, not which tool is right; skills transfer across AIs.
principles.quote: We must think in terms of “This is how things can be done.” not in terms of “This is the right tool.”

sources.title: Workaholic: why AI makes you work more, and 5 rules against performative productivity
sources.summary: Ruben argues AI removes the friction of both starting and stopping, so people ship more but move in the wrong direction. He names the enemy "performative productivity" and gives 5 rules plus two prompts to pick one goal and audit your week against it. He backs it with an 8-month Harvard study showing AI intensifies work.

principles.text: AI removes the friction of starting and stopping, so busyness feels like progress.
principles.quote: AI removes the friction of _starting_. That’s great. But it also removes the friction of _stopping_. And if stopping feels harder than continuing, you have an addiction.

principles.text: The hardest part of work is deciding what's worth doing; AI lets you skip it, producing circular momentum.
principles.quote: AI lets you skip the hardest part of work: deciding what’s _worth_ doing in the first place.

principles.text: Before prompting, state the problem in one sentence; otherwise AI generates noise you then edit all night.
principles.quote: If you can’t explain the problem in one sentence, AI will generate noise. And you’ll spend your night editing that noise.

principles.text: Subtract as deliberately as you add: kill 3 tasks for every 1 task AI helps you add.
principles.quote: For every new thing AI helps you ship, ask: what 3 things can I stop doing?

principles.text: Set a hard 'last prompt' time; rest is the most productive behavior.
principles.quote: Understand that the most productive behavior you can have is to rest.

principles.text: AI writes v1, but you decide whether v1 should exist; fast drafting is not a reason to draft.
principles.quote: Just because AI can draft something in 30 seconds doesn’t mean it should be drafted.

sources.title: 16 ChatGPT myths: how to use AI as a co-pilot, not an oracle
sources.summary: Ruben debunks 16 common beliefs about ChatGPT: it doesn't know the whole internet, forgets beyond its context window, hallucinates, carries bias, and isn't private or free. His core stance: treat AI output as a first draft, pair it with human taste and experience, and verify everything. He also announces a paid weekly video tier because AI courses go obsolete in weeks.

principles.text: Treat every AI reply as a first draft: verify, cross-check, then polish.
principles.quote: Treat every reply as a first draft. Verify, cross‑check, then polish.

principles.text: AI plus human beats either alone, so use it as a co-pilot; taste and experience are the moat.
principles.quote: On every possible benchmark, AI + human beats both AI or human alone.

principles.text: AI predicts the next token, not the next fact; confidence is not truth, so check sources.
principles.quote: It predicts the next token, not the next fact. When the data gap is big, it fills the void with fiction.

principles.text: Prompt specifically to pull the right knowledge: role framing makes answers instantly better.
principles.quote: if you say "Act like a data engineer", ChatGPT will directly go to its "data engineer database". The answer will be instantly better.

principles.text: Use multiple prompts and perspectives to detect AI bias and blind spots.
principles.quote: Use multiple prompts and perspectives to detect blind spots.

principles.text: AI course content goes stale fast, so ship weekly deep dives instead of static courses.
principles.quote: Because any AI course becomes obsolete… in 2 weeks.

sources.title: How ChatGPT makes you dumb (and how to use AI without paying cognitive debt)
sources.summary: Ruben unpacks an MIT study showing passive ChatGPT use hurts recall and brain connectivity, then argues the fix is order: do the hard thinking first, invite AI second. He backs it with productivity data (BCG, GitHub) and six workflows that keep the human in the loop.

principles.text: Do the hard thinking first, then bring AI in second.
principles.quote: do the hard thinking first, invite AI in second

principles.text: Draft solo before prompting; use AI to challenge your structure, not write it.
principles.quote: Write a quick outline or even a rough first draft on your own.

principles.text: Treat AI as a booster, not the steering wheel; stay in the driver's seat.
principles.quote: You stay in the cognitive driver’s seat; the model becomes a booster, not the steering wheel.

principles.text: Top performers don't copy-paste AI output; they iterate and blend it with their own expertise.
principles.quote: They iterate, reframe, and blend the AI output with their own expertise.

principles.text: Use ChatGPT as a relentless critic that sharpens your reasoning instead of writing for you.
principles.quote: turn ChatGPT into a relentless critic that sharpens your reasoning rather than writing for you.

principles.text: Quiz yourself on AI-assisted work so the information actually sticks.
principles.quote: convert ChatGPT into a just-in-time memory trainer so new information sticks.

sources.title: Claude for teams: a 5-day playbook to get a whole team using Claude
sources.summary: Ruben lays out a Monday-to-Friday plan to get a team actually using Claude: build one Project per recurring deliverable, add prompt templates, manufacture a before/after "wow", convert one overloaded teammate, then roll out with seeded DMs. The core idea is that adoption is a sales and context problem, not a training problem.

principles.text: Build a separate AI Project per recurring deliverable, each with only the context that task needs.
principles.quote: Each Project gets only what it needs (in terms of context).

principles.text: Remove the blank-chat problem: give teammates a one-sentence, single-input prompt template and let Project instructions carry the rest.
principles.quote: The template should rely on the Project instructions for everything else — tone, format, quality, guardrails. Don't repeat any of it in the template.

principles.text: Adoption comes from a specific output that makes people feel behind, not from features. Manufacture that proof with a real before/after.
principles.quote: People don’t adopt tools because of features. They adopt tools because someone showed them a specific output that made them feel behind.

principles.text: Treat adoption as a sales problem: convert one overloaded colleague using their own real work, then let others follow.
principles.quote: Adoption is a sales problem. Get one colleague excited, and the rest will follow.

principles.text: Pick the person who is drowning for your first conversion, not the tech enthusiast or the biggest skeptic.
principles.quote: The person who is **drowning**. Behind on emails. Always in meetings. Staying late.

principles.text: The first interaction decides whether someone keeps using a tool, so pre-configure the workspace and seed rollout with personal DMs.
principles.quote: The first interaction someone has with an AI tool determines whether they use it again.

sources.title: AI is a mirror: use AI for your strengths, with a context file of your taste, scars and audience
sources.summary: Ruben argues LLMs output the statistical average (70th percentile) in a confident tone, so people who use AI to fill skill gaps can't spot errors. His fix: extract your expertise (standards, constraints, landmines, audience) into a reusable context file, let AI draft v1, steer with follow-ups, and write the final 5% yourself.

principles.text: AI outputs the statistical average (70th percentile); exceptional work needs your input to reach the 95th.
principles.quote: AI always sounds like the 70th percentile. But you want the 95th percentile.

principles.text: Confident, clean AI output is a trap for non-experts: they mistake legibility for quality.
principles.quote: You’re mistaking legibility for quality.

principles.text: Expertise is felt taste, hard-won scars, known landmines, and deep knowledge of your specific audience, not knowledge.
principles.quote: Expertise isn’t knowledge. It’s a set of capabilities that takes years to develop, and that AI fundamentally cannot have

principles.text: Build a context file once (standards, constraints, landmines, audience) and upload it before every task.
principles.quote: Build your context file. Standards, scars, landmines, audience. 2-3 hours once.

principles.text: Treat AI's first draft as 60% there, then steer with short redirects; you add the final 5% only you can write.
principles.quote: AI does the prep. You do the surgery.

principles.text: Use AI for things you are great at, not your gaps, so you catch every mistake and push it further.
principles.quote: Stop using AI for the things you’re bad at. You can’t tell if it’s wrong.

sources.title: My mother & Claude: teaching AI to a retired pharmacist, step by step
sources.summary: Ruben walks his non-technical mom through Claude using a real task (planning an apartment succession). He shows a simple prompt formula, how to fix hallucinations with source rules, and how to turn an answer into a product. The second half is paywalled.

principles.text: Prompt with a goal, a success criterion, your context, and an invitation to ask questions.
principles.quote: I need [goal] that I will consider achieved once [success criteria]. I am [context about me, my situation]. If necessary, ask me clarifying questions first.

principles.text: Let the AI interview you so you don't fear missing details.
principles.quote: But that’s Claude’s job. That’s why we added, “If necessary, ask me clarifying questions first.”

principles.text: Beat hallucinations by restricting the AI to official domains and demanding citations.
principles.quote: you can force Claude or other AI to cite their sources and pick official ones only.

principles.text: Win AI skeptics by showing capability: documents and contracts, not just answers.
principles.quote: That’s how you expand someone’s brain about AI: they finally feel how it widens their options.

principles.text: Remove typing friction with dictation so non-typers can use AI.
principles.quote: So I showed her Wispr Flow, a dictation tool. We simply talked like she would to her notary.

principles.text: Technology can't be stopped, and the world splits between frontier-tech experts and likable people.
principles.quote: the world is dividing in two: either you’re extremely good at handling frontier technology (like AI), or you’re so likable people keep coming back to your shop

sources.title: 27 Claude tips after 1,800 hours: context hygiene, cost control and practical workflows
sources.summary: Ruben shares 27 non-obvious tips from heavy daily Claude use. Most are about keeping context clean (new chats, editing instead of correcting, fewer connectors and skills). The rest cover dictation, Artifacts, Claude Code and Cowork, and seat pricing. Several tips are product-specific and will date quickly.

principles.text: Use Projects only for repeated tasks with fixed material. For creative work, use a fresh empty chat.
principles.quote: use Projects for repeated tasks with fixed material (client reports, weekly formats). Use a normal, empty chat every time you want a new idea.

principles.text: Don't argue with a wrong answer. Edit the prompt before it, so the bad answer leaves the conversation.
principles.quote: When you correct Claude, the wrong answer stays in the conversation. Claude keeps working around it, and you pay for it on every message after.

principles.text: Dictate messy context instead of typing. Talking keeps the details typing makes you delete.
principles.quote: When you type, you organize your thoughts, and you delete context without noticing. When you talk, you don’t.

principles.text: Long chats get worse and costlier. Start a new chat after roughly 30-50 turns.
principles.quote: 30-50 turns is when it starts to be dumb.

principles.text: Show what you hate. Naming the exact thing to avoid beats vague adjectives like 'punchier'.
principles.quote: Adjectives do almost nothing, like when you prompt “make it nicer/punchier”.

principles.text: Don't chase every new technique. Focus on doing your job better, not on the technology.
principles.quote: Focus on doing your job better, not on falling in love with the technology.

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid grew LinkedIn to 770K followers with AI, taste and consistency
sources.summary: Ruben argues AI made effort and strategy worthless, leaving taste and consistency as the real edge. He breaks LinkedIn growth into three levers: reader-centric (not personal) topics, pattern-breaking hooks, and scrappy useful media, then insists on daily posting and picking a target to pursue with action.

principles.text: Write posts about the reader's problem, not your achievements; nobody cares about you, they care about being helped.
principles.quote: Either I help YOU now, or you won’t care enough to follow me.

principles.text: AI makes effort and generic strategy worthless; what remains scarce is taste and consistency.
principles.quote: AI made what was valuable terribly easy: the effort to start & a reasonable strategy. Both are now worthless and won’t make you a Linkedin star.

principles.text: The hook is the first two lines; its only job is to break the scroll pattern and earn the 'more' click. Generate many variants and let taste pick.
principles.quote: You must shock the reader. Break his patterns. Wake him up from his slumber and doomscrolling.

principles.text: Media dominates the screen, so it matters more than body text; the best format is a scrappy, unbranded, useful single image, not an ad-looking asset.
principles.quote: the more it looks like an ad, the worse the post performs. Be scrappy.

principles.text: Post daily: volume produces learning, which sharpens taste. There is no prompt that replaces consistency.
principles.quote: Action produces information.

principles.text: Don't stand still waiting for the perfect goal; pick a target, pursue it with AI, and build an unfair advantage through action.
principles.quote: Make your advantage so unfair it feels insurmountable to catch up with you.

sources.title: You can't beat AI: why judgment, taste and systems replace average work
sources.summary: Ruben argues AI makes intelligence a cheap commodity, so average work dies first and the market stops paying for it. Durable value shifts to judgment and taste, which you must extract into reusable context files, and to building repeatable systems rather than selling hours or answers.

principles.text: The threat isn't perfect AI, it's AI cheap enough to replace 'good enough'.
principles.quote: The threat is not that AI becomes perfect. The threat is that AI becomes cheap enough to replace good enough.

principles.text: When intelligence gets cheap, judgment gets expensive: the valuable person picks, decides and spots what matters.
principles.quote: When intelligence gets cheap, judgment gets expensive.

principles.text: Stop making average work; average now looks suspicious because it took seconds. Move above it.
principles.quote: Stop trying to make average work. Move above it.

principles.text: Turn your taste and expertise into reusable markdown context files so AI stops giving average answers.
principles.quote: A prompt is a one-time request. But a file (inside a folder) is reusable memory.

principles.text: Move from answer person to system person: build templates and workflows so you remove bottlenecks.
principles.quote: You stop being the bottleneck. You remove bottlenecks.

principles.text: Use AI where you already have taste, because you can't judge output in areas where you're weak.
principles.quote: If you’re bad at the thing, you can’t judge the thing.

sources.title: Replaced: Don't replace your team with AI, multiply it and hire for psychology
sources.summary: Ruben argues AI raises demand for knowledge work (Jevons Paradox), so the goal is making 5 people do the work of 50, not cutting headcount. He shows how he duplicated himself with AI tools, trained a team via recorded demos and SOPs, and hires for openness, humility and taste over technical credentials. The list of jobs AI will kill is paywalled.

principles.text: Ask how your team can do the work of 50 with AI, not how to replace people with AI.
principles.quote: Start thinking: “**How can 5 members of my team do the work of 50 with AI?**”

principles.text: Cheaper cognition expands demand for work (Jevons Paradox), so efficiency creates more projects and growth.
principles.quote: Cheaper/more efficient cognition → companies do way more projects, experiments, personalization, long-tail ideas that were once too expensive.

principles.text: Even at 10x efficiency you are capped by hours, so hire people to use AI for you.
principles.quote: Even if AI makes me 10x more efficient, I can’t have 10x more hours.

principles.text: Don't wait for perfect AI. Pick one real task (like research) and make it 10x better today.
principles.quote: Wrong: Wait for “perfect” AI.

principles.text: Teach AI workflows top-down: record yourself doing it, then write an SOP the team can follow.
principles.quote: I create a Loom/Screen Studio video of me actually doing it.

principles.text: Hire for psychology (humility, resilience, taste, openness), not AI certifications.
principles.quote: Wrong: Look for “AI experts” with degrees/certifications.

sources.title: How Ruben Hassid turns his voice into a text file any AI can use
sources.summary: Ruben argues your voice, taste and judgment are patterns that compress into one markdown file. He shares a two-prompt workflow: a 100-question AI interview, then a compression pass into a lean about-me file. Reuse it across Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and teammates, and keep editing it.

principles.text: Your voice, taste and habits are patterns, so they can be captured in one text file any AI can read.
principles.quote: Patterns. Every one of them is a pattern.

principles.text: Extract your voice via a 100-question AI interview; dictate answers by voice, which is faster and more honest.
principles.quote: Voice is faster and more honest.

principles.text: Compress the raw interview dump into a lean file, since a bloated file eats context window and costs tokens every turn.
principles.quote: But this file is too big. It eats too much of your context window.

principles.text: Keep only lines that change AI behavior. Cut generic values, flattery and biography; keep specifics, refusals and examples.
principles.quote: Optimize for maximum behavioral fidelity per token.

principles.text: Make the file portable: reuse it in any model and hand it to your team or ghostwriter so they draft in your voice.
principles.quote: You’re now a resource instead of a bottleneck.

principles.text: Do the hard work once to gain consistency, but edit the file often because your taste keeps changing.
principles.quote: Your taste changes a lot.

sources.title: Claude Skills: how to set up Claude once so you stop re-prompting
sources.summary: Ruben explains Claude Skills as reusable instructions that live inside Claude and fire on a /command or automatically. He walks non-developers through building one with the skill-creator, then shares seven lesser-known hacks and honest limits.

principles.text: Skills package long context and instructions into the AI, so you stop re-explaining the same task.
principles.quote: It’s like a very long context + instructions, living inside the AI.

principles.text: Start your first Skill with the task you re-explain most often.
principles.quote: Don’t know which task? Pick the one you re-explain the most. That’s the one.

principles.text: Be specific when describing a Skill; vague descriptions produce Skills that don't work.
principles.quote: “I write reports” is useless.

principles.text: Always run the evaluation on a new Skill before installing it; most people skip the step that matters most.
principles.quote: Take the time, it’s the most important step.

principles.text: Negative triggers ("Do NOT use for...") matter more than positive ones because they stop a Skill hijacking unrelated chats.
principles.quote: The _“Do NOT use for…”_ line in your description is more important than the _“Use when…”_ line.

principles.text: Debug a broken Skill by asking Claude when it would use it, then fix the description it quotes back.
principles.quote: Ask Claude: _“When would you use the linkedin-post skill?”_

sources.title: Vibecoding: what Claude Code is (and isn't) good for, and how non-coders use it
sources.summary: Ruben argues vibecoding won't make you rich but is worth it for two things: clickable mockups to brief developers and small custom tools for yourself or your team. He gives a setup guide, a CTO-style mega prompt, taste tricks, cost habits, and a rule for when to hand the project to a real coder.

principles.text: Vibecoding is not a get-rich-quick path; its value is mockups for devs and small custom tools.
principles.quote: Getting rich or having a functioning company is far more complex than just knowing how to prompt an AI. I won’t sell you a get-rich-quick scam.

principles.text: Build a clickable version of your idea so developers and designers stop guessing what you meant.
principles.quote: you build a clickable version of your idea and hand it to someone, like a developer or a designer, so they stop guessing what you meant.

principles.text: Build small tools just for yourself or your team; rough edges are fine when nobody else sees them.
principles.quote: you build a small tool that does the job better than a simple Claude-chatbot interface. Just for you, your team, or a few customers. Rough edges are fine because nobody else sees them.

principles.text: Describe the end result and let the AI pick the steps, then build one piece at a time.
principles.quote: Say what you want to exist, and let Claude pick the steps.

principles.text: Avoid generic AI-looking sites by feeding specific references, screenshots and design system files.
principles.quote: The more specific you are, the less generic it looks.

principles.text: Don't spend longer building a tool than you'll spend using it; avoid performative productivity.
principles.quote: Do not take longer to build it than to consume it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains how he grew a large AI audience by testing tools for himself and sharing only what works. His thesis: AI output is average and commoditized, so taste and a unique vision are what stay valuable. He also argues for building on the side of a job, ignoring money early, and learning AI by playing with one task.

chunks.heading: Taste is what AI can't commoditize
chunks.text:
- Ruben argues AI output is "average," but average is now so cheap that it beats what a freelance writer produced before ChatGPT. The same 2,000-word article that once earned $1,000 now looks like "just some words."
- His line "master AI before it masters you" means this: if you only produce average work, nobody has a reason to pay for it. You have to ask "what is so unique about my vision on doing something," whether you are a writer, accountant or lawyer.
- Lawyer example: contract templates get automated. What remains is service quality and human contact, such as having lunch with the client.
- He says he is open about using AI for his newsletter and records screens of how he does it. People think it is fast, but he spends a lot of time feeding AI his taste and steering its direction.
- He argues AI lets you pivot an article without having to convince anyone, which a human team would resist.

chunks.heading: Turning your taste into a reusable file
chunks.text:
- He published an article titled "I am just a text file" the same day. It came from about two hours of answering Claude's questions, after a prompt that said to ask him a long list of questions.
- Result: a markdown file of roughly 800 to 1,000 lines. It holds his opinions, taste, boundaries, how he writes, what he would never say, and his views on AI tools as of January 2026.
- Uploaded to a project in any AI, the model behaves "kind of like me," sometimes blunt and direct, with his little bracketed jokes.
- Idea: condense who you are into an encyclopedia you can carry across platforms, have conversations with, or let others use.
- Takeaway: shaping your taste, then steering the AI with it, keeps you ahead of the tool.

chunks.heading: Decision paralysis when you can build anything
chunks.text:
- He points to engineers after Claude Code with Opus 4.5 (end of December 2025). Hundreds of thousands reportedly said they "can code anything but don't know what to code."
- Coding used to take months, so people coded for others. Now it takes hours, so they need ideas, customer conversations and some marketing knowledge.
- He suggests the future skill looks like project management as a philosophy: know the goal, define the steps, and orchestrate multiple AIs with your taste.
- His fix for paralysis:
  - Turn off the AI news. His newsletter is deliberately not about news; it is about how to do something today.
  - Pick one easy thing you want to do and one AI to do it.
  - Spend about 15 minutes finding a reliable source of truth (not SEO articles). Being wrong is fine.
  - Play with it like a kid. His newsletter hero image is a child for this reason.
  - Mastering one thing is good enough.
- Analogy: nobody becomes a pro tennis player without first hitting a ball for 10 minutes with friends.

chunks.heading: Why AI pushes people to be more human
chunks.text:
- He told a heckler at VidCon in Los Angeles: "AI will force us to be more human." He also says he can list a thousand bad things about AI, as with the internet.
- Historical argument: in 1900, about 90% of people in the US worked in food (farming, animals, logistics). Freed from that, people could think about electricity, computers, Netflix and Amazon. He expects the same with AI.
- Industries he expects to grow because they are human: health, longevity, events, real human experiences.
- He is not a doomsayer. He says he never fear-mongers about job loss, but he does want people to discuss implications with kids, grandparents and partners.
- Safety example: he built an avatar and voice clone of himself two years ago and called his mother with the French version; she could not tell which was real. He believes video-call scams using fake voices and faces are already possible, and emergency-panic scams would work on him.
- Positive example: he colored black-and-white photos of his grandmother (who died when his mother was 12) with Nano Banana and animated one with Veo for a couple of seconds. His mother cried.

chunks.heading: Slow-build personal brand: keep the day job
chunks.text:
- He built his audience with a job. Before ghostwriting he worked at Trade Republic (a Berlin fintech) while running a music label (started at 18, ran about seven years). He moved from job plus ghostwriting to ghostwriting only, then to writing for himself.
- He argues against quitting your job to build a brand. Money pressure leads to decisions that hurt quality: "the more you forget about making money, the more money you make."
- Test he offers: if you cannot handle a job plus the side project, you probably could not handle the side project alone. How much you want it shows in whether you make the sacrifice.
- He cites Justin Welsh as agreeing, and says he had his team read an article on the subject.
- His own "overnight" success was not overnight: the music label and years of curating and writing came first.
- He thinks everyone has potential, but "mathematically very few are gonna make it."

chunks.heading: How he started (pattern: test, then teach)
chunks.text:
- As a 9-year-old he was obsessed with Guild Wars. Players had to pick eight skills from a near-infinite set. He tested builds with sticky notes and wrote French blogs about them, then learned English to reach the larger English forum. He did this for about five years.
- Music label work was mostly curating and sharing what he liked, as a "taste maker."
- ChatGPT origin: on November 30, 2022 he was a 25-year-old ghostwriter in Berlin who did not want to hire people. His first prompts were bad, then better. He found only technical material (Python, NLP, papers on chain of thought, few-shot prompting).
- He translated the papers into plain terms:
  - One-shot prompting: give one example before the request. Few-shot: give a few examples.
  - Chain of thought: give steps. Instead of "write an article," say step one outline, step two headings, step three the article.
- On December 7, 2022 he posted this on LinkedIn and woke to a million views. In the comments he asked what people needed and made content from the answers.
- About three months later he had 100,000 followers and went full time, moving from Berlin to Tel Aviv. He cites roughly 500 million LinkedIn views (he is unsure of the exact current figure).
- His method today: test things for himself like a scientist, discard what fails, and only publish when something is useful and not obvious.

chunks.heading: Bots, social platforms and his publishing cadence
chunks.text:
- He says the share of real comments on his LinkedIn dropped from about 100% genuine to roughly 50% (he hopes) as AI comments rose. His meme: a monkey handed a rifle.
- He expects platforms to verify humans (he mentions Instagram's CEO discussing ID verification). He supports measures like ID and a paid account.
- Bot cost argument: a bot costs a few cents a month, but at $10 per account per month, 10,000 bots cost $100,000 a month, which kills the economics. He describes this as Elon Musk's logic for paying on Twitter.
- Whether content is written with AI does not matter to him; the goal is talking to real people.
- Substack is his preferred place for effort because it is preserved as high-quality long form compared with LinkedIn.
- Cadence: newsletter twice a week (Wednesday and Sunday), 99% free. His plan is about 100 deep dives a year on one AI topic each. His advice: "skip the noise" and just read the newsletter.
- Example: Nelly, a reader of three years at Philips (12 years there), became the company's AI champion by playing with his content.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains his content philosophy: optimize for usefulness over personal story, write for a distracted reader on a bus, and post consistently without expecting ROI. He also covers using AI to be "greater, not lazier" through taste and volume, and how EasyGen and his own team's growth became its best marketing.

chunks.heading: Useful over personal: the core content philosophy
chunks.text:
- Ruben's guiding rule for his team: "be useful, not personal." He is "obsessed about being useful."
- He rejects the standard personal-branding advice to talk about your own story, opinions and experiences. His view: "I think no one cares, actually."
- He rarely posts "that's what I think about X." He frames himself as solving a puzzle and passing on the recipe, like a mad scientist handing over the potion so others don't have to spend the time solving it.
- Personal stories have a place in live settings (interviews, webinars, keynotes at VidCon in Denmark and Paris, Google in Tel Aviv), where he connects directly with the audience.
- He argues posts are already personal without trying: he picks the topic, the angle, the experience, the learnings and the conclusion. "I don't have to make it more about me than it already is."
- He says the best creators he follows work the same way.

chunks.heading: Writing for "the guy on the bus"
chunks.text:
- Ruben pictures a specific reader: someone on a crowded bus at 7:00 p.m., on the way back from the doctor, kid sick, partner upset, reading on a moving phone.
- He says the problem isn't poor reading skills. Life is simply full of messages and apps (Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram, Twitter, LinkedIn).
- Within 2 seconds the reader must know the context, what they will learn, and how the post helps them.
- By the end of the post the reader should be able to do something better, even if the gain is small.
- If the reader gets nothing in the first 15 seconds, "I'm probably not respecting him."
- Tactics that follow:
  - No long introductions; go straight to the point.
  - Actionable, step-by-step content.
  - No personal opinion pieces.
  - Always check how a post looks on a phone before publishing.

chunks.heading: Posting cadence and the content backlog
chunks.text:
- Ruben posts twice a day, every day, on LinkedIn alone. That excludes Threads, Twitter, his newsletter and YouTube.
- His rule: if a post doesn't bring value, don't share it. He isn't trying to fill a calendar.
- The more you publish with the "be useful" filter, the fewer ideas qualify: "I wish I had more bullets."
- He keeps a large backlog of queued posts and still wishes it were bigger. He says people who "don't know what to post today" should flip the framing and ask whether they have enough worthwhile ideas.
- His expansion path: LinkedIn first, then a newsletter, then Twitter and Threads, and YouTube when he has time. He repeats the cycle without a special strategy.

chunks.heading: EasyGen: building a tool from his own ghostwriting process
chunks.text:
- Origin: Ruben was a ghostwriter (for a financial analyst, while in Berlin) and wanted a "Mr. Beast-style" assistant who follows you around and absorbs how you work. He couldn't do that while moving between Berlin, Paris and Tel Aviv.
- Solution: train AI on his ghostwriting knowledge and SOPs. He started building it when ChatGPT's first API came out.
- He built it for himself first and says he grew from 8,000 followers to over 400,000 in 2 years using it. He made it public so his team could use it.
- How it works:
  - EasyGen is meant to take you "from 10 to 80, to 10 to 90," not from 0 to 100.
  - You arrive knowing the post topic, and it acts like a ghostwriter you brainstorm with.
  - Inputs include typed topics, audio, and uploaded images such as cheat sheets, from which it extracts the topic.
  - Formats include viral mindset quotes and cheat sheets.
  - You review, preview on a phone, and can generate an image.
- His own usage: he regenerates a post 20 to 30 times before choosing, and generates around 30 posts to pick the best lines.
- "AI is not just one button you press and then poof, everything happens." He still spends time making sure the post is what he wanted.

chunks.heading: How EasyGen sells: proof by use, not growth hacks
