chunks.text:
- Ruben says there is "no tactic, there is no black hat." He shares content on how he uses the tool, why, and how effective it is for him and his team.
- His team's accounts are the proof. Employees started posting in May, are now at about 23,000 followers each (Anisha is mentioned at 25,000), and their posts are written with EasyGen.
- Affiliates account for roughly 10 to 15% of EasyGen sales. His two biggest affiliates by far are his employees, because they grew their accounts with it.
- He positions himself as the number one user: "No one has ever used EasyGen more than me." He and his team (four people) use it daily.
- His "real black hat" is being useful, showing case studies, and skipping growth-hacking tactics.

chunks.heading: Using AI to be greater, not lazier
chunks.text:
- Ruben says the key question is "Am I using it to be lazier or to be greater?"
- His Midjourney analogy: top brands pay a lot for work by creative directors who have taste and experience, and who generate thousands of images with very different prompts and techniques. They build a huge mood board and then pick what works.
- He predicts people with taste and experience will "obliterate" those who just press an automated button.
- Outcome he expects: the mediocre baseline rises, but a portion of people become far better.
- Cross-industry example: a lawyer with an AI contract tool who uses the saved time to focus on the human side and close bigger deals will beat one who simply automates.
- Mindset he recommends: "I finally have the time to do this."
- Outlook: 2022 to 2024 was the chatbot era; next is the agent era, with AI embedded in Slack, CRM, Notion and Google Drive. He notes DeepSeek V3, an open-source model he describes as about 94% cheaper than ChatGPT.

chunks.heading: Turning content into opportunities (keynotes, no ROI expectations)
chunks.text:
- Ruben compares social media to the gym: show up daily with the right behavior and have faith, rather than calculating reps and results.
- His advice: "Don't expect any results." If you track ROI on everything, you get lost; if your motivation is being useful every day, good things happen because people see it.
- His own path had no strategy for keynotes. He kept being useful for free and opportunities arrived.
- The problem later flips: "how to say no to 99.9% of the things." He says no to podcasts using a pre-made template reply.
- He ties this back to his music-label days at 17: reach millions online for free, and a person connects better than a company or label. Personal beats made-up company, because a person "has a past, it has a future."

chunks.heading: Business model, revenue and goals
chunks.text:
- EasyGen ownership: 20% is held by CTO Pete Sena (a serial entrepreneur who built two digital marketing agencies); Ruben owns the rest.
- He chose a product over a ghostwriting agency because he doesn't want to deal with people or agency pain (tight margins, turnover). Pete told him his agencies' journey "was awful."
- Metrics he cites: about 33,000 weekly users and $500,000 annual recurring revenue ("half a million"), with a target of $1 million.
- Reach claim: his best day of the year was about 4 million people reached on LinkedIn.
- Long-term idea: build for other creators what he built with EasyGen, i.e. train an AI extension of a person's expertise that can serve tens of thousands of users, which no individual could serve alone.
- Guiding principle for decisions: "Having fun," and building like "an endless puzzle."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid explains how he grew the How to AI newsletter by publishing free, tested, step-by-step guidance. He argues AI lifts the average rather than everyone, so human taste and judgment remain the edge. He also covers how to get hesitant people started with simple, concrete tools.

chunks.heading: Why most people don't "get" AI: they never try it
chunks.text:
- Ruben says everyone in San Francisco talks about AI, but talking is not understanding.
- His blunt answer to who understands it: "the only people who've tried it, and tried it for long enough."
- Most people love discussing it, few actually test it or read the documentation.
- His edge as a writer: "I test what I write about." It is like explaining how to ride a bike after actually falling off one.
- Example: a law firm kept saying it "couldn't use Claude" for ethics reasons. He asked if they had read Anthropic's SOC 2 compliance or privacy documentation. They hadn't.
- He expects the next 5-10 years to be decided by people who live and breathe AI in their work, and the gap between them and everyone else to keep widening.
- He compares not using AI to not using the internet or phones: a basic part of the economy now.
- He frames it as a new way of working, like Excel's first ad where two executives in an elevator are amazed that you can "edit the numbers in a spreadsheet."

chunks.heading: "Clickers" and getting scared people started
chunks.text:
- He divides people into "clickers" and non-clickers. His mother is a pharmacist and asks permission before tapping anything on her phone, fearing it will blow up.
- Clickers open the tool, click everywhere, press the new tab, and aren't afraid to experiment. Like a toddler who keeps climbing and running.
- His mission is to turn more people into clickers; they may surpass him later, and that is fine.
- Common mistake: people equate AI with "agents" and email automation. He never writes about email automation because he thinks people don't want it.
- His entry-point tactic for beginners is Whisper Flow (voice-to-text):
  - Press a key, speak, and it types.
  - It learns names you correct ("Margo", "Scott" with double t).
  - Dictating a to-do list for a colleague shows them it is faster than typing.
- Why it works: beginners write lazy prompts because adding context is tedious. Speaking makes giving rich context easy, and the quality of ChatGPT/Claude answers improves.
- Result: the user realizes AI is not a monster that eats their computer, just a normal tool that makes their day better.
- His closing advice: book a 15-minute meeting with his newsletter twice a week and actually try the tutorial. After a year you "master AI before it masters you."

chunks.heading: Taste, and why "Don't Pick 27"
chunks.text:
- Core idea: AI does not make everyone better. It makes the average much better, and the average becomes "insanely good," but still average.
- Canva analogy: if only one designer had Canva templates 20 years ago, they would be the richest designer. Once everyone has them, a template is just a tool. A founder raising a billion-dollar round doesn't want a Canva-template deck.
- Law example: "I don't pay my lawyer to draft contracts. I pay my lawyer to find loopholes and pitfalls." He needs what is not inside the AI.
- If your work is just templates (Canva decks, simple contracts, filling PDFs), you have no advantage, and templates get cheaper and better daily.
- His book, "Don't Pick 27", has no deadline and may take 5 years:
  - Ask an LLM for a number between 1 and 100 and it often picks 27, because humans disproportionately pick 27 (and 47, 37).
  - If AI is the taste-maker and decision-maker, you always get the average.
  - Taste remains the one thing left: you ask the AI, and you decide what is good after it answers.
- His stated key message: "The average will get better and better, but the average remains average. Our role as humans is to understand what the average is, how good it is, and how to be better than the average."

chunks.heading: How he prompts: avoid delegating the thinking
chunks.text:
- He pushes back on the "ChatGPT makes you dumb" study: only 50 people, and it really showed that using it without thinking first activates less of your brain.
- Rule: know where you're going first, give enough context, then evaluate the result. Treat the output as not final; expect to tweak it.
- His standard prompt opener: "I want a task with success criteria," so he defines the goal up front instead of asking "tell me what to do."
- Don't ask for one answer. Better: ask for 20 totally different angles (his interview example: 20 ways to interview Ruben), give it all the info you have first and have it verify, then you pick the best 4.
- He calls this the "pick your own adventure" pattern, with AI and human in the loop. He often skips his own notes in a live interview because reading the room cannot be done by an LLM.
- He criticizes the "Jarvis people" (almost all men on Twitter): they build agent orchestrators and OpenClaw setups to look productive, but cannot show what they actually produce.
- Referencing a Steve Jobs exchange with a heckler: what matters is what people actually need and use, not what tech enthusiasts like. He asks to see real results for knowledge workers who don't code.
- He argues agents are hard to set up and maintain for non-coders. His newsletter "How to AI" is about what is practical and impactful today in writing, research and running a business.

chunks.heading: Tool stack for knowledge workers (spring 2026)
chunks.text:
- His view: most knowledge work is two things, researching information and writing information (memos, briefs, outreach, follow-ups).
- General-purpose pick: Claude, and specifically Claude Cowork. He sees no competitor today but expects ChatGPT, Codex, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot Cowork to catch up.
- For research: ChatGPT's extended thinking and deep research. He once ran a deep research on peptide markets that ran about an hour and a half.
- Specialized tools: Gamma for slide decks, Granola as a meeting note-taker (people forget around 70% of meetings), Whisper Flow for dictation.
- Context-connector workflow:
  - Connect Gmail, Slack and Granola to Claude.
  - For a contract negotiation, Claude pulls the email threads with his partner and lawyer, Granola meeting notes and Slack threads.
  - He uses it as a thinking partner, not an answer machine. He asks Claude to question him with the "ask user questions" tool (pop-up form: aggressive, calm, or another approach?).
  - He calls this the "IKEA effect": you build it with AI and human in the loop, which is where the flavor comes from.
- Cost note: a Claude Cowork plus Lovable, Supabase, Railway and GitHub setup lets non-coders build apps, but costs a lot; typical users probably don't want to spend more than $1,000 a month.
- His consulting client example: the largest salmon exporter (about half a billion dollars in revenue, small team). They don't need Lovable or Claude Code; a 10-20% productivity gain from sensible tooling is enough. He thinks traditional real businesses will benefit most, using the Pareto rule (the 20% that yields 80%).

chunks.heading: Content philosophy: the IKEA instruction manual
chunks.text:
- His analogy: he writes "IKEA instructions." The reader is a person at 2 AM with a box in the living room who has never held a hammer.
- "I'm just the instructions to get there." He wants readers to use his content, not be fans of it.
- Inspiration: French Touch artists (Daft Punk, Justice) who refused interviews and hid their faces so people focus on the music.
- Content principles:
  - Only the necessary steps; the right number (not 2, not 60).
  - Skip storytelling; work out the first step ("where do I start?").
  - Much of his work is change management for someone who must make a change at 2 AM.
- Origins: at age 9 he learned English because of Guild Wars. From age 7 to 14 he wrote blog posts on how to build characters (combining skills from a large pool, picking his own set of 8). He started in French, saw almost no readers, noticed the English forums, and switched to English. He sees this as the same thing he does today.
- Team principle: "Consensus kills creativity." He builds very small teams with one decision-maker. He alone writes and decides on his newsletter. He doesn't mind being wrong or failing. He contrasts this with mainstream news outlets that die of consensus and are all copies of each other.

chunks.heading: Newsletter growth and the free-first business model
chunks.text:
- Newsletter: "How to AI" on Substack, started May 19 (about one year before this episode). Said to be possibly the fastest-growing newsletter on Substack at the time. Went from a few thousand subscribers to more than 600,000, growing by a few thousand per day.
- He writes two newsletters a week; his team handles the rest. He published about 1,000 LinkedIn posts (two a day).
- He distributes across LinkedIn, Twitter, Instagram, Facebook; estimates 5-10 million people reached daily (his own estimate, hard to pin down).
- Everything is free on Substack. The paid tier is $200 per year only for access to a Circle community; he says on the signup page you can pick $200 or $0, and that most people shouldn't pay. The payment acts as a filter against spam and "buy what I have" posts.
- Rationale: "money finds its way to you." Giving enough free value means a small fraction (he estimates 10,000-20,000 people eventually) pay.
- Business stack: free content on LinkedIn and Substack, then the Circle community, then his consulting firm. The consulting helps companies adopt AI (he calls it "AI fluency") and builds roadmaps. He is deliberately brand-neutral, not tied to OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini, and picks the best model per use case (for example, he says Claude may be best for a French law firm, Gemini for a Hebrew-language Israeli insurer).
- Advice to new creators: keep a day job. "If you can't handle the pressure of two jobs, your creative work and your normal job, you won't handle the pressure of being a creator and building a business, because they're two different things." Mixing content and business pressure too early hurts both. Paywalls limit growth, which is why large paywalled media subscriptions shrink.
- Example of impact: a student creator at a LinkedIn event told him she had never paid but had learned most of her AI knowledge from his newsletter, and she sends it to many people. He says that is fine.

chunks.heading: Jobs, adaptability and the doom narrative
chunks.text:
- Message to people afraid of AI: build skills to build, become entrepreneurial in mindset, and don't stay static in a job. Past generations changed jobs twice in 40 years; now people may change roles many times in a few years.
- Historical analogy: 100 years ago about 70% of Americans worked in agriculture, now under 1%. He expects similar shifts to happen faster (copywriters, lawyers, customer support).
- Skills to keep: adaptability, learning and building. People in the trades (electricians, plumbers) are fine for now. Business owners of restaurants and cafes could use AI too: a Tel Aviv barista asked whether to ask AI for a business plan to host private dinners in a bigger kitchen, and Ruben told him yes.
- On the "AI will destroy humanity" claim he raised at an event: in the year 1000 the Pope wrote that war would end because of the crossbow. Humans love apocalypse narratives. Risks are real (nuclear weapons need rules), but nuclear catastrophe has not happened, and "you have to balance your own pessimism."
- Platform strategy comment: he thinks OpenAI shut down Sora and the Atlas browser to focus on developers and enterprises, copying Anthropic's enterprise approach (forward-deployed engineers). Anthropic and others are investing in them; Palantir and Mistral take similar enterprise approaches. His consulting positioning is as an independent advisor outside that race.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben chains three tools to produce a cited, 7,500-word academic paper in under an hour: Consensus to find papers, Sci-Hub to get the PDFs, ChatGPT to draft section by section. The workflow shows a repeatable pattern: structured prompts, one section at a time, quotes restricted to uploaded sources, and the full outline re-pasted to keep context.

chunks.heading: Research stack for a thesis: Consensus, Sci-Hub, ChatGPT
chunks.text:
Ruben wrote a full 20+ page thesis on "the differences between the EU and US approach to Iran over the last 20 years" to test how fast AI could do it. A friend needed the paper in about two weeks. He used three tools:
- **Consensus**, which he calls the best AI for finding scientific papers.
- **Sci-Hub**, to get the full PDFs.
- **ChatGPT**, to read the PDFs and write the text.

chunks.heading: Sourcing papers with Consensus and Sci-Hub
chunks.text:
- Type the research question into Consensus. Each result shows the paper title and the passage that answers the question. Opening a result gives key points, a summary and references.
- Consensus has a new CSV export. Ruben had been scrolling the page by hand before, so the export saves him that work. It includes the DOI, the unique identifier of each paper.
- Paste each DOI into Sci-Hub, which he describes as a piracy site that bypasses paywalls, and download the PDF.
- Splitting the question helps. He ran one query for the EU approach to Iran and one for the US approach over the last 20 years. He ended with 9 usable papers; some DOIs failed.
- If Sci-Hub keeps loading forever, it is most likely down or the paper isn't available. Skip it.
- He treated about 10 papers as enough for a 20-page paper, but said a more serious version would probably need around 30.

chunks.heading: Prompt structure for the first ChatGPT call
chunks.text:
- He builds the prompt as role, context, task, then a step-by-step process (chain-of-thought prompting).
- Role and context: "You are a PhD professor", later "from Harvard", writing a paper on the EU vs US approach to Iran. He asks it to respect academic writing style.
- He uploaded all the PDFs in one go. He said ChatGPT is best at handling several PDFs at once and was top of the LMSYS leaderboard at the time.
- Step 1: read all the PDFs and think of a strategy for writing the paper.
- Step 2: build a table of contents with an introduction, a conclusion, two big parts, and two sub-parts per big part. That gives 10 sections.
- He adds "take a deep breath and work step by step" as a small trick to improve chain-of-thought prompting.

chunks.heading: Controlling length
chunks.text:
- A 20-page double-spaced paper is about 5,000 words, so about 500 words per section.
- He says language models can't hit an exact word count. Asking for 500 won't give 500.
- His workaround is to ask for a different number and expect the model to land near the target. He asked for about 1,000 words for the introduction and got 1,263.
- He then told it to make the intro half the size and more like a Harvard-style academic paper. He found the first draft didn't read like an actual paper introduction.
- Body sections were requested at 500-700 words and came back around that (one measured 686).
- He checks length with a word counter.

chunks.heading: Section-by-section loop with real citations
chunks.text:
1. Paste the full table of contents again and say which section to focus on. Tell it the intro (and earlier sections) are already written.
2. Ask it to first extract all relevant quotes for that section from the uploaded PDFs only. It must not use any other PDF or invent any study.
3. Tell it not to start writing the next section until he says so. He added this after realizing it might jump ahead.
4. Then ask for the section at 500-700 words, using those quotes, in the voice of the Harvard PhD professor.
5. Copy it into a Word document: Times New Roman, about size 11, double spacing. The table of contents stays single-spaced and smaller.

- He verified the citations. He took one quote, opened the PDF, searched with Ctrl+F, and found the exact sentence ("The Bush administration embarked on a military invasion"). The quotes were real.
- The intro and conclusion need no citations.
- He kept a tokenizer open to watch the context window (about 128k tokens). Around section 6 it showed roughly 13k tokens used, so there was plenty of room.

chunks.heading: When ChatGPT drifts, and final result
chunks.text:
- By section 9 the model started with the wrong section number and stopped providing sources. He suspected the context window was getting long.
- His fix was to keep restating what is happening and the full table of contents, so ChatGPT knows what to do and what not to do. He re-ran the quote extraction and re-prompted.
- For the conclusion he reminded it of the nine written parts plus the ten-part table of contents. He asked for a final paragraph opening a new perspective the reader hadn't considered.
- Result: 26 double-spaced pages, 7,580 words and about 52,000 characters, built in about 51 minutes. He still needed to add the reference list and should read everything.
- The final paragraph argued that the real issue may be the shared assumption that Iran can be changed by outside pressure or engagement, and that its internal dynamics need more attention.
- He also asked ChatGPT for three distinct hypotheses for the thesis:
  - The EU's multilateral, diplomatic approach is more effective.
  - The divergent strategies reflect something deeper in the Western alliance.
  - Unilateral US withdrawal pushed Iran closer to Russia and China.
- Caveat he gives himself: with more time he might feed the papers one at a time instead of all at once.

chunks.heading: Building a product and the lesson for education
chunks.text:
- He sees a SaaS opportunity: connect the Consensus API, the ChatGPT API and Sci-Hub (he doesn't think Sci-Hub has an API), add the user's own material, and produce a 20-page paper in about 30 minutes.
- On top of that you could build an "AI detector" that pretends to detect AI. He says it can't.
- On schools: "this shouldn't be the way we assess students." It is too easy, so evaluation should come from something that originates in the students themselves. He doesn't know exactly what, but it has to be different.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains why generic ChatGPT prompts give generic output: LLMs are next-word predictors, so you must supply examples (few-shot) and steps (chain-of-thought) and treat the model like a precise but literal intern. He also covers using AI for brainstorming volume rather than education, and how EasyGen helped two employees hit 1M LinkedIn views in 25 days.

chunks.heading: Ruben's core mental model: an LLM is a very good but very literal intern
chunks.text:
- Ruben says people use ChatGPT like a "super Google" and expect a genius with all the answers. That is his number one mistake.
- An LLM (large language model) is trained mostly on text. Its simplest explanation is phone autocomplete "on steroids": it predicts the highest-probability next word.
- Trained on a gazillion examples the right way, it gets close to what humans produce day to day.
- A bare prompt like "write an article about Nvidia" returns something "as generic as possible, as dull as possible". He says that is not a flaw. It is "trained that way".
- To get a twist or new knowledge, you have to prompt in that direction.
- He compares it to a "very good student" and also "a very stupid" intern. It follows a process 24/7, is paid once, and is never sick and never on holiday.
- Like an intern, it does exactly what you ask. Anything you leave out because you are the expert, it will miss. You nudge it in the right direction.

chunks.heading: Zero-shot vs few-shot prompting
chunks.text:
- Ruben says prompt engineering terms sound technical but are simple.
- **Zero-shot:** you give zero examples before the output. "Write an article about Nvidia" is zero-shot. He says most people use zero-shot without knowing it.
- **Few-shot:** you give multiple examples before asking for the output.
- Example for the Nvidia article: "I want you to know how I write articles. Here are my top three articles, 1, 2, 3 (paste them). Now write an article in the same style for X."
- His pitch for why it matters: "you'll be way better on ChatGPT if you use few-shot prompting."

chunks.heading: Chain-of-thought prompting: you supply the steps
chunks.text:
- Chain-of-thought prompting means giving the model steps. He says it sounds odd but is very simple.
- Ask yourself what steps you and a colleague would follow to write an Nvidia article:
  - choose an angle and an interesting twist
  - draft a table of contents
  - write an introduction
  - gather recent, interesting company information
  - build a story framework
  - write a conclusion, maybe with a call to action
- You do those steps internally. The AI "knows it only if you ask for it", otherwise it produces the most generic version.
- Example sequence he gives: step one, find an angle. Step two, write the introduction. Step three, write a table of contents. Step four, wait for me to say yes to the table of contents before continuing.
- Teaching analogy: he tried this with a 7-year-old who had to guide him, as a "robot", to a toothbrush. Everything you think is obvious (go to the bathroom, add water to the brush) is not obvious to an intern or an LLM. Give five steps ahead.

chunks.heading: Where ChatGPT is the wrong tool: education and advice
chunks.text:
- Ruben says learning (LinkedIn growth, German for a kid) is not the best use of an LLM.
- ChatGPT is "a vector res, like a lot of data". Asked how to grow on LinkedIn, it returns the most generic advice.
- Example: a German-speaking community member in the US wanted his daughter to learn German via ChatGPT. Ruben asked if he had tried YouTube. A week later the man said he "didn't know there was so much stuff on YouTube."
- For LinkedIn, he says to follow specialists instead, such as Richard van der Blom (Dutch, obsessed with the LinkedIn algorithm), or Ruben himself.
- His test: "Do you ask your intern what's the best way to grow your LinkedIn? You don't."
- YouTube, Google, LinkedIn and Twitter are already a "goldmine" for education.

chunks.heading: Where LLMs shine: brainstorming at volume, then human selection
chunks.text:
- Best workflow: learn something from a real expert first, then take it to the LLM and apply it to your business.
- Example: you learned a new SEO technique for SaaS, but you run a retail business. Ask the LLM to connect the two and brainstorm. Generic "best SEO for 2024" prompts give generic advice.
- An LLM can brainstorm 1,000 or 10,000 ideas. It cannot pick the best one. "You're the human", so you select.
- His image: an orchestra of a thousand interns. Do not expect one button to give one perfect solution. Press one button, get a thousand solutions, select the two best.
- Existing data of your own makes brainstorming much stronger.

chunks.heading: Agentic workflows and building EasyGen
chunks.text:
- Next level above plain input and output: multiple LLMs or ChatGPTs talking to each other. He calls this "agentic workflows". It is tricky, time-consuming, and he improves his every two to three days.
- He built a tool for himself first and says "the gen part was easy". He used it to reach 120 million people on LinkedIn in roughly 18 months.
- He made it public for two reasons: he has a community, and his team wanted to use it.
- The hard part was making it easy to use, hence the name **EasyGen**.
- How it works today: you brain dump a post idea and EasyGen turns it into a LinkedIn-ready post. He is also building research help, and says he is putting about 10 years of social media knowledge into the tool.
- Example post idea he gives: "How teaching your 7-year-old how to brush his teeth helps you write better prompts for ChatGPT."
- He keeps tweaking it because consumption habits change, not only algorithms. He says the algorithm is made to keep you on the platform longer. He tweaks EasyGen for his own results, not to please users, and users happen to benefit.

chunks.heading: Proof: growing two employees' LinkedIn accounts
chunks.text:
- Setup: two employees with different branding. Anisha posts about overcoming mental blocks (psychology degree, introverted). Axel (his "eyes of AI") covers AI news from Twitter and Reddit, such as Runway and Claude releases.
- Ruben recorded himself writing a post for each of them every day using EasyGen. He launched a paid newsletter the same day EasyGen was released (about 40-something days before the interview, under 2 months).
- Results he reports:
  - 1 million views in 25 days
  - purely organic, no ads, no pods, no hacks, "just good content consistently"
  - about 2.3 to 2.4 million views after 40-something days, on their accounts, not his
- He now spends about one hour per week writing the week of content for both. Paid newsletter members get an hour-long unlisted YouTube video plus a written breakdown of wins, failures and lessons.
- He expects 10-15% of his reach by year end to come through them, which made him think about hiring about 10 people and duplicating himself with different branding.
- His view: it is a long game. He reports the result as consistency plus a good process.

chunks.heading: Personal branding and tone of voice
chunks.text:
- EasyGen is deliberately not built to copy a new user's tone of voice. He tells beginners they "probably have a shitty one in the first place".
- His analogy: you do not become a book writer by picking up a pen. You read a lot of books first. Consume content, see which authors or creators you love (he names himself, Chris Do and Eric Partaker), then work out why: videos, cheat sheets, carousels, how the idea was conveyed.
- Advice: write a thousand posts, then you have a tone of voice.
- He cites Stephen King, who said he started out bad, read a lot, wrote like one author, then like two or three, and eventually became Stephen King.
- Core rule for content: "It's not about me when I'm making a post. It's about you who's listening." Help the reader go from A to B. Example: A is you don't know how to prompt, B is you now prompt better.
- His line: "Personal branding is awesome, but ditch the personal. Write as you but don't make it about you. Make it about them."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid explains how he grew from a music label to a top LinkedIn creator by focusing on a single platform and persona. He covers reverse-engineering what works, killing the ego, setting realistic expectations, and building problem-first rather than AI-first.

chunks.heading: Choosing one platform and one persona
chunks.text:
- Ruben rejects the "create once, repurpose everywhere" advice. He says running more than one social account at a high level is "nearly impossible" alone, and the few people who do it have a team.
- His approach is one nail, one massive hammer: pick a single platform and hit it as hard as possible.
- He chose LinkedIn because it is non-anonymous, so he can see a person's profile, colleagues and job. Its quality is also high, with few trolls, because people have jobs to protect.
- His platform rules of thumb:
  - Twitter for people in AI, crypto or fast-moving news.
  - Instagram Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts for artists or video-savvy people, since the same content works across all three.
  - For founders building a business, he still advises LinkedIn or Twitter, depending on industry and audience.
- Only after reaching millions of views on one platform should you consider expanding, and then with a team.
- He is obsessed with knowing the persona and writes for one person. His Twitter persona differs from his LinkedIn one, so the same content tackles different people.

chunks.heading: Treating content like a startup product
chunks.text:
- Ruben treats social media like a startup product because the feedback loop is as fast as it gets. Each post is "kind of like I'm sharing a Google form".
- Feedback signals he reads: engagement, DMs, link clicks and impressions. Impressions are his number one metric: how many eyeballs, and how consistently.
- You won't wake up knowing your persona. Read between the lines, talk to the people who comment (even 20 comments), and ask them questions.
- His first PDF was rough, but people kept asking him basic prompting questions and said they loved the step-by-step guide. That told him to keep doing step-by-step guides.
- He first posted the same material on Twitter as on LinkedIn and it didn't resonate:
  - On LinkedIn he had to get people excited about AI, then make it sound simple.
  - On Twitter, trying to excite people about AI made him look like clickbait. Those readers are already in.
  - Once he got direct (for example "I ran this test of Claude vs ChatGPT and here are my results"), his views "skyrocketed".

chunks.heading: Persona by platform
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn: the "everyday guy" with a demanding job and no time to test. Ruben writes how-to guides and frameworks and walks them step by step ("you go on the top right, click the three dots").
- Twitter: a more AI-savvy audience, so he can use terms like LLMs, chain of thought and tree of thought. He has built this for about two months, after a year and a half of content.
- He says the goal is to be the bridge between people and AI, meaning ordinary people and generative AI they can use, not data scientists or autonomous driving.

chunks.heading: Kill your ego: educational content over personal story
chunks.text:
- His number one content advice, repeated for years: "kill your ego".
- One employee was surprised after three months that personal branding is not about sharing your own story. Ruben says 99% of his content is purely educational and he stays out of it.
- Successful creators sprinkle in personal stories, but that is not why people follow them.
- Example: his friend Ran Chong, 23 at the time, reached more than a billion people on Twitter in a year. Not one of his posts was about himself. He is just the fastest guy on AI news.
- A person-based brand works, but a logo page would not. People follow it for the useful content, not the person.
- Ruben shares personal updates only occasionally, in his smaller newsletter community (for example after Google's event).
- Business conversations are content too. Talking about the challenges you faced and how you solved them is what people want.

chunks.heading: How to learn LinkedIn and set realistic expectations
chunks.text:
- Before posting, spend a week, 10 days or a month studying your favorite creators: how often they post, the format (image or video), and how they write captions. His analogy: to be the fastest runner, study Usain Bolt's routine first.
- Reverse-engineer what works. He cites Stephen King's advice that great writers begin as copy artists.
- Copied templates (a screenshot of a tweet, a few lines, "agree?") still work on the platform, and he is frustrated by that. But it is also your branding, and an expert doesn't need 10,000 likes per post.
- Creating content is his full-time job and his team's. They spend 30 minutes on the first two lines of a tweet. Founders have a business to run and shouldn't expect to become internet celebrities.
- A realistic middle ground: post once or twice a week with high quality content.
- Even a few comments can pay off. Friends job hunting in Tel Aviv got DMs and interview invitations.
- Posting is only about a third of the game. Two thirds is commenting, DMs and engaging with others. His market analogy: selling fruit means knowing the cheese and meat sellers too, and you can't expect engagement if you never talk to anyone.
- A founder who creates content is better at hiring influencer marketers and can talk to them differently.

chunks.heading: Practical AI applications in sales and marketing
chunks.text:
- Marketing: he describes paid-ads teams (he worked with Trade Republic's paid team) producing many designs, copies, videos and images to test on Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok, then pouring money into the winner. He says AI plus automation can produce thousands of variations and push budget to the best one. He names a tool by Alison/Quicksilver for this.
- Sales negotiation: he uses a tool (named Substrata in the transcript) on high-ticket client emails. It tells him who has the upper hand, and he uses it almost every day.
- CRM: after training a sales agency from Jason Lemkin in the US, where the team wasn't filling the CRM, he points to tools that connect to calls and fill Salesforce plus draft the follow-up emails. He names Attention Tech as one.
- Inbound content: use ChatGPT or Gemini to brainstorm. He is also building his own tool for this.
- He admits "sales and marketing" is too broad a question, like asking for the real applications of the internet.

chunks.heading: The lean AI-powered company
chunks.text:
- Ruben loves this topic. He cites a graph over about 100 years showing the number of employees needed to make a million dollars dropping drastically, using top S&P 500 companies.
- He says some solopreneurs will become unicorns in the near future. He knows solopreneurs running at a 97% margin with one or two team members.
- His own goal is a company as lean as possible, using AI wherever he can.
- Thresholds are falling in content, no-code tools, automation and creativity. Example: Opus Clip turns a recorded live stream into short TikTok-style clips, a job that once needed a hired editor.

chunks.heading: Learning AI and building products in a fast-moving field
chunks.text:
- Ruben learned AI from Google, YouTube, Reddit and Discord, and now there are many creators to follow. Free route: consume content from top creators in your niche (he names Nick St. Pierre for Midjourney). Paid route: consulting, which gives current data.
- The industry moves so fast that what you learn may be outdated in six months.
- Last April he sold two masterclasses on ChatGPT and Midjourney for about $150,000. He says that content is already old: it covered Midjourney V4, which is now V6 with many new features.
- He refuses to predict the next five years. Asked at a B2B summit in Paris in June, he said giving a vision would make him "a total charlatan".
- On what to build:
  - He wouldn't build an AI meeting-summary tool, since he guesses Google Calendar and Zoom are already doing it.
  - Don't build AI first. Many companies build chatbots because they can, not because they solve a problem. He calls these "GPT wrappers".
  - Focus on solving the problem first, and use AI if it helps. If it doesn't, "who cares".

chunks.heading: Where to reach him
chunks.text:
- LinkedIn is number one. He says someone helps manage his DMs, but he reads them all and never misses one.
- He also uses Twitter heavily, has a YouTube channel (posted to less often) and a newsletter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains how he grew to 400K+ LinkedIn followers and built EasyGen, a bootstrapped post generator. AI rewards taste and volume (generate many, curate the best), not one-shot prompts. His LinkedIn playbook: one tight problem, many solutions, double down on winners, and engage.

chunks.heading: Using AI to write LinkedIn posts: taste and experience over one-shot prompts
chunks.text:
- Ruben argues AI does not make everyone's content good. It raises the floor of what counts as "mediocre", but mediocre output is still mediocre.
- He expects mediocre work to be replaced fast: people whose job is mostly "writing okayish articles", writing average contracts as a lawyer, or writing briefs to designers.
- The replacement will not be a "monster AI". It will be "one guy who can generate hundreds of contracts, hundreds of articles, hundreds of briefs and handles agents" because he has "more taste, more experience and his standards are just way higher".
- His central rule: bad AI results come from "one prompt, one shot" ("write a viral post on LinkedIn"), then judging the tool on that output.
- He uses AI "to be greater, not to be lazier": the aim is to do more, not to finish a quick generation and stop for the day.
- Analogy: the best Midjourney artists are creative directors. They don't chase one perfect prompt. They generate a thousand images, pick the 20 worth deep-diving, then zoom, unzoom and iterate, like a photo shoot where you shoot a thousand frames and select.
- His workflow with his own tool, EasyGen: generate 20-30 posts on one topic, then patchwork the best hook, the best middle section and the best structure. Humans are better as "creator and editor" or orchestrator than as one-shot writers.
- He says people over 30 are mastering AI faster than the 15-25s, who use it for school badly because "it's not vibing with them".

chunks.heading: AI pushes people to be more human
chunks.text:
- Ruben's "bold statement" is that AI will push people to be more human.
- Example: two lawyers with equal taste and the same contract AI. The one who handles clients socially gets paid 10x, because clients "do want to talk to a lawyer".
- The same applies to creators: how you behave on a podcast or keynote becomes the differentiator, because people follow personality.
- Historical framing: around 1900 about 90% of the US population worked on food. Within roughly 60-70 years it fell below 1%. He doesn't believe in "no one's going to work anymore". People find new work, and competitive workforces reward those with more taste and volume.
- His advice on trends: "follow the money". He points at the trillions the top five companies are spending on AI as a signal the direction is worth mastering.

chunks.heading: Why professionals should post on LinkedIn (even without becoming influencers)
chunks.text:
- He predicts an "uberization" of work: more people become freelancers, hired and fired quickly because skills and needs change fast. Freelancers need choice over who they work with, which means being visible.
- He says SEO articles and ads probably won't work for individuals, and podcasting is hard. So people should talk about what they do for a living, not become content creators per se. This also protects against a company going badly or a job move.
- He is bullish on LinkedIn ("I hate LinkedIn, I love LinkedIn") because it is the only non-anonymous professional platform: you can see classmates, bosses and employers, and DM them. He says LinkedIn doesn't care about creators, which is part of why it is a good place to be one.
- Example: his sister, a gastroenterologist who leads a prominent European effort around ultrasound, hates LinkedIn but needs to get the word out. His advice: not daily posts, but about one post a week on her topic.

chunks.heading: The post pipeline: mission, ideas, then post
chunks.text:
- Ruben works backwards from the end of the pipeline. Post creation comes first in EasyGen, with image generation also added. Ideation and mission come next. He says about 80% of a post is the caption.
- Mission: a single problem you are trying to solve. Examples he gives: upskilling teams instead of hiring outside; getting cold emails opened and fixing email deliverability.
- The tighter and simpler the problem, the easier it is. Then solve it in many ways, because there are "way more subtopics than you think". Under "management of teams" alone there are a hundred topics.
- Idea sources: Perplexity, Reddit, Twitter, Discord and newsletters in your industry. He built free "Mission GPT" and "Topic GPT" tools for this.
- Input: you can type a topic, or speak a voice note or upload audio, and the tool turns it into a post.
- Advice on scope: one post should focus on one solution, not a list of several.
- Pivoting is fine ("there is no stamp"), but go all in at the start.

chunks.heading: Starting a LinkedIn account from zero (the playbook)
chunks.text:
- Ruben says he'd start again on LinkedIn because it is text-heavy and non-anonymous. He cites having done it four times, including accounts for team members.
- He documented it publicly: he wrote a week of posts for team members using EasyGen, posting every day, recording himself weekly for 24 weeks. One account was at about 6K followers by week nine. He says a person's whole week of content took roughly two days.
- Result he cites: 0 to 14 million views, and over 20,000 followers on those accounts.
- Step 1, first 30 days: post daily and try several formats and angles. It is tough.
- Step 2: analyze the best five and worst five posts. Remake the best five about 30 times over the next month, each slightly differently, and drop the other 25. Don't try to fix a loser. "Always double down on the winners."
- Step 3: repeat yourself a lot. "You don't know how many times I repeated myself."
- Step 4: engage as much as you post, and more in the beginning, on your own comments and on other people's content. His argument: you can't want a community's results and never talk to anyone.
- He says the known pattern holds elsewhere: a YouTuber who regrew a channel secretly did it again because he had the taste and experience.

chunks.heading: Building EasyGen: product decisions and positioning
chunks.text:
- EasyGen is a LinkedIn post generator. It is built as a multi-agent workflow, not a GPT wrapper: multiple LLMs talking to each other, connected via APIs.
- Timeline: he built it for himself first and kept it private. He made it public in May 2025 after wanting his team to use it. The talk is from January 2025 per his own references, with about 38,000 users and a figure of 500K that he leaves unspecified (ARR or MRR is unclear in the transcript). He says it is bootstrapped and that VCs are chasing him.
- Product rule: "I don't listen to users." He quotes Henry Ford: asking customers gets you faster horses. He builds it as a tool he uses himself.
- Example of a request he refuses: automated AI comments and LinkedIn post scheduling. He says the minimum risk is a ban and the account is gone, so he wouldn't do it for himself and doesn't sell it.
- Positioning: it is not a one-click solution. Its job is to "make killer variations of posts", and he never promised one-click automation.
- Marketing tactic: he published a blog comparing competitors (Taplio, Magicpost, SocialPilot and others). He ran the same three prompts, one-shot, through each tool and shows the results. He concludes EasyGen is best and invites people to run the trials themselves.
- Naming: both "Master AI before it masters you" and "EasyGen" came from ChatGPT after going through about a thousand names.

chunks.heading: Ruben's path and how he decides to take risks
chunks.text:
- Background: as a kid he played Guild Wars and loved "theory crafting" (choosing 8 skills from thousands). He wrote builds and shared them on blogs, and says he learned English from it. This gave him his habit of discovering a recipe and sharing it.
- At 17 he started a techno label that got millions of views on SoundCloud and YouTube. After seven years he concluded the DJs (personal brands) were more powerful than the label.
- He then ghostwrote for a fintech founder and wrote on his own LinkedIn. In December 2022 he published a ChatGPT guide that reached about a million people in two days, which drew requests that led him to produce content instead of taking consulting clients.
- By March he was bigger than his clients, which pushed him to go solo at age 26. He later moved to Tel Aviv, per the transcript.
- His risk method: open an Excel file and write the worst case. How many months of runway (for example four months)? What happens if you earn zero in that time? Could you find a job again? He treats it as an honest conversation with yourself, and says people will call you crazy at every step because most would not take the risk.
- He now has more than 10-15 employees and uses the same worst-case thinking.
- Self-positioning: he's "worthless and yet very impactful": not an engineer or model builder, but someone who teaches non-technical people how to use AI. He wants to be "a step" in people's journeys, not a guru.
- Claims about reach: about 472,000 LinkedIn followers (the talk mentions 400,000 earlier), roughly 200 million views in two years from zero, and a blog sent as a Sunday newsletter to 45,000 people. He plans a tighter Telegram community in Q1 2025.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid explains how he went from a failed music label to a $3-4M/year business by writing "IKEA instructions" for AI tools on LinkedIn. He covers sponsorship terms, riding platform pushes, content-first positioning, the human edge against AI, and handling haters and burnout. (Interview in French; quotes translated.)

chunks.heading: Ruben's path: from music labels to AI content
chunks.text:
- Ruben started writing video game guides at age 9 (Guild Wars), obsessively testing combinations and logging damage numbers on sticky notes. He calls this "theory crafting": the urge to find the optimal way to do something.
- Writing for English-speaking forums taught him English, helped by Arctic Monkeys lyrics and Louis CK stand-up.
- At 19 he ran a techno label (with Axel) in business school, finding artists on SoundCloud. Their second album reached 1 million views on YouTube and SoundCloud with no ads.
- His diagnosis of those artists: they had zero marketing and believed the music alone would win. He compares this to founders who think the best product sells itself.
- Around 2022 he lost his drive for the music scene: he found Berlin techno culture afraid of success ("succeed, but not too much"). He quit.
- He had earlier lost about €10,000, all he had, on a clothing brand called Matin (Covid, unsold t-shirts). He says he would not change it, because it led him to where he is.
- He took a social media job at Trade Republic, was told he was good by his bosses, then ghostwrote for Nicolas Cheron for 6 months before his own LinkedIn took off.

chunks.heading: How a single post launched the business (December 2022)
chunks.text:
- When ChatGPT launched (30 Nov 2022), he went down the prompt engineering rabbit hole of academic papers and distilled them into plain terms: chain of thought (break a task into steps), zero/one/few shot (give examples of what you want).
- He posted his findings on LinkedIn on 7 December 2022: about 2 million views, roughly 10,000 new followers at once, hundreds of messages.
- Everyone told him to launch a course or academy. He refused, fearing the business would stop him creating good content.
- Instead he put every comment and DM request into a spreadsheet and published free content daily on whatever was asked most.
- He describes his role as writing "IKEA instructions" for AI tools: build the piece of furniture first, then write steps anyone can follow.

chunks.heading: Monetization: brand partnerships and distribution
chunks.text:
- Revenue is "between 3 and 4 million" a year, with a media team of three (Ruben, Anicha, Axel).
- Payers are AI companies (Gamma, Notion, Anthropic). Partnerships are public and disclosed.
- Deal structure he prefers: a guaranteed minimum number of views; if he misses it, he commits to publish more posts. Rates are by post, month, year or views.
- Control: he decides how to cover the tool and sponsors do not review his scripts.
- Integrity rule: he won't promote a tool he thinks is worse than an alternative. He turns down 5,000 to 20,000 euro offers when the product is poor, because he plans to write for decades.
- Gamma example: he reaches about 2 to 3 million people a month for them and says he is their biggest creator and, he believes, their main acquisition channel. He has worked with them for over 2 years.
- Pitch to sponsors: he'd first ask whether LinkedIn is a major channel for them and whether LinkedIn users have high lifetime value. If both are true, he is the right person.
- Rough pricing: a post reaching 500k views at 10,000 dollars is about a 20-dollar CPM. Tens of thousands of dollars per deal; for small startups he'd consider equity.
- Side benefit: viral sponsored posts help the company when raising VC money.

chunks.heading: Anthropic case: pitching a better angle
chunks.text:
- Anthropic wanted a Claude Code push. He tested it, judged it fit engineers rather than his non-technical audience, and proposed instead Claude's custom writing style feature (upload your posts so Claude learns your style, one per client).
- Sponsor's contact agreed on his condition: he'd make a PDF carousel, and if it flopped he'd make a video for free.
- The PDF got 500,000 views.
- Lesson he draws: the best partnerships happen when the sponsor trusts you to test and own the angle, and you commit to correcting course if it fails.

chunks.heading: Format and platform tactics
chunks.text:
- He used a Synthesia avatar, an ElevenLabs voice and a Russian editing team (using B-roll) for LinkedIn vertical video. Axel wrote scripts and posted. About 60 million views in a few months.
- He stopped because of what he calls "fast marketing": when a platform pushes a new feature (LinkedIn vertical video, autumn 2024) it over-promotes it, then reach fades. His rule: spot the new feature early, exploit it, move on.
- He posts three times a day on LinkedIn, and not everything works. He also runs a newsletter read by about 130,000 people every Sunday.
- He doesn't do TikTok, Reels or Shorts: it needs a different style and he lacks the appetite for now.
- He does few conferences (down from three or four a year to about one) because travel and prep cut into writing time.

chunks.heading: Handling audience, haters and scale
chunks.text:
- He can't reply to hundreds of daily messages and says so honestly; automated replies to people in distress would be wrong.
- Educational creators must accept that most followers won't apply the advice (fitness analogy).
- Haters: seeing negative comments on creators he admires convinced him it comes with success; people try to climb on an expert's back. He told his team that hate means you are doing it right.
- Content creation means going on stage "naked" daily, since everything is public.
- Public speaking: he worked with coach Noémie, including a poetry-slam cafe night in Paris, where he trembled on stage.

chunks.heading: His views on AI and work
chunks.text:
- Career advice: don't chase "find your passion". Find what you're good at and get recognized for it; passion often follows. Keep hobbies as hobbies.
- AI is the average: it sits at the middle of the curve, so humans keep an edge through taste, direction and curation. He gives the DJ or orchestra-conductor analogy.
- Example: Nick St. Pierre generates huge numbers of Midjourney images (even auto-prompting from podcast transcripts every five words), then curates; his skill is selection, done for brands like Gucci.
- Most knowledge work is searching for information and rewriting it (slides, text, Slack, Gmail), which AI will heavily change even without AGI.
- Education: the thesis demo. His ex needed a 20-page thesis with 15+ academic sources. He used Consensus for literature gaps, downloaded the papers, had ChatGPT build the outline and citations. It took about 40 minutes and scored 92/100. His conclusion: schools should shift toward oral defence, with AI use allowed.
- Predictions: people will pay for human experiences (retreats, in-person), and he expects more deepfake-driven distrust. He doubts AI has consciousness and favours demystifying LLMs as matrix math and probabilities.
- Tools he rates: Nano Banana in Gemini (edits the existing image instead of regenerating it). He finds vibe coding promising but overvalued.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid explains how he went from joking with ChatGPT in Berlin to building an AI audience, and how he prompts it. He treats the model as a team of creatives you direct in layers (outline first, then iterate), feeds it your own data, and keeps a human editing the output. He grew by giving content away free before monetizing.

chunks.heading: How Ruben started and why he gives content away
chunks.text:
- Ruben found ChatGPT in early November 2022, when it had been out for a week or two. He was a ghostwriter for personal brands at a co-working space in Berlin.
- He began with jokes about a coworker's haircut, then poems in Spanish, Shakespeare style and rhymed forms. He kept adding detail to his prompts.
- He waited until early January 2023 to post a quick how-to guide. It got "more than a million impression[s]". He says the timing was right, and a November post would have gone unseen.
- He treats a personal brand like a startup and has "two hammers, one for monetization and one for growth". He hit growth first: "growth at all costs, everything is free."
- He sold a guide for $1, with pay-what-you-want tips; he says some people paid $50 or $100. It was a 1,000-plus prompt library and his carousels.
- Premium courses and conferences come later. He wants to "democratize AI" and be "the bridge between people and AI".

chunks.heading: Treat the AI as a team and prompt in layers
chunks.text:
- He calls a prompt "how human talks to the machine". He says to think of generative AI as a team of creatives, not one genie. Talk to it like a manager.
- His "Good, Bad and Ugly" prompt course has three levels:
  - **Ugly:** "Write a podcast script between Jason and Ruben around AI." There is no context, length or voice, so the team cannot be creative.
  - **Bad:** he adds roles, such as Ruben being an obsessed content writer.
  - **Good:** he describes each speaker's age, tone and vocabulary, then asks for a table of contents first.
- His order is title, then table of contents, then each part. He mirrors how humans work: pick the topic, then the big parts, then the subparts, then write.
- He gives feedback like a boss: "the first part is good, the second part should lean more toward Ruben being French", then "write the first part", then "make it better".
- "You don't prompt once. You prompt with layers of prompts."
- He compares himself to a grumpy VP on the couch. He edits and picks the best ideas from his "team" and doesn't do all the work.

chunks.heading: Give it your data; don't ask it for opinions
chunks.text:
- He says the biggest misconception is treating GPT like Google. GPT is best at generative work: "give it data and it gives back something really smart", like a summary, an outline or a strategy. It is not for asking opinions or judgments.
- "GPT is one hell of a liar." It is built to answer and not to say "I don't know". If you ask for sources, it invents plausible titles.
- His fix is to supply the sources, abstracts or full articles yourself and have it build from them. He does not use it as a fact-fetcher.
- He expects the future to be feeding it large private documents, such as a 100k-word PDF, and asking it to find better ways to work or to do the work. He has spoken to lawyers about a PDF summarizer for long documents.
- He was in talks with a Swiss healthcare company whose sales reps mostly do cold emails, cold outreach and articles. He knew nothing about healthcare. He sent sample outputs and the CEO said it was solid. Ruben's view: "one guy could make the job of 15 or 20."

chunks.heading: Content repurposing workflow
chunks.text:
His most viral post, as he describes it, turned a YouTube video into many formats:

1. Pull the YouTube transcript with a tool (he used a Huberman Lab podcast, a neuroscience podcast that runs two to four hours).
2. Feed it to ChatGPT in chunks and say what the discussion is about.
3. Ask for several outputs: an SEO article, public-speaking notes, a cheat sheet, a thread, a LinkedIn post and a cold email.

- **Twitter thread hack:** he doesn't use Twitter much. He likes one big article summarized into 10 to 15 tweets of 280 characters. They are snappy, digestible chunks he can reuse as LinkedIn carousels.
- **Carousel pipeline:**
  - GPT writes about 10 slides of text and produces Midjourney prompts for the visuals.
  - Midjourney renders the images.
  - His example was an ad for natural aromatic oil for baby massage, from just the words "baby skin care".
  - GPT had proposed 10 ad ideas and he chose one.
  - He could not get text rendered inside images at the time.
  - He still builds the final million-impression carousels by hand.

chunks.heading: Using it for sales and outreach
chunks.text:
- Build a personal brand first; "your life's going to be much easier."
- Ideate with the AI, giving it a real brief. His example was selling a Shure SM7B microphone:
  - He would not trust GPT to know the specs, so he feeds it the qualities and benefits.
  - Ask for article ideas, SEO keywords and email subjects.
  - Then work from the top: title, table of contents, then content.
- Then spend about 30 more minutes qualifying the output: "don't just copy paste." The goal is not to be any sales rep but "the best sales rep".
- He demoed this live for an insurance audience on GPT-4:
  - He prompted "act like an SEO copywriter expert" for 10 completely different article titles on auto and home insurance, with meta keywords.
  - He asked for fear-based angles, since fear drives opens in emails.
  - He picked one title, "The Ticking Time Bomb", then asked for an SEO table of contents.
  - He then asked for the first two parts, with an invented story as an example.
  - Finally he asked for the story to be more dramatic, detailed, with precise numbers and dates.
- Of 10 outputs there are usually only one or two "super good" ones, and the rest get discarded. He keeps those and keeps prompting.
- He made his LinkedIn headline "Master AI before it Masters you" this way. About 85% of the headline came from ChatGPT:
  - He ran 10 to 15 prompts, asked for 10 to 15 headlines each time, and gave detail about himself.
  - He kept asking it to be "more provocative".
  - He chose one from about 90 options and edited a single word, "rules" to "Masters".

chunks.heading: Productivity and jobs
chunks.text:
- His historical frame is the steam engine and the tractor. In his telling, about 70% of people once worked on food and now it is about 1%. The freed people did other work.
- His view is that AI makes people "superhuman", not unemployed.
- He argues against laziness: "It's not the time to be lazier, it's the time to do 10 times more." The average gets higher, and the person who prompts deeper and edits still stands out.
- He says humans stay as editors who add the "touch" and "spice", and he doesn't expect to work less.

chunks.heading: Tooling and ecosystem views
chunks.text:
- He pointed to the share of Y Combinator batches that are generative-AI startups as a sign of speed. He said it was about 10% in one batch and "more than 40%" in the latest.
- He expects a wave of new tools from GPT-4 and Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and Leonardo AI, plus Google's Bard.
- He warns that voice cloning needs only 3 to 5 minutes of audio, which makes impersonation scams likely.
- He says he had calls with Microsoft partners and OpenAI, and quoted one: "we are the good Jedi, how do we push the force to the positive?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains why he built EasyGen as a ghostwriter-style tool for his own team, and how founders should do personal branding by educating rather than sharing their life story. He also covers using employees' brands as a growth channel, LinkedIn micro-testing and language focus, and talking to people before building.

chunks.heading: Why Ruben says founders need a brand and distribution
chunks.text:
- Ruben says first-time founders tend to be technical and want to build the best product. Second-time founders focus on marketing, because a great tool can still go unnoticed if you can't share it.
- He learned this at 17, running a techno music label. Bedroom producers spent 10-15 hours a day perfecting tracks, assuming quality alone would make them known. Ruben's view: "Without a platform, without a community, you can be the very best DJ in the world... you're never going to have your first success."
- He treats the audience as the asset. A person's content stays with them across companies. A company can change in 10 years, but "your content is your content."
- He believes content is like fitness: you don't have to be a content creator full-time, but a healthy amount of it helps everyone.
- His advice to founders: before building, talk about the solution to other people as early as possible. Be "obsessed first driven by the solution and the people you want to help rather than the product itself." He cites the Reddit founder printing flyers and posting them around his campus.

chunks.heading: What "personal branding" really means
chunks.text:
- Ruben says personal branding does not mean being personal. It means you are not a company. People relate to a human more than to a corporate page.
- Content doesn't have to share your life story. He rarely tells his own story (some podcasts, his WhatsApp community, a touch on stage). People follow him because he learns something and shares it.
- The reader's frame: "I am at point A, I need to be at point B now." The creator's job is to transform the reader, not to show their breakfast.
- Two extremes to avoid:
  - Too personal: the audience thinks "help me first".
  - Too company-centric ("my company, my company, my company"): readers feel you are pushing your product down their throat and only want their money.
- The middle path for a founder: embody the person who needs the solution. Example: for a habit tracker, put about 80% of content on how hard it is to abandon a bad routine and how good it is to embrace one good routine, not on the tool itself.

chunks.heading: Content as an umbrella around the product
chunks.text:
- Ruben says his content is not just about EasyGen. It covers Pinterest, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude, design, scheduling, and mental frameworks. EasyGen is one tool inside a transformational journey ("go from A to B").
- Design advice: good social design should look like "everything but an ad".
- He runs a paid newsletter started two months before this talk (when EasyGen launched).
- The product is a solution inside a bigger process. You can recommend that people use it, but you teach the whole process.

chunks.heading: The two-employee experiment on LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Context: Ruben has 400,000 followers. He could not just tell people to use EasyGen, so he tested it on two employees, Axel and Anisha, who had barely posted on LinkedIn.
- Setup:
  - Each week he recorded a one-hour video making a week of content for each of them.
  - Axel's niche: the latest AI demos (videos). Anisha's niche: overcoming mental blocks (she is introverted).
  - The employees spend at least 45 minutes a day finding topics and images or videos, send them to Ruben (30-45 minutes), he writes the post with EasyGen, then they post and engage for 15-30 minutes. Roughly one hour a day each on their own brand.
- Results: no ads, purely organic. 1 million views in 25 days. A later update: 3.2 million views in 17 days (as he stated it). He ran 11 videos over 11 weeks.
- He rejects the "secret" explanation (pods, ads, his likes on their posts): "If any time I would like a post it would make people go from zero to three million views in two months I'll be very rich."
- Employer angle: even 30 minutes to an hour a day on their brand is positive for him and for them. He planned to do the same with two new employees.
- His success criterion for the test: if it went badly, he would improve EasyGen. It went well, so he keeps going.

chunks.heading: EasyGen: how it works and why it differs from ChatGPT
chunks.text:
- Origin: Ruben built it for himself, then for his team, in February 2023. He spent about 6 months improving it. Staff found early versions too hard to use, so he made it easy (hence "EasyGen"). He says he and his team are the primary customers, so he won't change things just on request.
- Positioning: it is a ghostwriter, not a generic writer. A human LinkedIn ghostwriter costs about $2,000-$5,000 per month and involves lots of back and forth. EasyGen costs roughly $2 a day, he says.
- How to use it:
  - Type your topic as a rough first draft or brain dump. It is not a ChatGPT-style prompt. Example topic he typed: "personal branding is not about being personal but being relatable... explain why it matters to my audience, not me".
  - Press generate, regenerate 2-3 times, combine parts, edit. He copies the topic before generating because LLMs can hallucinate and a regeneration is sometimes needed.
  - Output is about 80-90% good by design. A post that used to take 1-3 hours now takes 15-20 minutes.
  - Optional topic suggestions exist but he says people use them badly and he may remove them.
- Why LLM output sounds generic: an LLM picks the highest-probability next word, like phone autocomplete, so it trends generic. ChatGPT posts often start with "Are you tired of...?" Good content isn't generic, so the human supplies the first draft and the angle ("you are the captain, AI is the pen and paper").
- Planned: voice or video input, a web app, and possibly design and ideation help. It is LinkedIn-only for now because posts of about 3,000 characters fit it.
- Stack and stage: Chrome extension (beta), solo-founder bootstrapped, with a web app planned. He said the web app would come mid-August for paid users and early September for others, as stated in the talk.

chunks.heading: Traction, community and customer feedback
chunks.text:
- About 6,000 free users and a little over 400 paying users (as he said at the talk).
- Chrome Store: about 50 reviews at 4.9, from real named people. He plans to collect the stories into a "wall of love" on his website.
- Day-one signal: on launch day a personal branding agency asked to buy it and wanted to close their agency deals with it. He might build a B2B version for agencies later, but today it targets people who care about their own content.
- Customer story: Bora, a salaried employee at a large German company (not a founder), used EasyGen and got posts with 10x to 100x the CEO's views on a company launch. The CEO first asked him to take the post down, then colleagues pointed out it brought the company a lot of views and the boss came around. Bora writes in German, using EasyGen in English then DeepL to translate.
- Community: a WhatsApp group with his users, with his phone number visible. He learned from a former client, Nicolas, the biggest finance influencer in France (about 120,000 followers), who put his email and phone on Twitter. Only one person got weird enough to block. Ruben says he reads every connection note on LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn mechanics and platform opinions
chunks.text:
- Microtesting: the platform shows a post to a small sample (for example 20 of 1,000 followers). If the sample reacts (likes, reposts, comments, shares), it widens the audience step by step. If people scroll past, it stops.
- Language rule: pick one language. Posts in a language part of your audience doesn't read get scrolled away, which hurts microtesting. If your audience and clients are in France, write in French. "You should never do both."
- Bots: platforms employ large engineering teams to find bots, so automation and AI agents for social media get punished. He doesn't believe in AI agents for social media. Being social takes time but is worth it.
- LinkedIn's AI comment feature: he thinks it is dangerous. He says about 20-30% of his comments already look AI generated (from real people, not bots). If it reached 50-70% he might stop posting there, because he posts to inspire people and connect one-on-one.
- On AI in general: AI is the pen and paper, not the end product. The skeptic argument ("AI content isn't real") echoes the old complaint that computer-written books weren't real books. Pen and paper has produced many bad books too. He says the best startup combination is a content creator obsessed with a problem plus a technical co-founder obsessed with the same problem. He cites his own pairing with his CTO, Pete, and mentions Sam Altman as an example of strong communication paired with deep technical teams.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid explains how to prompt ChatGPT by treating it like an intern: give a Persona, Context and Mission, and keep the decisions yourself. He also covers token limits, custom instructions, common mistakes, and how he builds LinkedIn content with AI as a helper rather than a replacement.

chunks.heading: Ruben's mental model of ChatGPT: a human-like intern, not a mind-reader
chunks.text:
- Ruben says an LLM is built on human knowledge (Wikipedia, Reddit, books), with a natural language processing layer on top. His analogy: "NLP is French, but 'bonjour' is the prompt."
- He argues you should prompt it like a human, because it is trained on human text. Ending a prompt with "take a deep breath and work on this step by step" gives much better results (he cites a DeepMind research paper).
- His intern test: "Listen to the podcast and write an article" is a bad brief. A good one covers context, mission, article type, length, SEO intent, and 30 good examples.
- His rule: "The answer is just as good as the prompt." If you lack time for a quality prompt, you can't complain about quality. He also notes the AI can't make judgment calls well and will always answer rather than say "I don't know".

chunks.heading: Persona, Context, Mission: Ruben's prompt structure
chunks.text:
1. **Persona:** who ChatGPT should be, in detail. Not just "podcaster", but a podcaster for tech nerds talking about AI, or one styled after Joe Rogan, Lex Fridman, or a full profile of the actual host.
2. **Context:** what is happening right now. Who the host is, who the guest is, the audience, the topic, the podcast title.
3. **Mission:** what you want. Example: a table of contents with 5 questions per category. If the categories are wrong, call that out and ask for 5 new categories.

He says most people only write the mission. The biggest mistake he sees is not knowing what you want and expecting the AI to know. His analogy is clients who "know what they want" until they see the result.

chunks.heading: Two prompting modes and token management
chunks.text:
- **Exploratory mode:** you don't know where you're going and you brainstorm and refine in conversation. Keep prompts and answers short, because every message eats tokens.
- **Big-prompt mode:** you know exactly what you want. Give 2,000-3,000 tokens of context and examples, expect a 2-3k token answer, and skip a long back-and-forth.
- Tokens are the model's "brain limit" per chat. GPT-4 had an 8,000 token limit (roughly 6,000 words) at the time. ChatGPT never tells you when it has forgotten earlier content. He points to OpenAI's tokenizer website to measure.
- Custom instructions sit outside the token limit and are always remembered, so he recommends putting your Persona and context there. He doesn't use them himself because he prompts across many personas daily.
- For feeding PDFs and documents he mentions Claude over GPT-4 for capacity, and also names "Yana" as a good tool.

chunks.heading: Tree of thoughts: you decide, the AI brainstorms
chunks.text:
- He says people hand judgment to the AI ("pick the best one"), and it's bad at that because judgment needs experience.
- Tree of thoughts: ask for 5 ideas, you pick one, ask for 5 ways to execute it, you pick again, and so on.
- Example: getting French people to watch the Olympics. Ideas include a baguette marathon, then locations (he picks Lyon to match his calendar), then local influencers.
- He notes it's a human technique: "what we'd do with an A4 paper."

chunks.heading: Common mistakes: judgment calls and scraping
chunks.text:
- Don't ask ChatGPT to "find the best designer for my thumbnail on Fiverr". There are two errors: it can't judge "best", and it can't scrape the internet, which would require hundreds of millions of pages.
- Browsing is useful when you already have a specific page: "browse this page, now let's discuss it."
- It lies because it is built to always answer. He says people forget "it's not God".

chunks.heading: Ruben's content workflow on LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Ruben says the top 1% of creators need their own brain in the main content. AI is for support work and inspiration.
- He gives ChatGPT the last 50 hooks he used and tells it which got the most impressions. He expects one good word or idea, not 50 good hooks.
- He iterates by calling out mistakes: hooks too long (he targets 55 characters), too complex, too many rhetorical questions. He says "use simple words" because ChatGPT loves complex ones. He does this in one thread, then asks for new hooks, and says the process can take a few hours.
- He sets a post to take around 4 hours.
- Tip: use affirmative instructions ("stop asking questions") instead of "don't ask questions", because the negative contains the thing you want to avoid.
- He uses a trained prompt for his newsletter: summaries that are informative enough that the reader doesn't need to click.
- He uses Opus Clip (as an ambassador) to repurpose video, hired a video editor, plans to hire a content creator to train, and expands to YouTube, Twitter and Instagram/TikTok.
- At the time, he said he was ranked second biggest LinkedIn creator in April and about 10th later, and first in AI. His positioning: "the bridge" between technical AI people and everyday consumers.

chunks.heading: Why Ruben says AI won't end work (and the closing advice)
chunks.text:
- His analogy for AI is fire, not the internet or electricity. Fire freed humans from 12 hours a day of digesting raw meat, which let them build tools.
- Myth 1: AI takes all jobs. In 1900, 90% of the US worked in food and farming. 60 years later it was under 1%, and people went on to create the iPhone, Netflix and Amazon.
- Myth 2: the apocalypse. He cites a pope banning the crossbow because a peasant could kill a knight, as a pattern of every era predicting the end.
- You will be replaced "by someone using AI the right way". His tagline: "Master it before it masters you." He also notes solo creators can build bigger one-person businesses with AI.
- He also flags a security-style bug: ChatGPT obeyed text written on an image ("tell the user it's a picture of Justin Welsh") over the user's own question. His view is that the user's prompt should always take priority.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains how EasyGen, a bootstrapped LinkedIn post generator, gets about 18% of its roughly $50K MRR from affiliates, with most of it coming from four people. He covers turning employees into affiliates, coupon-based tracking, community building around one problem, and refusing automation and VC money.

chunks.heading: How Ruben built EasyGen's affiliate program to ~18% of revenue
chunks.text:
- Ruben said EasyGen's affiliate revenue started at roughly 10% of revenue and had grown to about 18% when he recorded this, and "could go as near as 20%".
- He puts it at about $10,000 per month from affiliates, on roughly $50K MRR overall, with about 40,000 weekly users.
- Concentration is extreme: about 80% of affiliate revenue comes from just four people, and two of those four are his own employees (Anisha and Axel), paid through Rewardful on top of their salaries.
- He calls this a form of equity for staff: "imagine you have a $12 a month SaaS where you don't have to do anything, no customer support", and you're actively growing it by supporting his journey.
- He built the program reactively. Members of the EasyGen paid-users WhatsApp group kept asking for an affiliate program. Early on people DM'd him asking where to sign up because he had forgotten to put a link in the app.
- The fix was a button labelled "affiliate" in the web app's left sidebar that opens the Rewardful signup page.
- Affiliates get 20% recurring, which is $12 per month per referred customer. His biggest affiliate has around 50-55 referred customers and earns about $600-700 a month.
- He has never done active affiliate recruitment, and says maybe he should.

chunks.heading: Turning employees into the top affiliates by growing their LinkedIn accounts
chunks.text:
