- Ruben used his own team as case studies. He had planned to prove EasyGen by creating a fake LinkedIn ghostwriter account, then dropped the idea. His warning: never create a fake LinkedIn profile, because it breaks the terms and puts the real account at risk.
- Instead, around April 2024, he offered Anisha and Axel (both on his media company team) a deal. They picked their own topics and personal brand, and he handled the content.
- Process:
  - He recorded a weekly YouTube playlist (a paid newsletter product) showing how he wrote a week of LinkedIn posts for each of them.
  - It took roughly one hour a week.
  - He ran this for 23 consecutive weeks, using EasyGen plus Canva and Perplexity to refine topics.
- Anisha's brand: empowering people to write their first LinkedIn post. She was at 6,000 followers by week 5 and later passed 30,000.
- Axel's brand: "my eyes of AI". She tracks AI news and demos across LinkedIn, Twitter, Reddit and Discord, and turns that into a daily post. She went from 0 to about 25,000 followers.
- Each post ends with a line like "by the way, this post was made by EasyGen, and if you want $10 off your first month use my code".
- Result: both became two of his biggest affiliates.

chunks.heading: Coupon-code tracking and who makes a good affiliate
chunks.text:
- Ruben tracks affiliates with Rewardful's coupon-based tracking rather than links.
- His reasoning: people tend to go straight to the Stripe payment page, and when someone clicks a link they worry it isn't working. With a coupon they can see the discount applied in Stripe, so it feels trustworthy. He says it is "much sturdier on my end".
- The affiliate pitch for a SaaS is recurring income with no investment, no customer support and no payroll or cash-flow costs. He notes some people refuse because they know he keeps 80%, but says it is still a good deal if you believe in the product.
- What makes a good affiliate, in his view:
  - They believe in the channel. For EasyGen that means believing organic LinkedIn is a huge opportunity. His argument: LinkedIn has about 1.15 billion users and only around 0.6% post weekly, a gap he says doesn't exist on Instagram, TikTok, Twitter or YouTube.
  - They genuinely use and love the product. Zach, a top affiliate, is often the first to report bugs.
  - They benefit from inbound leads. His example is Emanuel Oren, a broker who matches clients with 3D design agencies for a 20% cut. He stopped cold calling and now posts 3D case studies on LinkedIn, so leads come to him. He became a super affiliate.
  - Good fits are sales, HR and VC people who need inbound.
- Ruben says the best affiliates are customers who use the product daily, and that he makes sure he is the most prominent user of EasyGen himself. His employees are the second best users and also his biggest affiliates.
- He suggests affiliates publish a "tech stack" list the way beauty creators publish Amazon lists, and share it whenever someone asks what tools they use.

chunks.heading: How EasyGen got its first users: friction and a WhatsApp waitlist
chunks.text:
- At launch EasyGen was a Chrome extension that was not on the Chrome Store. Users had to join a WhatsApp waitlist, which he accepted manually, then watch a Loom video and install the package by hand.
- He did this deliberately to filter for people who really wanted it and to have conversations with them. He had hundreds of signups per day and about 4,000 people across four WhatsApp groups of roughly 1,000 each.
- Once the product was paid, he moved paying users into a VIP group, which is still active.
- The most common request was an automation that schedules a whole week of posts. He refuses to build it: "if you behave like a bot", platforms with large teams hunting bots will target your account. He keeps a blog post titled "never automate".
- He also refuses to connect to the LinkedIn API for analytics, because accounts get blocked.
- He stopped the waitlist later, and says the WhatsApp community let him educate users, since good LinkedIn posting was not even a topic ten years ago.

chunks.heading: Distribution channels: content-led, no SEO and no paid
chunks.text:
- Ruben calls himself a non-traditional founder: no SEO, no paid ads, barely any influencer marketing.
- He says 99% of revenue outside Rewardful comes from his own LinkedIn plus a little from other channels and his newsletter.
- His newsletter has about 46,000 subscribers and goes out free every Sunday. It covers how AI grows LinkedIn, across all his systems, not just EasyGen.
- His method is to share his real process as content. Example: he clipped a Donald Trump Stargate clip with Opus Clip, researched it with DeepSeek, generated about 10 post versions in EasyGen and patchworked a final one. The post got 1.1K likes, 400 comments and 100+ reposts, and he plans to explain the process in the next newsletter.
- On LinkedIn he went from 8,000 to 400,000 followers over about two years. He argues AI is "not to be lazier but to be greater": he generated around 100 posts and hand-picked the most impactful one.
- His reach last year was 125 million people on LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Community philosophy: aim for 1,000 true fans, not millions of views
chunks.text:
- Ruben says going viral is useful for attention and data, but going viral for any reason isn't a goal. The strongest community he has is only about 1,500-2,000 people.
- His rule of thumb: aim for 1,000 community members over three years, which is about 300 per year or roughly one new person per day.
- A community member is someone who actively follows your journey, not someone who reads one post.
- Pick one mission and solve one problem. Example he gives for the host: affiliate programs for SaaS founders. Then you become the category: "you have a SaaS and you need affiliate, read this content and check Rewardful".
- He compares being a "stepping stone" in someone's journey to niche YouTubers (a grilled-cheese channel, a Japan restaurant POV channel) he saves for later use.
- Most people quit because they lack patience for one person a day over three years. His analogy: nobody expects muscle on day one at the gym.
- He believes everyone will eventually need to market themselves (for promotions, freelance leads, or portfolio), even with a full-time job.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping, team and EasyGen roadmap
chunks.text:
- He is bootstrapped and declined VC offers. His first month took his bank account from zero to about -$50K of his own money. He had budgeted that he could sustain it for about a year, and treated it as investing in himself rather than the S&P 500.
- His preference: "a business making 100K a month where I own 80% of the company and have a lot of fun" over one making $10M a month while being crunched by VCs.
- Team: a CTO who owns 20%, two developers (one team in India), a project manager, and a newly hired customer support person. Marketing is just him plus Rewardful.
- He says he builds the prompt engineering himself, and EasyGen is an agentic flow of multiple LLMs rather than a single-model wrapper. He satisfies his own taste first and sometimes ignores users with small followings.
- He explicitly positions EasyGen as a replacement for a ghostwriter you'd pay about $2,000 a month, not a ChatGPT alternative.
- Roadmap for 2025:
  - Mission and ideation (what to post based on trends in your niche).
  - "Sessions": one topic generates 10-20 post versions fast, with the ability to patchwork between them and edit sections by prompting, similar to ChatGPT Canvas.
- Focus is his stated edge: he is bad at doing many things at once but very good at being hyper-focused.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben walks through scraping a profile's LinkedIn posts cheaply via Apify, having Claude analyze them into a report and SOP, then turning that into a reusable /skill that generates new posts from proven patterns. He also shows how to clone the recipe of a single viral post, and is candid about the limits: AI mirrors rather than creates, and only works if past posts were good.

chunks.heading: Scraping your LinkedIn posts for $2 per 1,000 instead of using your own account
chunks.text:
Ruben says not to run the extraction from your own LinkedIn account ("never do any automation"). Instead, use a third-party tool that safely and legally pulls publicly visible posts, since all LinkedIn posts are public on the web.
- He uses Apify and says he is not affiliated: "it's just the best way to do it."
- Cost is about $2 per 1,000 posts. A free Apify account comes with $5 of credits, enough for roughly 2,000 posts.
- Steps:
  1. Create a free Apify account.
  2. Open the LinkedIn profile-posts actor.
  3. Enter a LinkedIn profile URL plus the settings, then click save and start.
  4. Wait a couple of minutes.
  5. Export the results as a spreadsheet.
- His own run scraped 489 posts for about $1, covered by the free credits.
- The method works for any account with 30+ posts, not just your own. His demo used Alex Hormozi's posts.

chunks.heading: The report prompt: turning the export into a decision-ready analysis
chunks.text:
Ruben uploads the spreadsheet to Claude Cowork with one long prompt, run once. It makes Claude act as a coach producing a serious analytics deliverable (50 to 5,000+ rows).
- **Fixing misleading columns.** The `type` column says "post" for every row, so format is derived from which media columns are filled: document means carousel, `postVideo` means video, `article` means shared link, `postImages` means image, otherwise text-only.
- **Engagement.** Likes + comments + shares. The reaction mix (like, empathy, praise, funny) is used to read emotional register.
- **Dates.** There is no date column, so the prompt decodes the timestamp from the activity ID: take it as a 64-bit integer, shift right 22 bits, and read the result as Unix milliseconds. This feeds cadence and best day/time analysis.
- **Rigor.** Quantitative stats are computed in code across all posts so numbers are exact, and the outlier multiple used must be stated.
- **Visual review.** Claude must open the actual images, video thumbnails and carousel slides (via the transcribed-document URLs) rather than judging from captions. It describes the hook text, style (selfie, screenshot, chart, quote card, meme) and layout, and ties them to performance.
- **Required report contents:** bottom line in 3-4 sentences; winning formats with average, median and sample size; winning angles and hook patterns; biggest over- and under-performers with links; Stop / Continue / Start; cadence, best day/time, length, comment-to-reaction ratio, fatigue signs and the single highest-leverage change.
- **Outputs:** two new files, a written report and an SOP for the next post reverse-engineered from the top outliers (hook formula, format, angle, visual template).
- **Integrity checks.** If data is missing (too few videos, dead media URLs), Claude must say so, and re-check headline numbers against the file before finishing.
- His Cowork run took about 8-10 minutes and spawned agents to go through the whole file.

chunks.heading: Turning the report and SOP into a reusable skill
chunks.text:
To avoid re-pasting the same prompt and context, Ruben continues in the same chat and asks for a skill.
- Prompt pattern: `/skill-creator Create a skill combining what matters inside the content report and the SOP to write viral posts for [person]. Call the skill "[name]".`
- The skill must use the AskUserQuestion tool, tailored to what the person does best, to collect input before generating angles, hooks and captions. The user then picks favorites and assembles the post with Claude.
- After saving, he invokes it in a new Claude tab with the `/` command. It returns five angle options (he says he could ask for 500). After he picks one, Claude searches the web and produces the full caption plus guidance on the image to pair with it.
- Everything is optimized only from the person's own best posts, "nothing from the internet (which is probably outdated anyway)."
- He notes you could technically start a ghostwriting agency this way.

chunks.heading: Recreating one ultra-viral post as a skill
chunks.text:
For someone who "went ultra-viral once," meaning a post that did really well for their own standards (5 usual likes and one with 100 counts), Ruben builds a skill from that single post.
- Example: an Alex Hormozi post with 9,500 likes.
- Method: screenshot the post (and describe the video if there is one), upload it to Claude using Opus 4.8, and run a `/skill-creator` prompt.
- The prompt asks the skill to capture the recipe: the format, the hook (first two visible lines), and the entire caption, covering how it is written (line breaks, cadence, tone of voice).
- The skill stores the full viral post for reference. When invoked, Claude iterates through questions and answers until the new post is generated, and the new post can be about anything, for anyone.
- Claude even tells you not to use AI where appropriate, which Ruben likes.
- Warning: don't repeat an ultra-viral recipe over and over. "It's not because burgers are tasty that you want to eat burgers every day."

chunks.heading: Where the approach falls short (his own caveats)
chunks.text:
- **AI isn't creative.** It follows instructions well, but the value comes from combining its capacity to digest lots of context (400+ posts) with your human pattern-matching.
- **Not faster.** A good post still takes time; the gain is spending time more efficiently for better odds of going viral.
- **Expensive.** Claude costs him $100/month.
- **Not for one post.** Worth it only if posting at least weekly and with enough past posts.
- **Garbage in, garbage out.** If you are bad at LinkedIn, training on 400+ bad posts won't help; feed it good posts first.
- **Only good at repeating.** Ultra-viral is often novelty, but everyone starts by mirroring (not copying) the best.
- **Don't be a copycat.** He dislikes people who copy and add a tiny "credits: Ruben" comment.
- On a reader's question (only 3 posts so far), the essay's answer is implied by these limits: it needs a body of good posts, so a newcomer would study someone else's profile.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn credentials and newsletter positioning
chunks.text:
- Ruben says he gained 340,000 new followers last year with $0 spent on ads.
- He runs a paid LinkedIn "Circle": 3,700 people joined at $200 a year. LinkedIn caps connections at 30,000; he has 18,000 and can still connect with about 12,000 more. He sent 3,000+ connection requests manually.
- He says he is not tied to any model ("I don't care about Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini") and is not paid to make the newsletter.
- His stated goal: be "the greatest filter to the AI noise," publishing twice a week on the "How." The newsletter has 700,000+ readers, most arriving through a trusted person's referral, so he asks readers to share it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues that one-line prompts give average, generic output because Claude lacks context. His fix is Claude Cowork pointed at a folder of text files (style, rules, goals) that act as a permanent prompt. He pairs it with Obsidian so non-developers can read, search and edit those files, and adds Skills for repeated tasks.

chunks.heading: Prompting is the weakest way to use Claude: context files beat long prompts
chunks.text:
Ruben argues that short prompts give "average results" because Claude lacks context on tone, audience and rules. Typing 500 words of instructions for every first draft is something nobody does, so outputs "sound like everyone else" and people blame Claude for it.

- **Projects** (upload files once, reuse across chats) are better, but still force a new project per topic, repeated uploads and re-explained rules. He says that is not how a "Second Brain" works.
- **Claude Cowork** is the fix. He calls it "the biggest thing to happen to AI since ChatGPT".
  - It connects to a folder on your computer.
  - You save text files in it covering your style, rules and goals.
  - Claude reads them automatically before every session: "The files are the prompt. Forever."
  - It then creates documents (docx, ppt, Excel) inside the folder, "like a real employee".
- He claims software lost about $2.5 trillion in valuation since Cowork and that it made Claude's growth parabolic, surpassing ChatGPT. This is his belief ("I believe...").
- Payoff example: with a one-line prompt, Cowork read his whole folder (writing style, taste, dislikes), ran an "Anti-AI Writing Style" audit unasked, and saved a solid LinkedIn post into an OUTPUTS subfolder.

chunks.heading: Minimal Cowork setup (recap)
chunks.text:
- Cowork exists only in the Claude desktop app (free to download). It needs a paid plan: $20/month minimum; Ruben pays $100/month.
- Create a folder called "Claude Cowork" with 3 subfolders:
  - **about-me**: three files. `about-me` (him and his taste), `anti-ai-writing-style` (because he hates sounding like an AI), `my-company` (business info).
  - **claude-output**: where Claude stores its work; you don't touch it.
  - **templates**: saved work templates; you don't touch it.
- Set Global Instructions (Settings > Cowork > Global Instructions) so Cowork always reads `about-me` and leaves the rest alone.
- His earlier free Cowork guide was read by over 3 million people, and he offers to DM his files to commenters.

chunks.heading: The Cowork problem: markdown files are unfriendly to non-developers
chunks.text:
- Cowork runs on `.md` text files, but non-developers have never managed them.
- Double-clicking opens a geeky editor full of hashtags and asterisks that "looks like coding", so people rarely edit the files and close them.
- Ruben's diagnosis: this is why most people never try Cowork ("too much work to set up").
- What he wanted: something as easy as a Google Doc that saves automatically. He tested 6 tools over two weeks and picked one.

chunks.heading: Obsidian as the interface for Claude's "brain"
chunks.text:
- Obsidian is a free app that opens a folder as a "vault" and renders it like a clean knowledge base: formatted files, sidebar navigation, search across everything, in-place editing that writes to your actual folder.
- Setup is two steps: download from obsidian.md (works on Mac, Windows, Linux), click "Open folder as a vault", and select the Cowork folder. No import, conversion or sync.
- Daily workflow:
  1. Open Obsidian to browse, search, read and edit files.
  2. Open Cowork to create work and deliverables.
  3. Both see the same folder, always in sync.
- "Obsidian is where you update your brain → Cowork is where you build."

chunks.heading: Five ways he uses Cowork + Obsidian
chunks.text:
1. **Stop prompting.** Demo: he edited the first line of `about-me` to say he eats only coconuts. A new Cowork session on the same folder read the file first and answered accordingly. Edits in Obsidian become the new prompts. When Claude does something he hates, he updates the file with "Remember [this]" or "Replace [this] with [that] always."
2. **Edit context files properly.** Update job title, targets, new tools, or new things he hates from Claude. He calls the last one "usually the best update you can make". Example rule he added: always ask him questions before executing any task, so they outline it first. Then a one-line prompt triggers questions, the anti-AI-writing-style check, and a draft that is "already 80% there".
3. **Finding things.** Obsidian searches everything he and Claude wrote. He says "Claude's internal search engine is terrible."
4. **Reading outputs.** Past outputs (e.g. his newsletter on Claude usage limits) are readable in one folder with proper formatting, and new Cowork files appear in Obsidian automatically.
5. **Combining capabilities.** Cowork can produce multi-tab Excel files with formulas and charts, Word docs, PowerPoints with speaker notes, PDFs (fill, merge, split, extract tables), full websites and dashboards, research reports, CSV analysis, scheduled tasks, and use connectors to Slack, Google Drive, Notion, Gmail and 50+ apps.

chunks.heading: Skills: saved workflows for repeated tasks (advanced)
chunks.text:
- Problem: weekly tasks (LinkedIn post, newsletter, client brief, specific contract) need the same extra instructions repeated, like "under 1,300 characters" or "single image only". Saying it 30 times is inefficient.
- Skills are one file per task, called with a `/` command (e.g. `/contract`, `/negotiation`).
- Creating one:
  1. Open Cowork, start a new task (he uses Opus 4.6, with the Cowork folder selected).
  2. Prompt: create a skill called "negotiation", interview me about the deals I negotiate daily, build the best negotiation skills based on different experts, and save it as a skill callable with `/negotiation`.
  3. Answer Cowork's questions and click "Always allow" so it can edit.
  4. Claude reviews the skill with examples and benchmarks. Tell it "It's ok now", then click "Save skill".
  5. Type `/nego` and the skill appears.
- He moves the generated skill file from the OUTPUT folder into a new `SKILLS` folder via Obsidian.
- Skills stack with other pieces: Cowork + his folder + `/negotiation` + the Gmail connector so it reads his email.
- To change a skill, edit the text file in Obsidian, then re-upload it into Claude.
- Ideas: `/newsletter`, `/client-brief`, `/sales-email`, `/weekly-report`, `/meeting-notes`.
- He says most people don't need skills.

chunks.heading: Why Obsidian won over six alternatives
chunks.text:
- His criteria: free, local on the computer, easy and clean for non-developers.
- Rejected:
  - **Notion**: cloud database, would need re-import every time Cowork updates a file. Good for project management (his team still uses it for the content library), "terrible for this".
  - **Google Docs/Drive**: not `.md`, constant conversion.
  - **Apple Notes**: closed format, can't point at a folder.
  - **VS Code / Cursor**: made for developers; "If I see a code editor, I close the tab."
  - **GitHub**: needs git, commits, pushes.
  - **Typora**: $15 one-time, but one file at a time, no folder-wide sidebar, search or linking.
  - **MarkEdit**: free, Mac only, but one file at a time.
- Obsidian wins because it:
  - reads the existing folder with no import, conversion or sync,
  - is free on one device ($4/month to add a phone),
  - has a clean interface for non-developers,
  - never touches files in a way that breaks Cowork (no hidden metadata or format changes), so `.md` files stay `.md`.
- He states he is not paid, affiliated or sponsored, and likes that Obsidian's CEO Steph Ango says they don't know their user count (no forced accounts, no analytics).

chunks.heading: Distribution and call to action
chunks.text:
- He asks readers to block 20 minutes that week to set up Claude ("Acting > Reading") and to share with anyone using Claude who hasn't tried Cowork.
- Distribution note: his newsletter "mostly grows because of your shares", with 1,000+ shares on each free article, which he calls his "north star" and says keeps it free.
- Lead magnets: 100+ infographics (like the Skills recap) given to free subscribers, and his Cowork files via DM to commenters.
- His suggested learning plan: read only the Cowork newsletter and this one, then spend 2 x 20 minutes twice a week.
- Best share channel: colleagues' group chats (Teams or Slack).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid argues you can skip learning prompt engineering by running a rough one-liner through his free "Prompt Maker" GPT, then pasting the output into a fresh chat. He shows the two-step workflow with LinkedIn hooks and newsletter ideation, and ends with a simple newsletter growth ask.

chunks.heading: Using the Prompt Maker GPT instead of learning prompt engineering
chunks.text:
Ruben offers two routes to better prompts: use his free "Prompt Maker" custom GPT, or learn prompt engineering yourself (Chain-of-Thought prompting, Zero vs. Few-shot prompting, Role - Ask - Steps - Example(s) - Iteration). His framing: ChatGPT is only as good as its input, so the prompt matters, but you can delegate the writing of the prompt.
- The Prompt Maker is a free GPT inside ChatGPT, reported at 700,000+ users, built to convert bad prompts into good ones.
- He updated it on the day of the essay (Jun 8, 2025).
- Access: ChatGPT left menu > "GPTs", or the direct link chatgpt.com/g/g-hhh4w3eov-prompt-maker. The "About" tab on the GPT shows user reviews.
- He says his newsletter will eventually teach the manual techniques too, but this essay focuses on the tool.

chunks.heading: The two-step Prompt Maker workflow
chunks.text:
Ruben reduces the process to two steps:
1. Send your bad (even one-line) prompt to the Prompt Maker and get back a better prompt.
2. Copy that prompt (the tool always adds a "Copy" button at the top right), paste it into a new ChatGPT chat, add your own material, and pick the model (he chose o3, via the model picker at the top left).

His expectation-setting on quality: the output is not "the best prompt possible" for the task, but it is "a fantastic start from a one-liner terrible prompt... The best you could have."

chunks.heading: Filling in the placeholders in a generated prompt
Example 1: LinkedIn hooks across models
chunks.text:
- Input to Prompt Maker: "A prompt to write drastically different hooks for a Linkedin post I share."
- He ran the resulting prompt on three models and compared outputs:
  - ChatGPT o3 (his first choice).
  - GPT-4.5 for "a different twist" ("also good").
  - Claude, with the pro tip: "Use Claude-Opus 4 + Extended thinking."
- Takeaway: the same generated prompt is portable across LLMs, and switching models is a cheap way to get a different style of output.

chunks.heading: Example 2: Newsletter topic research
chunks.text:
- Input to Prompt Maker: "A prompt to read my last 3 newsletters I input to search the web & give me ideas for new topics."
- He pasted the generated prompt with model o3; ChatGPT then asked him for the newsletters, which he pasted in.
- Result: the answer "blew me away", so long, detailed and on point that he couldn't screenshot it, so he shared the conversation as a ChatGPT share link instead.
- Pattern shown: the generated prompt can make ChatGPT ask for the inputs it needs, so the user does not have to anticipate every field up front.

chunks.heading: How Ruben markets the newsletter (as stated in the essay)
chunks.text:
- He reports 40,000 people opened the email.
- His stated referral math: if 1% forward it to a colleague, that is about 4,000 extra subscribers, which he frames as what keeps the newsletter "free forever."
- He calls his own pitch "the annoying marketing part" and keeps it short and self-aware, a pattern of acknowledging the ask openly instead of hiding it.
- The essay itself is distribution for his free tool: the GPT drives traffic to the newsletter and vice versa.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues that asking ChatGPT to write your prompt gives vague results, because prompting is thinking, not typing. His method: find a reference and convert it to markdown, reverse-engineer it into a short blueprint, write a 4-question success brief, then stack all three into one prompt and keep chatting to steer toward the result.

chunks.heading: Prompting is thinking: prepare three artifacts before you type
chunks.text:
Ruben argues that most bad prompts fail before the first word is typed. "Most people think prompting = typing. But prompting = thinking." The model only knows what you type, so a fuzzy input produces a fuzzy output "every single time."

- He lists three causes of bad prompts: vague descriptions, no definition of what success looks like, and trying to fit everything in one shot.
- He splits LLM requests into two types. Quick requests (a Google-style lookup, finding something in a PDF) don't need a complex prompt, only the right settings. Serious tasks (heavy brainstorming, parsing a legal contract, a multi-step marketing plan, an agency brief) need a specific method.
- His rule: "No, ChatGPT won't help you write better prompts." Asking ChatGPT "Make a prompt for [desired result]" gives a vague, generic prompt.
- He admits that his own Prompt Maker GPT (built about two years earlier) helped create this belief. He says its prompts beat "Write me an email" but still fall short of the method below.
- Before prompting, he prepares three things: a reference, a blueprint, and a success brief.

chunks.heading: Step A: find a reference and convert it to markdown
chunks.text:
Ruben starts from a real example of the output he wants, not vague inspiration.

- Find something that makes you say "I want exactly this": a contract, memo, proposal, landing page, email or report.
- Convert it to markdown with a tool like MarkdownDown (or any markdown converter) and save the .md file. He calls markdown a text file made for LLMs like ChatGPT. He also quotes the line "AGI will be a single markdown file."
- Use a Project in ChatGPT when the task repeats with the same desired output (weekly reports, client proposals, team updates). Upload the reference once, and every future prompt starts with that context.
- For a one-time task, upload the file straight into the chat. Repeating task means a Project.

chunks.heading: Step B: reverse-engineer the reference into a blueprint
chunks.text:
Ruben uploads the markdown reference and asks the AI to analyze it so it can recreate something similar later. His prompt:

- "Analyze this reference so you can recreate something similar later."
- Ask for a short, actionable blueprint covering what it is, tone, and key patterns, under 100 words total.
- The blueprint should work as instructions: someone who never read the reference could recreate it start to finish. Put everything in a codeblock.
- Save the output. This is the blueprint.

chunks.heading: Step C: fill out a four-question success brief
chunks.text:
The success brief is the only part you actually type. It defines what your version must achieve.

- **Type of output + length:** contract, memo, report, proposal, landing page.
- **Recipient's reaction:** what they should think, feel or do after reading.
- **Does NOT sound like:** what to avoid (generic AI, too casual, too legal, jargon-heavy).
- **Success means:** they sign, approve, reply or take action.

His examples:
- C-level briefing: executive summary, 1 page max; reaction "I understand the situation and know what to decide"; not jargon-heavy consultant speak; success is a decision in the meeting with no follow-up questions.
- Legal contract review: contract risk summary, 2 pages; reaction "I know exactly what to negotiate"; not legalese that needs translating; success is the client walking into the negotiation prepared.

chunks.heading: Step 2: "Show, don't tell" by stacking the artifacts into one prompt
chunks.text:
Once he has the reference, blueprint and success brief, Ruben assembles them in a fixed order.

1. Upload the reference markdown file first.
2. Write: "I uploaded a reference to what I want to achieve. Here's what makes this reference work:" and paste the blueprint (wrapped between ### markers).
3. Write: "Here's what I need for my version:" and paste the success brief (also wrapped in ###).
4. Close with: "Now that you know all of this information, let's create the plan to complete it step by step in a chat (5 steps maximum). Define the outline, and ask me one question so you can move on to the first step."

The AI gets a concrete example to follow, a breakdown of why it works, a brief defining success, and context about your situation. He contrasts this with "write me something like..." and hoping the AI figures it out. He adds that you shouldn't skip chatting with it afterward.

chunks.heading: Chat is the point: why multi-turn beats one shot
chunks.text:
Ruben calls not chatting "the biggest mistake you make when you use AI," regardless of tool (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok or Claude).

- He explains GPT as Generative Pretraining Transformer, roughly "fancy autocomplete machine that replies, using training data."
- He argues the real revolution on November 30th, 2022 was adding "Chat": the ability to discuss, call out mistakes and steer the conversation.
- He says this conversation is now embedded in the technology: when an AI is "thinking," it is talking to itself, and results are much better (smarter, better at following instructions).
- He cites three papers: "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv:2203.02155, 2022), "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (arXiv:2201.11903, 2022), and "A Survey on Multi-Turn Interactions with Large Language Models" (arXiv:2504.04717, 2025).
- The goal is to avoid bloating the chat, so he sets strict guidelines (next section).

chunks.heading: Six rules for steering a chat
chunks.text:
Ruben's rules for chatting with an AI without bloating the context:

1. **Correct errors immediately and explicitly.** When the model makes a factual or logical error or drifts, call it out directly, e.g. "That's incorrect, X is actually Y because [brief reason]. Fix this and continue." Don't let errors compound across turns.
2. **Keep every message concise.** No long preambles, chit-chat or unnecessary politeness. State the correction (if needed), the next instruction and any required context reference. Long user messages bloat the context window and encourage long AI replies.
3. **Reference prior output precisely.** Quote or point to specific parts instead of repeating information, e.g. "In your previous response, you said [short quote]. Build on that by adding..."
4. **Use directive language.** Phrases like "Respond briefly," "One paragraph only," "Bullet points, no fluff," or "Revise your previous answer to be ≤200 words." He says modern models follow these well.
5. **Steer aggressively toward convergence.** Each turn should push closer to the final output, e.g. "Now produce the final version incorporating all fixes" or "Summarize everything so far into a clean, complete answer." Avoid tangents unless strictly necessary.
6. **Reset when the context feels bloated.** If the conversation passes roughly 8-10 meaningful exchanges, or you see repetition or declining quality, copy the current best output, start a new chat, paste it and continue with "Here is the refined version so far, now improve/finish it by..." This avoids token waste and context decay.

chunks.heading: Distribution mechanics: the cheat sheet and subscriber prompt library
chunks.text:
Ruben ends the guide with a lead-magnet offer tied to his newsletter, How to AI.

- He packaged the method into a one-page cheat sheet to bookmark, without the full instructions.
- The cheat sheet sits in his prompt library under a "Cheat Sheet" category, offered as a free gift to people who subscribe to How to AI.
- He cites "230,000 other weekly readers" as the newsletter's size.
- Subscribers who can't find the library link are told to comment under the article, and his team will DM them the link personally.
- He links back to a free companion guide on ChatGPT Projects and settings ("How to better use AI before prompting") for the quick-request case.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues most ChatGPT prompts fail because they are wishes rather than briefs. He lists seven common prompting mistakes with before/after fixes and offers the R-E-X framework (Role, Examples, Expectations). Iterating in short steps beats writing one long prompt.

chunks.heading: Prompts are briefs, not wishes, and Ruben's seven fixes
chunks.text: Ruben's core claim: most ChatGPT prompts fail because they are wishes, not briefs. "Good outputs start with good inputs. Prompting isn't magic; it's a good brief." He says to prompt quicker, not longer, because iteration beats length.

chunks.heading: Sin 1 and 2: No context, vague instructions
chunks.text:
**No context.** The model guesses the job, audience and constraints, and guessing multiplies errors. Fix: add role, task scope and constraints.
- Before: "Analyze this."
- After: "You are a product analyst. Analyze the attached transcript for founders from seed to Series A to find the vision outliers. Output a 5-bullet decision memo. Max 180 words."

**Vague instructions.** The prompt never defined success. Fix: define success and acceptance tests.
- Before: "Write about marketing trends."
- After: "Write a 1,000-word brief on the three most important B2B AI marketing trends for Q3 2025. Include one data point per trend with a source and a one-line implication."

chunks.heading: Sin 3 and 4: Treating AI like Google, asking for everything at once
chunks.text:
**Treating it like Google.** Asking questions is "level 1". Give directives instead. Fix: turn questions into jobs with deliverables.
- Before: "What are good onboarding ideas?"
- After: "Draft a 5-step onboarding flow for a B2B SaaS. Include the email subjects, timing in days, and one KPI per step."

**Asking for everything at once.** One giant ask hides failures and produces spaghetti outputs. Fix: split into steps and chain the outputs.
- Bad: "Create our GTM plan, website copy, and investor memo."
- Step 1: list the 5 core customer jobs-to-be-done, with a one-line pain each.
- Step 2: using the chosen JTBD 2 and 4, write 5 homepage H1 options of 8 words max each.
- Step 3: expand H1 #3 into a 150-word hero section.

chunks.heading: Sin 5: Not iterating
chunks.text:
Ruben's point: "It's a chat. So have a chat with it." The critique-then-revise loop is the key. Example for an article:
1. Ask for 5 potential angles on the topic, aimed at a given audience and niche.
2. Using the chosen angle, ask for 10 SEO-ready titles with one-line summaries.
3. Using the chosen title and one-liner, ask for the article outline.

Each step builds on a choice he made from the previous output, instead of a single "Write the article" request.

chunks.heading: Sin 6 and 7: No format or tone, no examples
chunks.text:
**No format or tone.** Models default to generic structure and a bland voice. Fix: force the shape and the voice.
- Before: "Announce the feature."
- After: "Write a LinkedIn post. 220 words. Hook (2 lines), 3 bullets, one CTA. Tone: direct and practical, no buzzwords, plain English."
- Side note: for LinkedIn posts specifically, he would use easygen instead of ChatGPT.

**No examples.** "Examples are how models learn your taste." Fix: add 1-2 gold standards, and optionally one anti-example.
- After: "Model the tone and density on these two snippets [paste]. Avoid this anti-example [paste]. Keep sentence length under 16 words."

chunks.heading: The R-E-X prompt
chunks.text:
Ruben says the R-E-X prompt "works 99% of the time". It defines a Role, gives Examples and sets Expectations.
- **Role:** who the model is and the constraints of the job (domain, audience, risk tolerance).
- **Examples:** paste one or two gold outputs to imitate, with a short note on why they work. Optional anti-example.
- **Expectations:** format, length, tone, banned words, a scoring rubric and the iteration loop.

Checklist: write the Role line, paste the Examples, set Expectations (format, word range, tone, rubric, loop).

His worked example is a marketing analyst prompt:
- Role: senior marketing analyst for non-technical leadership, plain English, no hype.
- Example to imitate: "CTR 1.8% vs 1.2% (+0.6pp). CPC $2.45 vs $3.10 (−21%). So what: shift budget to exact-match."
- Inputs the user pastes: timeframe, channels, metrics, benchmarks. If anything is missing, the model asks one precise question and stops.
- Task: compare against benchmarks and flag any KPI with a gap of 15% or more, better or worse.
- Output order: Summary (max 5 lines plus one "so what"); Comparisons by channel; Findings (5-7 lines with likely cause and H/M/L confidence); Actions (top 3, with impact %, test days, difficulty L/M/H); Notes (methods and data risks).

chunks.heading: Prompt Maker and the shortcut
chunks.text:
Ruben built a free custom GPT, Prompt Maker, and says he gets nothing from it. Flow: write a bad prompt, receive a better one.
- His self-critique: it sometimes makes the prompt too long, so he trims it before copying and pasting.
- Shortcut if that feels too long: write a quick, clear prompt, then ask ChatGPT to ask you clarification questions. Answering them forces you to be clearer.
- Closing principle: "the more you prompt, the better you are at it."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben Hassid summarizes recent academic papers on prompting modern LLMs. Key lessons: keep questions neutral, drop "step by step", verify every AI-cited source, limit prompts to about 3 rules, and give a clear goal instead of examples. The final "One Prompt" template is paywalled.

chunks.heading: Never use tag questions or leading prompts
chunks.text:
- Ruben cites a Cornell Tech study (Tapan Parikh, 27 Jul 2026) that tested 45 AIs with one-word changes.
- "\[X\] is the better choice, right?" makes new models disagree with you. "\[X\] is the better choice, maybe?" makes all 45 models agree with you more.
- His conclusion: asking an AI for its opinion is a bad idea, because the answer is biased more by how you ask than by the model's actual view.
- Fix: keep it neutral and avoid yes/no questions. Instead of "Buying is the better choice, maybe?", write "Compare buying and renting for my situation."
- His analogy: don't make a friend answer the way you want them to answer.

chunks.heading: "Step by step" no longer helps; a short role does
chunks.text:
- Ruben used to tell everyone to add "Take a deep breath and work on this step by step". That came from the OPRO paper ("Large Language Models as Optimizers", September 2023), which tested Google's PaLM 2-L.
- He says that is outdated: Claude and ChatGPT models are now about 10x more capable, and prompting techniques from that era no longer work.
- He cites an IBM Research paper (Preet, Lin & Patel, 7 May 2026) with 430,738 evaluations across 8 prompting techniques. "Let's think step by step" lost to asking normally.
- The winning combo was the plain question plus a role in a few words, e.g. "…as a reliability engineer". Role prompts ranked on top and chain-of-thought near the bottom.
- Caveat he raises: the paper used "reliability engineer" for every topic (medicine, physics, math), so it is unclear whether picking a well-matched role improves results further.
- Bad pattern: "\[question\] Gather information, devise a plan, answer step by step." Good pattern: "\[question\] . . . as a reliability engineer."

chunks.heading: Don't trust confident AI output; verify every source
chunks.text:
- Ruben cites a Microsoft audit by Mark Russinovich (CTO of Microsoft Azure), Siva Kumar and Salem (1 Jul 2026) of 2.6 million references at top AI conferences.
- Finding: 1 in 4 NeurIPS 2025 papers, which had passed expert peer review, contained a hallucinated citation. Reviewers missed it and scored those papers slightly higher.
- The affected-paper rate rose 1.9x since ChatGPT; one paper had 20 hallucinated references.
- His takeaway: if professional reviewers can't catch hallucinated papers, you won't either, so open every link.
- He admits the practical problem ("who in their right mind will open 210 sources") and says he wishes he could trust AI research more.

chunks.heading: Keep prompts to 3 rules maximum
chunks.text:
- Ruben cites Meta Superintelligence Labs (Mariya Vasileva, 14 Aug 2026), which tested 15 models, including GPT-5.5, Claude Opus and Gemini Pro, on prompts with 1 to 12 rules. An example of 3 rules: "Exactly 3 paragraphs. Under 150 words. No emojis."
- At 8 rules, models get each individual rule right 41% of the time, but satisfy all 8 at once only 5.7% of the time. The gap between per-rule and all-rules success was 35 percentage points at k=8.
- 12 of the 15 models can't reliably hold more than 3 rules.
- Bad example: one LinkedIn-post prompt stacking about 8 constraints (3 paragraphs, under 150 words, no emojis, required keywords, no competitors, end with a question, grade-6 reading level, voice sample).
- Fix, two runs:
  - First run: write the post with 3 rules: must include "AI-native", "workflow", "ship"; no emojis; end with a question.
  - Second run: "Check your draft against each of these requirements ONE AT A TIME, then revise: 3 paragraphs, under 150 words, grade-6 reading level, no competitor mentions."
- His broader lesson: prompt engineering is about giving a clear goal.

chunks.heading: Goals beat examples in modern prompts
chunks.text:
- Ruben cites a study from EPFL, Apple and Mistral AI (Pushkin, Jiang, Lotfi, Sandon, Abbé, 4 Aug 2026) finding that examples in a prompt can hurt modern models.
- Mistral's model scored 74% with the standard examples prompt and 83.8% after the examples were deleted. In his chart, every few-shot configuration sat in the low 70s and zero-shot in the mid 80s.
- Bad prompt: "You are a world-class newsletter strategist", two worked examples, then "Find a plan, and answer step by step: How can I improve my newsletter?"
- Good prompt: state the situation and goal concretely ("My newsletter open rate fell from \[X\]% to \[Y\]% over three months. I send one issue every Tuesday. I did not change the format, the send time, or the subject. What are the most likely causes?") and add "Ask me for the data you need before you answer."
- His summary: "Specifying a goal is the ultimate key to a good prompt."

chunks.heading: How Ruben keeps up with prompt research, and the "One Prompt" template
chunks.text:
- Method: he reads new academic papers daily (arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent, 100+ new AI papers a day) because model behavior changes fast and older techniques go stale.
- He distills the findings into five rules: never end with "right?", skip "step by step", don't trust confidence, stick to 3 rules max, goals over examples.
- He packaged all five into a single reusable "One Prompt" template, plus a keyboard shortcut so it doesn't need to be copy-pasted each time. The template itself is behind the paywall and not covered in the source.
- Distribution note: the essay is a paid Substack post (Aug 19, 2026). He asks readers to save it (about a 15-minute read), send it to anyone searching for better prompts, and share it, saying the newsletter grows from shares and calling it his "weekly north star".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben shares a two-word prompt, "Use ASD-STE100", that forces Claude into simplified technical English and removes typical AI slop patterns. He notes it fits instructions and clear explanations but fails for creative writing and LinkedIn posts. Most of the essay (prompt, research workflow) is paywalled.

chunks.heading: Simplified English as the fix for AI "slop" writing
chunks.text:
- Ruben says people hate AI's default writing style: "It's not [X], it's [Y]", meta commentary, exaggeration, "It's the expression of something", and "that is important" filler.
- He claims a 2-word prompt fixes this for about 80% of chats: "Use ASD-STE100."
- Tested on Claude, he prefers the ASD-STE100 output in every side-by-side comparison. He asked for a calendar, then for more information, and in each case found the STE answer "clearer" and more "direct", describing it as "an organized, desloped Claude".
- He says the trick works on any AI: ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, and coding platforms like Cursor, OpenClaw and Hermes.

chunks.heading: What ASD-STE100 is and why it works on AI
chunks.text:
- ASD-STE100 is simplified English for instructions. It is an international standard for writing clear, simple, safe technical manuals, and is very well known in aerospace.
- Ruben's reasoning: models already know the standard well enough to reply in simplified English when asked to follow it, so the name alone acts as a compact style instruction.
- He treats it as a shortcut: one standard's name replaces a long list of "don't write like AI" rules.

chunks.heading: The /ste Claude skill
chunks.text:
- Ruben built a more rigorous version: a Claude skill that encodes the actual ASD-STE100 rules so Claude "truly" talks like STE instructions.
- He built it with Claude's top model plus Research mode (he names it "Fable-5-High").
- It is a free download as a zip file. Install steps: open Claude, go to "Customize", then "Skills", then "Upload a skill", and drop the zip. It also works on ChatGPT.
- Invoke it with the command "/ste".

chunks.heading: When not to use ASD-STE100
chunks.text:
- Ruben says do not use the prompt or skill all the time. It "falls short on some tasks".
- Creative writing: it is "really bad", for example a poem that is not fun to read.
- LinkedIn posts: "too cold. Almost German."
- Best fit: instructions, explanations, plans and informational answers where clarity and directness matter more than voice.

chunks.heading: Ruben's pre-writing research workflow (partly paywalled)
chunks.text:
- He pairs a copy-and-paste research prompt, run on Claude or ChatGPT before any piece of text, with screen recordings of himself writing.
- The recordings show him writing a newsletter and the matching LinkedIn post live.
- His stated goal: never sounding like an AI, "even when you didn't intend to".
- He cites his own reach as context: newsletter of 885,000 readers and 900,000 LinkedIn followers. (Elsewhere in the same essay he mentions 800,000 people; the figures are not reconciled in the free text.)
- The prompt itself and the rest of the workflow are behind the paywall, so they are not captured here.

chunks.heading: Distribution mechanics visible in the essay
chunks.text:
- He gives away the core trick free in the opening ("You can stop the newsletter here") and asks for 10 more minutes for the skill and workflow, using a free value-first hook.
- He puts a free download (the skill) in the middle and gates the deeper workflow for paid subscribers.
- He asks readers to share: "This newsletter is free because people like you share it to people they love."
- He ends a skill section with a hiring line: "And yes, I am hiring."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains that Claude re-reads the whole conversation on every message, so cost compounds as chats grow. He lists 23 habits, from converting files and planning in Chat to editing instead of following up, to cut token waste and hit limits about once a month.

chunks.heading: Convert files and plan cheap before building expensive
chunks.text:
- Ruben's core model: "Claude counts tokens. A token is roughly a word." Each message makes Claude re-read the entire conversation from the top, so message 1 is cheap but message 30 re-reads 29 prior exchanges first.
- Every habit comes back to one idea: avoid wasting tokens so they can be spent on what matters.
- Documents are costly. A single PDF page costs 1,500 to 3,000 tokens. A full 1000x1000 screenshot is roughly 1,300 tokens; a tight crop can drop under 100. DOCX and PPTX carry invisible metadata bloat.
- Uploading the same 15-page PDF to 4 chats burns 180,000+ tokens on something convertible to about 2,000 tokens of clean text.
- His workflow: open a Google Doc (type doc.new in the URL bar), paste the needed text, download as markdown (.md), upload that.
- Plan in Chat, build in Cowork. Anthropic confirmed file creation (spreadsheets, docs, presentations) uses more of the limit than regular chat. He plans structure, sections and assumptions in Chat, then pastes the result into Cowork (Opus 4.6 + Extended thinking) with "Build this exact file."
- Match product to task: quick question = Chat with Haiku; report from files = Cowork with Opus; chart from data = Code with Sonnet. Chat is lightest, Cowork heaviest. Chat's Research feature also uses a lot of tokens.

chunks.heading: Prompt less, ask more: short prompts, AskUserQuestion, voice input
chunks.text:
- A 500-word prompt costs 500 tokens on every re-read. Instead, write about 15 words and let the AskUserQuestion tool generate clarifying questions once; answers are cheap clicks.
- His go-to prompt, under 30 words, used for about 80% of his Cowork sessions: "I want to [task] to [success criteria]. Read my folder. Ask me questions using AskUserQuestion before you start."
- Keeping a stable prompt structure helps: Anthropic confirmed frequently used similar prompts get partially cached (mechanism unpublished). He recommends a stable prompt library, swapping only the variable part.
- Wispr Flow (voice-to-text) reduces total tokens: typed prompts tend to be lazy ("Make it better"), causing follow-ups that force more re-reads. Speaking gives richer one-shot context, e.g. "The tone is too stiff. I want it to sound like I'm texting a friend who runs a 200-person company. Keep the data but make it casual. Only redo section 2."
- Fewer messages means fewer context reloads.

chunks.heading: Avoid redos, follow-ups and wasted output
chunks.text:
- Don't say "redo the report." Say "only redo section 3. Keep everything else to save tokens." A full redo regenerates all output (e.g. 2,000 output tokens again).
- Add "No commentary. No explanations. Just the output." when the desired result is clear; otherwise Claude's "Happy to help! Here's what I did..." costs tokens.
- Batch tasks into one message: three prompts = three full context reloads, one prompt with three tasks = one reload. Example: "Summarize this article, list the main points, and suggest a headline." Answers also tend to be better with the full picture.
- In Chat, use the Edit button on the original message and regenerate, instead of sending "No, I meant..." or "Actually, change X to Y". The old exchange is replaced, not stacked. He calls it his favorite hack and uses it constantly.
- In Cowork, where prompts can't be edited, use "Restart the conversation from here" on an earlier message. The higher up, the more tokens saved. If the whole session went sideways, start fresh with a one-line summary.

chunks.heading: Keep conversations short and start fresh deliberately
chunks.text:
- Cost grows fast: a 20-message session burns roughly 105,000 tokens; a 30-message session roughly 232,000.
- He cites a developer who tracked usage and found 98.5% of tokens went to re-reading history and only 1.5% to actual output.
- Every 15-20 messages, ask Claude to summarize what matters, copy the summary, open a new session, and paste it as the first message.
- At the end of a Cowork session, prompt "Write a session-notes.md with the key decisions and next steps." Next session start with "Read session-notes.md first."
- New topic = new chat, always. Old messages about a LinkedIn post or client proposal remain dead weight when asking about dinner.

chunks.heading: Trim context: files, folders, features, memory
chunks.text:
- Cowork reads the folder before every task. His about-me file was 22,000 words; he trimmed it to under 2,000. Rule: keep ABOUT ME files under 2,000 words each.
- Don't dump 50 files "just in case"; oversized files also get summarized loosely. For tasks needing no files (e.g. an email draft via a connector), select zero folders.
- Turn off unused features: web search, connectors and "Explore" mode add tokens to every response. His default is everything off, enabled per task. (He still uses Extended thinking almost always, but pays for the $100 plan.)
- Be specific with connectors: "Search Slack from the last 7 days for messages about the Q2 launch" beats "Search Slack for anything about launches."
- Use Projects for recurring documents: upload once, it is cached and referenced by all chats in the project without re-tokenizing. Anthropic confirmed reused project content doesn't count like fresh uploads. On paid plans Projects use RAG, retrieving only relevant chunks. Useful for contracts, brand guides, research papers.
- Turn Memory off (he always does) and set Settings > General > Personal preferences plus Styles (e.g. "Concise" or custom) so new chats skip 3-5 setup messages.

chunks.heading: Model choice, Claude Code and scheduling
chunks.text:
- Use Sonnet or Haiku for grammar checks, brainstorming, reformatting, short answers. "Opus + Extended thinking is your heavy machinery. Don't use heavy machinery to move a chair." His rule: if Claude would answer in under 30 seconds, it probably doesn't need Opus. Switch models before the session (2 clicks, sometimes under "More models").
- Scheduled tasks: for weekly reports, digests or research, use the /schedule plugin instead of a growing Cowork session.
- Claude Code: he uses it for briefs for his tech team and quick data visualizations. It goes wide (explores files, reads directories) unless scoped. Example: "Create a bar chart from this CSV showing monthly revenue for 2025. Save it as chart.png."
- CLAUDE.md loads every task, so put recurring instructions there (folder, language, naming conventions) but keep it short; Anthropic warns bloated files make Claude ignore instructions. Move occasional workflows into Skills, which load on demand.

chunks.heading: Plans, timing and using the right tool for the job
chunks.text:
- Claude uses a rolling 5-hour usage window. Burning the whole limit in one morning wastes daily capacity; split into 2-3 sessions (morning, afternoon, evening) so earlier usage rolls off.
- Ruben pays $100/month specifically to avoid worrying about this; he moved up from the $20 plan after hitting limits by 2 pm. With the habits he now hits his limit about once a month.
- Don't use Claude for what it's bad at: it can't generate images (use Gemini instead of spending 5 messages on workarounds); for real-time search he says Grok is faster and more accurate. He notes ChatGPT has recently been good at both.

chunks.heading: Where to start (his prioritization)
chunks.text:
- Pick 3 habits, not all 23.
- Daily Cowork users: habits 1 (convert files), 2 (plan in Chat), 5 (no full redos).
- Mostly Chat users: 8 (edit instead of correcting), 15 (new chat per topic), 17 (Projects).
- $20-plan users hitting limits: 6 (batch prompts), 13 (cheaper models), 22 (spread sessions across the day).
- Distribution note: his free articles routinely get 1,000+ shares, which he calls his "north star" and says keeps the newsletter free; he asks readers to share with colleagues in Teams or Slack groups.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains how employees who use personal ChatGPT or Claude accounts at work can cut their legal and career risk. He covers switching off model training, anonymizing data, using temporary chats and avoiding connectors, then points readers to his paid tiers and consulting.

chunks.heading: Setting up personal AI accounts for work: the privacy checklist
chunks.text: Ruben's premise: most employees already use personal ChatGPT or Claude accounts at work because the company pays for nothing or for the wrong tool ("ahem… Copilot"). He argues the risk is real but manageable, and he lays out a setup routine ("block 10 min this week & set up your account right"). His closing thesis is that the real fix is a company-paid AI plus team training.

chunks.heading: How common shadow AI use is
chunks.text:
He cites these figures (he attributes the first to an MIT study):
- Workers at more than 90% of companies use personal chatbots for work, mostly without telling IT.
- 57% have typed sensitive information into one at least once.
- 22% still use a personal AI even where the company already pays for an AI tool.

His takeaway is "you're normal", but you can't keep doing it without fixes first.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Turn off model training on personal plans
chunks.text:
On personal plans (free or paid), the AI provider may train on your chats by default.
- **Claude:** Anthropic changed its consumer terms in August 2025. On Free, Pro and Max, chats and coding sessions are used to improve Claude unless you opt out, and conversations can be kept for up to 5 years. Path: profile > Settings > Privacy > turn off "Help improve our AI models".
- **ChatGPT:** profile > Settings > Data controls > turn off "Improve the model for everyone".
- **Grok:** profile > settings > data controls > turn off everything.
- **Gemini:** harder. Use myactivity.google.com/u/1/product/gemini and turn it off there; he found no easier way.
- The opt-out only applies going forward, to new and resumed conversations. Conversations already in a started training run are not pulled back, and models can't "unlearn" data, so turning it off sooner keeps more data out.
- He added an update for the new Claude Fable 5, whose footnote means (in his reading) "we will take your data for 30 days". His advice: "Use it at your own risk."

chunks.heading: Step 2: Understand the firing and legal risk
chunks.text:
He says both firings and lawsuits have happened, with the caveat that he is "not a lawyer" and is citing public cases.
- **Samsung, April 2023:** engineers allowed to use ChatGPT leaked internal source code three times within 20 days (code pasted to find bugs, more code uploaded to fix defects, and a recording of an internal meeting). Samsung banned ChatGPT company-wide and opened disciplinary investigations.
- **NDA breach:** a chatbot run by another company counts as an outside party.
- **Trade secrets:** under the US Defend Trade Secrets Act, a secret stays legally secret only while kept secret, so handing it to a third party under loose terms can undermine the company's own protection.
- **GDPR (Europe):** pasting a customer's name, email or phone number into a personal account can make the company liable for an unlawful data transfer. He cites West Technology Group v. Sundstrom, where a salesperson recorded confidential meetings with an AI tool and kept access after leaving; the company sued.
- **His test before pasting:** "Would I be fine if this exact text showed up in the company-wide channel, with my name on it?" If yes, paste. If no, anonymize it or use the company's tool.

chunks.heading: Step 3: What never to paste into a personal account
chunks.text:
- Source code or anything from the company codebase
- Customer or patient data (names, emails, phones, addresses, order history, health info)
- Unreleased plans, roadmaps, designs, prototypes
- Non-public financials (revenue, margins, budgets, forecasts, deal terms)
- Anything marked confidential, internal-only or under NDA
- Logins, passwords, access keys, security settings
- Full contracts or legal docs with real names and terms
- Recordings or transcripts of internal meetings

Side-project warning: if you use your company's AI to vibecode a side project, "your company now owns your project". Vibecoding with your personal AI on the company's computer is also risky: "Just don't do it."

chunks.heading: Step 4: Anonymize before you paste
chunks.text:
The AI only needs the shape of the problem, not the identifying details.
1. Swap names for roles ("the client", "Company A", "Project X").
2. Use fake values of similar size (real numbers become fake numbers; emails become name@example.com).
3. Paste only what is needed. Don't upload the original PDF or spreadsheet, which can carry author names, comments, tracked changes and hidden columns. Copy out the relevant part.

Example he gives:
- Don't: "Draft a renewal email to Sarah Chen at Medtronic. Their $2.3M contract expires Aug 31 and they're unhappy about support delays."
- Do: "Draft a renewal email to a client contact. Their $5M contract expires end of next month, and they're unhappy about support delays."

Anonymizing "drops your risk a lot" but "doesn't make it zero". For truly regulated data (health records, legal files, anything re-identifiable), the only clean answer is a company-paid AI.

chunks.heading: Step 5: Use temporary chats for work tasks
chunks.text:
Even with training off, normal chats save to account history. For work tasks, start a temporary chat before typing:
- Claude: "Incognito" (top right)
- ChatGPT and Gemini: "Temporary chat"
- Grok: "Private chat"

A temporary chat isn't saved to history and isn't used for training. Close it and it's gone. He suggests making it the default for private chats.

chunks.heading: Step 6: Connectors are the most dangerous feature
chunks.text:
Connectors (integrations or "apps" linking Gmail, Drive, Calendar, Slack, Teams, Outlook) are, in his words, "the most dangerous thing you can do with a personal AI account."
- **Access is enormous:** Gmail exposes the whole mailbox; Drive exposes every file you can open, including old shared documents. Connecting work Gmail to a personal AI pipes the company inbox into a tool the company has no contract with.
- **Hijack risk:** researchers showed twice in 2025 that a connected AI can be tricked by content it reads. He calls the cause the "lethal trifecta": an AI that can reach private data, read outside content you don't control, and send information out can be made to steal your data.
- **Rules:**
  1. Never connect work accounts to a personal AI.
  2. Connect the least, with the narrowest access (read-only or a single folder; if you can paste the one thing you need, skip the connector).
  3. Use only official connectors from the AI's own directory; a remote third-party connector can quietly change behavior after approval.
  4. Review and disconnect monthly, including the Google or Microsoft "third-party access" page.
- His conclusion: connect almost nothing on a personal account and save the connected setup for the company tool, where someone is paid to secure it.

chunks.heading: The best solution and Ruben's funnel
chunks.text:
His top fix: get the company to pay for the best AI and train the team on it. He notes that Microsoft Copilot "isn't the best AI out there".

His tiered offer, framed by what people can afford:
- Free: this newsletter, read by about 700,000 people ("Go & do it yourself!").
- Paid: 3,659 paying subscribers get access to his Circle community, to "figure things out together".
- Workshops: live, starting with mastering Claude Cowork, via a separate free email list (how-to-ai.co/interested).
- Enterprise: a consulting firm in NYC that helps "dozens of enterprises" adopt AI (a lot of Claude). He limits it to 3 new clients per month, with a minimum team size of 50 people.

chunks.heading: Distribution approach
chunks.text: He says the newsletter grows from shares and that he keeps hitting 1,000+ shares per post, calling it his "north star". He repeats share prompts throughout the post ("Sharing is free & helps others use AI more safely") and ends with explicit asks to save and send it to colleagues. He also embeds consulting and workshop calls to action inside a practical, fear-driven safety guide.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben reverses his earlier advice to build Cowork around folders and files. He now recommends only Skills for repeatable capabilities and Projects for specific contexts, with minimal settings, voice dictation, and tactics to cut token costs. He also covers shared team projects and onboarding new hires with Claude.

chunks.heading: Ruben's current Claude Cowork setup: Skills plus Projects, no folders
chunks.text:
- Ruben says he was wrong about his earlier Cowork guides ("Cowork" and "Cowork 2.0", about 20 million views combined) and tells people not to read them.
- He still stands by the prediction that Claude will become bigger than ChatGPT because of Cowork, launched in January. He has urged people to switch to Claude since December 21st 2025.
- His claim: "If you don't code, you must be using Claude Cowork."
- What broke the old setup: enterprise workshops with teams of hundreds using Cowork together. His files-and-folders system didn't work for collaboration.
- He says how Anthropic wants people to use the product differs from how people actually use it. He isn't paid by Anthropic, so he says whatever setup works best.
- Access:
  - Download the app at claude.com/download.
  - A Pro account ($20/month) is required. He pays for the $100/month plan.
  - Click the Cowork tab between Chat and Code.
  - Use Opus for complex tasks. He uses Opus 4.8 (High) most of the time, Max effort when needed, and Fable-5 once available.
- Why Cowork beats normal Claude: it answers with many Claude sessions at once. One session reads the Excel, another searches the web, another plans. Tasks can run 30+ minutes. One example took 8 minutes of many sessions from a single prompt.

chunks.heading: Why he dropped folders and files for Cowork
chunks.text:
His old setup was a local Cowork folder with an "about-me" file and an "output" file or folder, selected at the start of each session. After months of use he found two problems:

1. **Folders leak.** Even when told "never check my output folder," Claude sometimes read it, poisoning context with outdated outputs.
2. **Files are impossible to maintain.** Nobody with a full-time job can spend hours a week updating an about-me file. It became a painful bottleneck.

- He also says he rarely opens Claude's output files anyway. He exports spreadsheets, text docs, PDFs and slides to Google Drive with one button (the Google Drive integration, opening as Google Sheets/Docs).
- His conclusion: "You really don't need folders."

chunks.heading: Skills vs Projects: the core of the new setup
chunks.text:
- **Skill** = a capability you call with a slash command (e.g. /linkedin-post). It travels into any chat, and into other AIs like Gemini or ChatGPT.
- **Project** = a place you go to. Files and instructions stay loaded, it remembers, and it can be shared with a team. Every chat in a Project has the full Project context, and it doesn't pollute chats outside it.
- His test:
  - A skill you can teach someone → **Skill**.
  - A specific context (a client, a campaign) → **Project**.
- Teach teams the difference. Otherwise they end up with hundreds of skills that should be a few projects, or dozens of projects that should be shared skills.
- Best practice is to combine them:
  1. Make skills for your most recurring capabilities (e.g. drafting a contract).
  2. Run them inside a client Project with that client's information uploaded.
  3. Connect Gmail/Outlook and Slack/Teams first for extra context.
- His team gets access to his skills and projects in their own Claude.
- Some skills carry hundreds of pages of posts, hooks and SOPs as data.

**Ways to create a skill**
- Use Claude's built-in /skill-creator, answer its questions, test, save, then invoke it with the slash command.
- Use his free tool makemyskill.com (free account, no paid version). It scrapes the web more deeply than Claude usually does. Download the skill, then go to Cowork > Customize > Skills > Add > Create skill > Upload a skill.
- Ask Claude in an existing chat to "make it a skill."
- Run Research in Chat on a topic (he pasted a tweet praising experts). Claude generated a deep research report and decided to create 7 skills from it.
- His advice: create many skills, test them, improve them.

**Sharing**
- Projects: create them in Chat (not Cowork), make sure they're set to shared (top right), then start any task from Cowork. He admits "It's weird, I know."
- Skills: Customize > Skills > click one > Share > select the workspace.

**Problems he dislikes**
- Skills can auto-fire from their description. He wants a switch to only activate on invocation.
- Projects have a file-upload limit.

chunks.heading: His minimal settings philosophy
chunks.text:
- His belief: "you shouldn't give too many instructions to an AI." Too much context makes Claude fall into the same answers every time and lose creativity. That's fine for drafting the same contract, but bad for brainstorming.
- His current setup:
  1. No folders.
  2. Minimal account settings, with no personal info given.
  3. Everything off except Connectors (the + menu, e.g. Gmail) and the setting that enables interactive charts.
  4. Global Instructions kept free of context.
- Instead of settings, use Skills for recurring tasks, Projects for recurring projects, and AskUserQuestion to prompt better.
- Turn the old about-me file into a skill so it's invoked only when wanted.

chunks.heading: The AskUserQuestion trick
chunks.text:
- His #1 trick. Prompt Claude to use AskUserQuestion and it builds a form you answer. Claude then thinks more about how to reply, giving a much better output.
- It works for follow-ups too. Claude keeps interviewing you until there's enough context that failure is hard.
- When you don't know what to ask next, ask Claude to ask you.
- His view: most people don't know how to prompt LLMs. It takes practice and an understanding of how the technology works, since models are built to answer rather than state truth, which causes hallucination.

**Spreadsheet prompt template**
```
Create an Excel spreadsheet from: [DATA]
Purpose: [who uses it, what decision it supports, 1 sentence]
Sheets needed: "[Sheet name]": [columns, row meaning, calculations]
Formatting: [currency/date formats, conditional highlighting, frozen header, totals row]
Before building, list your top 10 assumptions so I can sanity-check them, then execute.
```
- His example was a customer support capacity and cost model for a B2B SaaS company with 4,800 accounts growing 8% month-over-month. It had 7 sheets (Assumptions, Ticket Forecast, Capacity Plan, Cost Model, SLA & CX, Dashboard, Scenarios).
- Key rule: every assumption is an editable, labeled input, never hardcoded in a formula.
- To edit afterward, go back to Cowork (ask Claude to ask you what to change), or use the free ChatGPT extension in Google Sheets (Extensions > ChatGPT, Heavy mode).
- He says he tested every way to create spreadsheets with AI and Cowork is the best.

chunks.heading: Onboarding new employees with Claude
chunks.text:
1. Create a Claude Project with the company mission, deck, CEO/C-level interviews, and support best practices (which usually cover everything a new hire should know).
2. Invite the new hire to the Project.
3. Add a skill called /answer-onboarding that explains how to use the Project data to answer onboarding questions.
4. New hires start with the Project, run /answer-onboarding plus their question.

His company rules:
- "Please ask me as many questions as possible. Failing is winning."
- "Never ask me a question before giving me a potential answer."
- Find the potential answer via project plus skill first. This shifts people from "I'm new, I can't think for myself" to "I work actively to find the answer, but I still need help."

chunks.heading: Picking the right tool, and speeding up with voice
chunks.text:
**Which tool**
- **Chat**: nothing to build, nowhere to keep it; a question or quick rewrite.
- **Claude Code**: the deliverable is software.
- **Cowork**: everything document-shaped (decks, analysis, client work).
- He references how-to-ai.guide for the visual.

**Voice with Wispr Flow**
- His claim: "its biggest blocker is most of the time… you."
- Typical session time he cites: prompt 30 seconds; skills read 50 seconds; plan 50 seconds; clarifying questions 50 seconds. Answering around 8 questions at 60 seconds to 2 minutes each means 8-15 minutes of the human being the slow part.
- Typing is about 60 words per minute; speaking is about 150.
- Wispr Flow is a dictation tool: hold a key (he uses Shift), talk, release, and the words appear wherever the cursor is, including Cowork's chat box. No integration needed.
- Free tier is 2,000 words/week. Paid newsletter subscribers get a free month (not required).
- The bigger benefit is richer context: people give more context when talking ("we are yappers by nature"), and speaking feels natural and puts you in flow state.
- Use it for three things:
  1. The initial prompt.
  2. AskUserQuestion custom answers (dictated, no self-editing).
  3. Feedback and pivots, e.g. "The tone is too stiff... like I'm texting a friend who runs a 200-person company. Only redo section 2."

chunks.heading: Saving tokens and money in Cowork
chunks.text:
His framing: at company scale, saving tokens saves thousands of dollars.

1. **Restart instead of following up.** Claude counts tokens, not messages, and re-reads the whole history every turn.
   - His figures: message 30 costs 31x more than message 1; at about 500 tokens per exchange, 20 messages burn 105K tokens and 30 messages burn 232K.
   - Use "Restart the conversation from here" on an earlier message (higher is better), or Edit your own prompt, which deletes what follows. He calls it "the biggest hack."
2. **Fresh session every 20 messages.** He cites one developer who found 98.5% of tokens went to re-reading history and 1.5% to output. Ask Claude to summarize, copy it, start a new session, and paste the summary first.
3. **Batch tasks into one message.** Three prompts means three context reloads; one prompt with three tasks means one. Wispr Flow helps with this.
4. **Use Sonnet or Haiku for quick tasks** (grammar, brainstorming, formatting, short answers). He says this frees 30-70% of budget for deep work. Save Opus with extended thinking for hard work.
5. **Fable-5 ("Mythos-level")** is better than Opus for the hardest tasks but the most token-intensive. He uses it freely on the $100 plan with no problems, since his team doesn't code and so uses fewer tokens.
6. **Spread work across the day.** Claude uses a rolling 5-hour window; split into 2-3 sessions and avoid peak hours (5-11 AM Pacific on weekdays). He admits he never does this: "If I want to work, I work."

- His view on cost: "a couple of dollars per day is worth it to have a godlike intelligence by my side."

chunks.heading: First 20 minutes, and how Ruben monetizes
chunks.text:
**Setup plan**
- 0-3 min: empty your settings, turn everything off.
- 3-8: build your first Skill (something you keep doing).
- 8-13: create your first Project (upload a client's PDFs, Excels).
- 13-17: use the skill inside the Project.
- 17-20: download his Claude Skills library (free in his welcome email).
- Creating skills should be the priority once Cowork is set up.

**Business model and positioning**
- His newsletter is free; he makes money consulting for companies of 50-500 employees with his team in NYC (about 20 people), through discovery calls and tailored enterprise AI workshops.
- In the PS he targets companies with 100+ people, arguing that AI adoption is "not a 'send them a newsletter' problem. It is a systems problem" (different roles, clients, tools, workflows, permissions, data, risks, habits). Workshops map where AI saves time, where it shouldn't be used, and how to adopt it without chaos.
- Audience and positioning: about 750,000 readers; he publishes twice a week; he wants to be the "filter to the noise": what to ignore and what to set up this weekend.
- Growth and lead-gen mechanics:
  - A free skills library is given to new subscribers in the welcome email, and to existing subscribers by comment and DM.
  - A free tool (makemyskill.com) is "free because it costs almost nothing to run."
  - Share and thank-the-sender calls to action appear throughout.
  - A paid-subscriber perk is a free month of Wispr Flow.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues that LinkedIn growth comes from writing good, targeted posts around one clear mission, not from pods, automations or AI comment spam. He covers profile setup (headline, featured link, experience section) and a Mission + Solution + Angle + Format post framework. The essay is paywalled, so the step-by-step 0 to 10,000 plan is not visible.

chunks.heading: Ruben's LinkedIn thesis: win by solving one problem, consistently
chunks.text:
- Ruben reached 650,000 followers on LinkedIn. His blog on getting the first 10,000 is framed as how he would start over.
- 10,000 followers is not "being successful". Doing it the right way, and continuing to do it, is what makes you successful.
- Wrong ways he rejects:
  - Cold email automations.
  - Joining pods to cheat the system.
