  - Spreading AI comments "like the plague".
  - Copy-pasting what another successful person did.
  - LinkedIn AI agents pretending to connect with leads.
  - Posting at an exact "right time" because a blog said so.
- The right way is writing good posts. Good means targeted, helpful, consistent, and getting better over time.

chunks.heading: Find one mission: one problem only
chunks.text:
- Ruben says most people's LinkedIn topics are too broad. Half the posts resonate with the community and the other half don't, so focus is needed.
- Rule: solve one problem, and one only. His own: "How to AI with English, not code." He does not post about robots, coding or politics.
- Test: if you can't explain your mission in one sentence, you need help.
- Examples of one-clear-mission creators he likes:
  - Justin Welsh: run a solopreneur business without ruining your life.
  - Codie Sanchez: own a small, profitable business.
  - Rory Flynn: AI for images and videos.
  - Dan Go: why to get and stay fit.
  - Reno Perry: land better jobs.
- He built a free "Mission-GPT" in ChatGPT to help people define their mission.

chunks.heading: Profile setup, element by element
chunks.text:
- Colors and fonts: he made a free "Color Theory" GPT to pick them.
- Profile picture: HD 1080 x 1080, super-zoomed, smiling, clear background. AI image tool Flux (not affiliated) is an option.
- Banner: HD 1584 x 396 px that says one thing. A slideshow banner is available with paid LinkedIn and surprises people.
- Headline: the mission with a twist, cheeky and clear.
  - Mission: "How to AI with English, not code."
  - Headline: "Master AI before it masters you."
- Featured section: one link, big text, no description.
  - No description means one click goes straight to the website. "Less clicks = More conversions."
  - Don't feature your best posts; he finds it weird.
- About section: he deliberately has none, so visitors reach the featured section faster.
- Experience section: put "who you are" here and write a lot, extensively. When people ask ChatGPT or Perplexity "Who is Ruben Hassid?", the answer mostly comes from his LinkedIn experience tab.
- LinkedIn Premium: gives the special link under your name when posting. "More links visible = More clicks = More conversions."

chunks.heading: Post formula: Mission + Solution + Angle + Format
chunks.text:
- Mission is the one problem. A post is one of many solutions to it.
- A post needs the right solution, the right angle on that solution, and the right format for that angle.
- Worked example for a finance creator:
  - Mission: make investing understandable for rookies.
  - Solution: what is an ETF?
  - Angle: explain ETFs like grocery shopping.
  - Format: infographic.
- Workflow:
  1. Research with Perplexity (select "Research"). Prompt: "Act like an experienced financial educator; explain ETFs through grocery-shopping analogies, contrast them with stocks & mutual funds."
  2. Design: search Pinterest for "ETF infographic" or "Finance infographic", copy and improve it, use Canva, or pay a cheap designer.
  3. Caption: paste the research as "Topic" into EasyGen.io.
- EasyGen bonus for repurposing viral posts: Trending tab, find the highest "Outlier Index" (most viral), click "Repurpose", add a new topic, get a new viral post. He notes few people will do it, and those who do win more.

chunks.heading: Consistency: 30-day content calendar
chunks.text:
- After one good post, the question is how to do it every day.
- He made a free "Calendar GPT" that turns a viral post into a content calendar.
- His sequence to start: mission, a good profile, three posts, a monthly calendar.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben explains why he stopped using ChatGPT for a month and moved his AI work to Claude Cowork. He gives four reasons (follows long instructions, avoids infinite loops, no memory overfitting, creates real files) and five non-technical use cases. The core lesson: control the full context yourself and think in workflows, not tools.

chunks.heading: Why Ruben quit ChatGPT for Claude Cowork
chunks.text:
- Ruben says he went almost a month (as of Feb 2026) without opening ChatGPT because of Claude Cowork. He says he is non-technical and doesn't know how to code, and that anyone can replicate his setup.
- His claim: "Claude Cowork replaced ChatGPT and any other AI." He still uses Gemini sometimes (images, videos) and Grok sometimes (to search).
- He frames Cowork as "a philosophy more than a tool". Just as learning to prompt ChatGPT teaches you to prompt any AI, the lesson is to think "This is how things can be done" rather than "This is the right tool."
- He calls it the tool that changed how he works more than any since the original ChatGPT launch, while admitting it isn't perfect.
- Setup:
  - Install the Claude app.
  - Use a Pro account (he quotes seventeen dollars a month).
  - Open the "Cowork" tab.
- Reader comments note Cowork was macOS only at the time.

chunks.heading: Reason 1: It follows long instructions, so context quality compounds
chunks.text:
- Ruben's complaint about ChatGPT: you give it a 500-word prompt with context, requirements, formatting rules, do's and don'ts, and it ignores half. When reminded, it apologizes, then ignores the other half.
- In Cowork he uploads:
  - His voice profile (over 2,000 words on how he writes, what he hates, phrases he never uses, preferred structures).
  - His copywriting rules.
  - Reference documents.
- He says it reads and follows all of it, so output sounds like him, not "AI trying to sound like me."
- His principle: the quality of AI output depends on how much context you can give. If the AI ignores your context, you're stuck with generic results.

chunks.heading: Reason 2: Long sessions without the infinite loop
chunks.text:
- ChatGPT problem he describes: about 45 minutes into a complex task it repeats itself, contradicts earlier statements, or loops on apologies and the same wrong output, so you restart or give up.
- In Cowork he has run 2-hour sessions with back-and-forth, revisions and mid-conversation pivots. His four observations:
  1. It doesn't lose the thread.
  2. It doesn't get trapped.
  3. It remembers what was decided 90 minutes earlier and builds on it.
  4. It creates a form to ask him about a new direction when he's unhappy with the output.
- His principle: real work takes time and multiple pivots. If your AI breaks after 20-minute sessions, you can only do small tasks, which is a ceiling on what's possible.
- His rescue prompt when things go wrong, using the AskUserQuestion tool so Claude prompts him:
  - "We are getting sidetricked. We need to start over without losing the context of this chat. First, generate a first AskUserQuestion form for me to answer so we get to decide what went wrong and where we must go instead. From my answer, generate a second AskUserQuestion form to now be able to complete the task."
- Summary line: "Claude Cowork is the one prompting me."

chunks.heading: Reason 3: No memory is a feature (avoiding overfitting)
chunks.text:
- Ruben argues ChatGPT's cross-conversation memory causes what he calls overfitting. It matches what you said last week too hard, makes assumptions from stale context, and gets weird in ways that are hard to diagnose.
- Cowork starts fresh every time. He gives context explicitly, per conversation and per task, usually via his markdown files. His line: "I decide what matters. Not some algorithm guessing."
- He concedes an AI that knew exactly when to pull the right past information would be great, but says it doesn't work that way today. So use AI the way it works best: control the full context before starting the task.
- Tactic: if you're tired of introducing yourself, create a markdown file with everything about you and upload it to any AI at the start of conversations when necessary.

chunks.heading: Reason 4: It creates real files, not text to copy-paste
chunks.text:
- ChatGPT gives text you copy, paste into another tool and format yourself, "every single time." Cowork writes the actual files into your folder:
  - Presentation request gives real slides.
  - Spreadsheet request gives an Excel file with working formulas.
  - Document request gives a formatted Word file.
- Cowork can generate slides, Excel and PDFs inside your computer.

chunks.heading: Five things he built with Cowork
chunks.text:
**Slides via Gamma.** Gamma is his favorite AI for slides, and Cowork connects to it. His process:
1. Tell Cowork what you need.
2. Use the AskUserQuestion tool so Claude prompts you on the outline.
3. Once the outline is good, create content for each slide.
4. Final prompt: "Use Gamma MCP connector to create the slide in [style]."

**Triage a huge reading pile.** He is writing a book with a publishing house, which sent him 4,992 files. He asks Cowork what he should really read and why.

**Excel.** Cowork absorbs existing Excel files and produces an upgraded version. He separately wrote a newsletter on Claude in Excel.

**Expense report from receipts.** 47 receipts from a work trip.
- Old way: open each photo, read amounts, type into a spreadsheet, categorize, total. At least 2 hours.
- His prompt: "Create expense report. Categorize by type. Include date, vendor, amount. Calculate totals."
- Result: an Excel file with every receipt logged, dates extracted, vendors identified, categories assigned and totals calculated.
- Claude flagged 3 blurry receipts ("Could not read clearly. Please verify."). He filled 3 cells manually. Total time: 10 minutes.

**Research brief with sources.** For a newsletter on AI agents.
- Old way: 23 browser tabs, quotes pasted into a doc, losing track of sources.
- His prompt: "Research AI agents in 2026. Major players, product launches, company use cases. Create a brief I can reference while writing."
- Result: a markdown file organized by theme, with key points summarized and source links, in about 2 minutes and without opening a browser tab.

chunks.heading: Going from top 1% to top 0.1% in AI, and his offer
chunks.text:
- He sees three ways to move from top 1% to top 0.1% in AI:
  1. Play with AI. He notes you learned through games as a kid.
  2. Use AI without its current limitations. He says Cowork has the fewest today.
  3. Join a community of obsessed AI users, such as his Slack with 1,000+ professionals.
- Consulting offer: he consults Fortune 500 companies in the US to deploy this system, setting up Claude Cowork per department and duplicating seniors' knowledge. He had a spot left for Q2, taken via LinkedIn DM.
- Content approach: he teased plugins and connectors for Cowork as a future newsletter and asked readers what he should cover next, saying his team uses Claude to select the best comment suggestions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues AI removes the friction of both starting and stopping, so people ship more but move in the wrong direction. He names the enemy "performative productivity" and gives 5 rules plus two prompts to pick one goal and audit your week against it. He backs it with an 8-month Harvard study showing AI intensifies work.

chunks.heading: AI removes the friction of stopping, so people work more, not less
chunks.text:
Ruben argues that AI did not reduce workload; it intensified it. He says he met "dozens of people this year" who work past midnight, ship more than ever, feel productive, and are also more stressed, lost and exhausted. His diagnosis: most AI users sprint fast in the wrong direction.

- Every earlier tool (Excel, email, Google search) felt like work. Prompting feels like chatting with a friend, so it doesn't register as work.
- People prompt before bed, at lunch, in meetings and while files load.
- "AI removes the friction of *starting*. That's great. But it also removes the friction of *stopping*. And if stopping feels harder than continuing, you have an addiction."
- Doing more is not the same as doing better.

chunks.heading: Harvard 8-month study: three ways AI intensifies work
chunks.text:
Ruben cites a Harvard (HBR, Feb 2026) 8-month study at a 200-person tech company where nobody was forced to use AI, yet everyone ended up working more. Three patterns appeared across the board:

- **Role creep:** people did other people's jobs because AI made it feel easy. Product managers wrote code, researchers did engineering tasks, and everyone absorbed work that used to require extra hires.
- **Work spilling into breaks:** evenings, lunches, commutes and "quick 5 minutes." The casual, conversational style of prompting let work into the time the brain needs to recover.
- **More multitasking:** multiple AI threads at once, constant output-checking, a permanent state of juggling.

Every person in the study felt more productive, and most felt busier. Ruben paraphrases one engineer: you thought you'd work less because AI makes you faster, but you work the same or more.

chunks.heading: The real enemy: performative productivity
chunks.text:
Ruben calls the hidden problem "performative productivity." His scenario: it's 11 pm, you shipped a landing page, rewrote the sales deck, drafted a content calendar, fixed an email sequence, and you can't name one thing that moved you forward. The common complaint he hears is "I did so much today, and I have nothing to show for it."

- AI lets you skip the hardest part of work: deciding what's worth doing.
- Before AI, starting something was hard, which forced you to ask whether it was worth starting. Now you type a sentence and something exists, so nobody pauses to ask "does this actually matter?"
- The result is momentum that is circular: fast movement, no progress.
- He is still pro "fast shipping + 'show don't tell' using AI" ("It's magic"), but says you must fight directionlessness so you pursue something worth pursuing.

chunks.heading: Ruben's 5 rules against performative productivity (his own company gameplan)
chunks.text:
1. **Write one sentence about what you're solving before you prompt.** If you can't state the problem in one sentence, AI generates noise you then spend the night editing. Example: "Grow my newsletter 10% faster."
2. **Kill 3 tasks for every 1 task AI helps you add.** AI makes adding easy and nobody teaches subtraction. For each new thing shipped, ask which 3 things to stop. He calls this taste: saying no to more things so you can say yes to the right ones.
3. **Set a "last prompt" time.** Like a cutoff for email, set a hard stop for AI. His example: after 8 pm, no prompts. He has talked to people prompting at midnight or 2 am ("just one more"). "The most productive behavior you can have is to rest. The work will be there tomorrow. Your brain won't be if you don't let it rest."
4. **Ask whether you're doing more things or the right things.** If you can't honestly say you're closer to your actual goal, "you're busy. Not productive." He uses a matrix (from his "Happy New AI Year" post) and shares a Google Sheets template to build your own.
5. **AI writes v1, but you decide whether v1 should exist at all.** He calls this the most important rule. That AI can draft something in 30 seconds doesn't mean it should be drafted. Illustration: anyone can make a LinkedIn post in 30 seconds, but very few can grow an account to 10,000 followers in 17 days (he says his team did, going from 49 to 10,000 followers in 17 days). If the answer to "does this need to exist?" is "I don't know, but it's easy, so why not," that's a problem. "Don't sprint before knowing where you're going."

chunks.heading: Two-prompt workflow to find your real goal and audit your week
chunks.text:
Ruben's concrete starting method: open Claude (or whatever tool you use) and run two prompts, in order, without skipping the first. The idea is to use AI to "see clearly" rather than to produce more.

- **Prompt 1, find your real goal:** list everything you're working on, and ask the AI to ask tough questions to determine which ONE item matters most to your growth in the next 90 days. Instruct it to challenge you, not let you pick 3, and force you to pick 1.
- **Prompt 2, audit your week:** give it your one goal plus everything you did that week. Ask it to score each task on whether it directly moves you toward the goal or was performative productivity, "be brutal," then produce a plan for next week containing only what matters.
- He says you'll want to argue with the answer, and that is how you know it's working.
- His framing: "Most people use AI to *produce more*. Start using it to **see clearly**." That is the difference between an AI-holic and someone who knows what they're doing.

chunks.heading: Going from planning to mastering AI
chunks.text:
Ruben's three steps for moving from planning to mastery:

- Join a community of obsessed AI users (he cites his Slack with 1,039 professionals).
- Pick one tool, most likely Claude for most readers, and master it.
- Use AI for your strengths, not your gaps.

He also mentions consulting Fortune 500 companies in the US on AI assessment and workshops, with 1 spot left for Q2, taking inquiries by LinkedIn DM only.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben debunks 16 common beliefs about ChatGPT: it doesn't know the whole internet, forgets beyond its context window, hallucinates, carries bias, and isn't private or free. His core stance: treat AI output as a first draft, pair it with human taste and experience, and verify everything. He also announces a paid weekly video tier because AI courses go obsolete in weeks.

chunks.heading: Common ChatGPT myths Ruben debunks: knowledge, memory and accuracy
chunks.text:
Ruben's essay "16 chatgpt myths." (July 20, 2025) corrects widespread misconceptions about how ChatGPT works. The first group concerns what it knows and how reliable it is.

- **"It knows the entire internet."** He says ChatGPT is not connected to the internet by default. The search feature must be toggled on, and even then it reads only the first few links, which are hard to control unless you share a specific link.
- Without search, it draws on training data (mostly books, Wikipedia, Reddit, YouTube transcripts, papers). That is "a lot of the internet, but not the entire internet", and it stops at June 2024.
- You have to "call" that data with the right prompt. His example: "Act like a data engineer" sends it to its "data engineer database", and the answer is instantly better.
- **"It remembers everything."** A chat forgets anything outside a ~100,000-token context. A token is part of a word. 100,000 tokens is about a 300-page book. Turning on the "Memory" feature in settings gives it much more memory.
- **"It never lies."** ChatGPT and nearly every other AI hallucinate, meaning they fabricate data. It predicts the next token, not the next fact, so when there is a data gap it fills the void with fiction.
- It can invent sources, quotes and entire studies. His line: "Confidence ≠ truth."
- His rule: treat every reply as a first draft. Verify, cross-check, then polish.
- **"It's unbiased."** Training data is the open internet, packed with cultural, political and historical bias. Reinforcement learning fine-tunes behavior, but humans with their own bias set the rules. He recommends using multiple prompts and perspectives to detect blind spots, and points to his post "How to make AI battle for you" on confirmation bias.
- **"It predicts the future."** It extrapolates trends and nothing more. Future facts are probabilistic guesses, "sometimes right by luck. Like the Simpsons." He advises asking for multiple scenarios, not certainties.
- **"It understands humor."** It understands patterns, not punchlines. Sarcasm relies on lived context it lacks, and sound-based wordplay ("knight/night") often falls flat. His advice: give it clear setups and tweak the timing, "or just write your own jokes".

chunks.heading: AI as co-pilot: the "replaces experts" myth
chunks.text:
- Ruben says ChatGPT does not replace experts: "Think co-pilot, not captain."
- His claim: "On every possible benchmark, AI + human beats both AI or human alone."
- He believes "taste & experience is the ultimate MOAT no AI can reach. Yet."
- He frames ChatGPT as "a tool, a very smart intern (that can turn into a parrot)".
- He warns against "ChatGPT psychosis": people get validated in their own worldview until they reach total psychosis and paranoia. He says it is real and links a recent X thread as an example.
- He says he does not want to live in the movie *Her*, but "we're heading there". He says a terrible thing is when people fall in love with AI. He still prefers AI that can be flirty within limits: "I hate vanilla AI. The real world isn't."

chunks.heading: Pricing and plan advice: the "ChatGPT is free" myth
chunks.text:
- **"It's free."** Ruben says nothing is free, "Not even Google."
- Free tiers reduce speed and context.
- Each token costs OpenAI energy and money. He cites "something like $15 million a day" and stresses "A DAY."
- His view: the real price is either your data or your subscription.
- He argues the $20 plan is "much, much better" than the free one. It gives access to:
  - gpt-4.5, which he calls "awesome at writing".
  - gpt-o3, "the smartest".
  - Deep research, "the best at searching".
- The $200 plan is "an overkill for 99.9% of you. I don't even pay for it."

chunks.heading: Privacy, confidentiality and data handling
chunks.text:
- **"ChatGPT is private."** By default, chats are stored on ChatGPT servers and may train future models. OpenAI staff can review flagged content for safety. His fix: turn off "Improve the model" or use the enterprise tier if privacy matters.
- **"It's safe for my confidential files."** He says it is not, unless you have the Team plan.
  - Files can be stored up to 30 days for abuse checks.
  - They may be used to improve the model unless you opt out.
  - On the Team plan, "you're good. But most aren't."

chunks.heading: Image ownership and copyright
chunks.text:
- **"ChatGPT images are yours."** Ruben says ownership comes with strings.
  - OpenAI assigns you the copyright, but you must respect trademarks and likeness rights, and "it's on YOU to respect it. Most don't."
  - Celebrity faces or branded logos can trigger takedowns.
  - He advises running a reverse-image check before commercial use. He admits there is no 100% safe way to protect yourself instantly and wishes such a tool existed.
- **"ChatGPT owns the image you upload."** You keep the original rights, but derivatives are tricky.
  - If your upload is someone else's IP, you still need permission.
  - Remixing a copyrighted photo can create an infringing twin.

chunks.heading: Search engine, browsers and the move to a paid Substack
chunks.text:
- **"ChatGPT uses Google to search."** He says it uses Bing from Microsoft, not Google.
- He says he can't wait to use Perplexity Comet, a new AI browser meant to compete with Google Chrome. He says it is time to "step up the very thing we're using for hours every day", and that he loves Perplexity. He says it is not an ad.
- His "How to AI" newsletter is "exploding". His stated premise: "People want to master AI with words, not code."
- Next Sunday he planned to launch his first paid Substack edition, on "How to set up (properly) your ChatGPT."
- Why a paid newsletter rather than a course: "any AI course becomes obsolete… in 2 weeks", so he shares weekly deep dives to keep content relevant.
- The model he announces:
  - The written newsletter stays free "forever".
  - The paid part is a weekly video walkthrough where he makes a video course of that week's newsletter.
  - Paying gives access to all past, present and future video courses, which he calls his "most advanced & hands-on" content.
- To gauge demand and build support for the paid launch, he asked readers to leave a comment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben unpacks an MIT study showing passive ChatGPT use hurts recall and brain connectivity, then argues the fix is order: do the hard thinking first, invite AI second. He backs it with productivity data (BCG, GitHub) and six workflows that keep the human in the loop.

chunks.heading: Do the thinking first, invite AI in second
chunks.text:
- Ruben opens with a warning: he uses ChatGPT every day, and passive use can make you "dumb."
- His takeaway from the MIT study is that the damage comes from passive use, not from AI itself.
- He argues that "do the hard thinking first, invite AI in second" keeps your memory circuits active while the AI polishes, fact-checks or expands ideas you already own.
- Practical rule: write a quick outline or rough first draft on your own. Only then open ChatGPT to challenge the structure, add counter-arguments or surface examples you missed.
- In his words, you stay in "the cognitive driver's seat; the model becomes a booster, not the steering wheel."
- His closing recipe: draft with your own neurons first, interrogate the AI like a sparring partner rather than a fortune-teller, and own the final cut (tone, ethics, responsibility).

chunks.heading: What the MIT "cognitive debt" study found
chunks.text:
- The study had 54 students writing SAT-style essays: 18 with ChatGPT only, 18 with Google search, 18 with their own brains only.
- Four minutes after writing, 15 of 18 ChatGPT-only participants (83%) could not recall a single sentence. The comparison group not using ChatGPT was at 11%.
- Brain-only writers felt "total ownership" of their essays. ChatGPT users said theirs "felt half-mine at best."
- EEG showed brain-to-brain connectivity roughly halved with ChatGPT: about 80 active "lines" for brain-only writers versus about 40 for ChatGPT writers.
- Ruben's reading: if the model does most of the thinking, you practice less thinking yourself. Researchers call this gap "cognitive debt," because users skim, accept and move on.
- He lists four blind spots: only essay tasks, a short time frame (4 months), an unrealistic lab setting (32-channel caps, one tab, no Slack or WhatsApp), and no control for prior writing skill or knowing how to use AI. He says that last one "makes all of the difference."

chunks.heading: Evidence that active AI use pays off
chunks.text:
- In the study's 4th session, brain-only writers were finally given ChatGPT. Their brain-network activity surged above every earlier session and graders gave their essays the highest scores.
- A field experiment with 758 Boston Consulting Group employees found GPT-4 users finished tasks 25% faster, with work judges rated 40% higher in quality.
- Ruben notes that half of a consultant's work is research plus making slides, so pairing deep research tools (ChatGPT, Perplexity) with slide tool gamma.app makes someone better at the craft.
- GitHub data he cites: Copilot users cut coding time by 55% and time-to-merge halved.
- Creative work: studies in Science Advances found AI-assisted stories judged more creative and engaging, especially for less-experienced writers, though a human still has to curate and vary ideas to avoid sameness.
- His conclusion: top performers never copy-paste and call it a day. They "iterate, reframe, and blend" AI output with their own expertise, ending up both faster and better.

chunks.heading: Workflow: "Draft, Then Ask"
chunks.text:
Goal: understand the problem before the model suggests phrasing or arguments.

1. Do a 10-minute solo draft. Ignore spelling and time yourself, which overcomes writer's block.
2. Gap scan: mark areas that feel thin, repetitive or weakly evidenced.
3. Open ChatGPT and give it full context (share a paper as a PDF). Then ask specific questions, such as "Give me three counter-arguments to Point B" or "Suggest two historical examples for my thesis."
4. Curate, don't copy: paste only what strengthens your narrative, rewrite in your tone, or train ChatGPT on your tone by giving it a snippet.

chunks.heading: Workflow: "Socratic Chat" and "Reverse-Prompt"
chunks.text:
**Socratic Chat** (for people afraid of confirmation bias). It turns ChatGPT into a relentless critic that keeps your executive-control loops active.

1. State your thesis (example: "I argue that universal basic income boosts entrepreneurship").
2. Ask GPT to destroy it: "List the three strongest objections, with evidence."
3. Rebut each objection or concede and adjust your claim.
4. Ask GPT to rate the new draft 1-10 for internal consistency and name the weakest point.
5. Repeat until GPT's score is 8 or higher and you can verbalize every point without the prompt visible.

Ruben has a separate guide on this, "How Socrates prompts ChatGPT."

**Reverse-Prompt** (for tightening ambiguous drafts, specs or prompts).

1. Feed GPT your text.
2. Say: "Guess the exact prompt that generated this. Show it."
3. Any section that comes back generic signals vagueness, so tighten the objective, constraints or style.
4. Rewrite the original with precise constraints and cut fluff.

chunks.heading: Workflow: "AI Pop-Quiz Loop" for retention
chunks.text:
Goal: turn ChatGPT into a just-in-time memory trainer, directly countering the 83% recall failure.

1. Finish your AI-assisted document and close extra tabs so only ChatGPT is open.
2. Prompt: "Generate five short-answer questions that test the key facts, stats, and arguments in my essay. Hide all answers."
3. Answer from memory in the chat, with no scrolling back.
4. Type "show answers" and score yourself, or ask GPT to grade you while acting like an expert on the matter. Follow with "Explain differently the questions I missed."
5. Redo missed questions until you hit 5/5.

He frames this as ideal for students or anyone who needs to learn something.

chunks.heading: Workflows: "Chain-of-Thought Reveal" and "Silent Dialogue"
chunks.text:
**Chain-of-Thought Reveal** (for people who can spot a mistake fast). Goal: see every hop in GPT's reasoning so you catch leaps, assumptions or hallucinations before they infect your work. He recommends o3 because you can see its reasoning.

1. Prompt: "Solve <problem>. Show every reasoning step, no matter how small."
2. Highlight any step that feels like a jump.
3. Cross-examine: "How did you get from Step 4 to Step 5? Cite data."
4. Keep only the steps you can restate in your own words.

**Silent Dialogue** (for people who love to speak). Articulating a problem out loud surfaces hidden assumptions, so GPT acts as a silent listener.

1. Open the ChatGPT phone app with Advanced voice mode on.
2. Set the role: "Act as a silent rubber duck. Reply only 'go on' every 60 sec unless I ask a direct question."
3. Talk the problem through from the top.
4. Note the line where you stumble; blockers usually appear where you can't explain a rationale.
5. Ask a pinpoint question about that gap (example: "Why would variable X be undefined here?"), integrate the fix and repeat.

chunks.heading: How Ruben himself writes with AI
chunks.text:
- He read the entire academic paper (a roughly 200-page EEG preprint), challenged it, and changed his mind about AI.
- He says ChatGPT wrote 50% of the post, and he published the full conversation link and a screenshot as proof, since his newsletter is called "How to AI."
- His model: "I didn't think for Ruben; I thought with Ruben" (the closing note he lets ChatGPT write as co-author). Every stat is fact-checked by him, every analogy trimmed by him, and every workflow stress-tested against his real writing practice.
- The full sequence he recommends: start AI-free with a draft, stress-test with Socratic loops, seal retention with a pop-quiz, reveal reasoning to correct it, use silent dialogue for blockers, and reverse-prompt your own text.
- His stated positioning: "Master How to AI with English, not code."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben lays out a Monday-to-Friday plan to get a team actually using Claude: build one Project per recurring deliverable, add prompt templates, manufacture a before/after "wow", convert one overloaded teammate, then roll out with seeded DMs. The core idea is that adoption is a sales and context problem, not a training problem.

chunks.heading: Setting up Claude as a 5-day team rollout (seats, Projects, templates, proof, then launch)
chunks.text: Ruben's pitch: adoption fails when teams are told to "switch" and left with a blank chat. His fix is a one-week playbook, 15-60 minutes a day, that pre-loads context so a teammate's first interaction already works. He frames it as "what most companies hire a consultant to do in 5 months," with no IT ticket, leadership deck or training session.

chunks.heading: Choosing the Claude team plan and seats
chunks.text:
- Team plan is at claude.com/pricing/team. Minimum 5 seats, maximum 150. Enterprise goes through claude.ai/create/enterprise/qualification.
- Seat advice: Premium if someone uses Claude every day, Standard for less than twice a week. In between he still leans Premium.
- Claude does not train on team data, "like every AI-team plan." He says people keep asking this.
- He prefers Claude Cowork for personal use but Projects for onboarding a team.

chunks.heading: Monday: build one Claude Project per recurring deliverable (45-60 min for 3-5 Projects)
chunks.text:
**Goal:** a separate Project for each task the team repeats weekly (client updates, proposals, meeting recaps, campaign briefs, internal reports). Each gets only the context that deliverable needs. Example: a law firm gets Projects for client memos, case summaries, demand letters and internal reports. Client memos get the tone guide and client roster; court filings get formatting rules and statutory references. "Your sales proposals don't need your brand guide. Your meeting recaps don't need your pricing sheet."

**Steps:**
1. **Let Claude identify the Projects.** Prompt #1 has Claude interview you one question at a time (use AskUserQuestion) about daily work, deliverables, repetitive tasks and work that gets redone. It outputs 3-5 deliverables, a Project name for each, and exactly which documents to upload. His fake firm "RubenLegal" got five Projects after four Q&As.
2. **Create the Projects:** Claude > Projects > Team > New Project. Name each as Claude suggested, add a short "what are you trying to achieve," and set it visible to the whole workspace.
3. **Load only the right context:** one gold-standard example of the deliverable, any relevant background doc (client list, pricing sheet), and the brief or template the team already follows.
4. **Generate instructions per Project.** Prompt #2 (run in regular Claude on Opus with Extended thinking, with examples uploaded) outputs a paste-ready block: what the deliverable is, who it's for, tone and format, quality bar, and guardrails (e.g. never speculate on timelines, always include next steps, never exceed one page). Turn on Extended thinking for most Projects; Web search is optional.
5. **Test and validate.** Prompt #3 asks Claude to produce a sample for a fictional scenario, then critique its own output and say what to add. Tweak instructions if off, about 2 minutes per Project. His test output was an 8-page document he called impressive.

chunks.heading: Tuesday: write a one-sentence prompt template for every Project (15-25 min)
chunks.text:
- Teammates otherwise "stare at the empty chat and think, 'What do I type?'"
- Prompt #4 asks Claude, inside each Project, for the shortest possible copy-paste template: one sentence max and ONE [INPUT] field (raw notes, rough draft or bullets). It must rely on the Project instructions for tone, format, quality and guardrails and not repeat them.
- Save each template in the Project's Knowledge (probably on Drive). About 5 minutes per Project.
- Result: a junior pastes notes, hits enter, done.

chunks.heading: Wednesday: manufacture a before/after "wow" (20-30 min)
chunks.text:
- "People don't adopt tools because of features. They adopt tools because someone showed them a specific output that made them feel behind."
- Pick a task you did manually this week that took 30+ minutes, has a visible "before," and that a teammate also does regularly.
- Run it through the new Project. Optionally record the screen (he uses ScreenStudio) and store the video on Drive with the template and Project link for onboarding.
- Screenshot your manual version and the Claude version, and save everything in one document. This is "actual side-by-side evidence," not "trust me, Claude is good."

chunks.heading: Thursday: convert one person instead of training ten (20 min prep + 15 min session)
chunks.text:
- Core claim: "Adoption is a sales problem. Get one colleague excited, and the rest will follow."
- **Pick the drowning colleague:** behind on emails, always in meetings, staying late, visibly short on time, and someone whose reaction will make others curious. Not the tech enthusiast (will self-serve) and not the biggest skeptic (too much resistance for day one).
- **Message to send** (Slack/Teams): offer to show a tool that could save them serious time on a specific task, 15 minutes, using their actual report/email/brief from this week, no prep needed.
- **15-minute session:** open the Monday Project, paste the Tuesday template, show the Wednesday result, using THEIR work. They learn nothing and take no course; "the context layer you built Monday through Wednesday did the work."
- **Make them co-owner:** add them to the shared Project, show where templates live, and ask "What other tasks should we template?"

chunks.heading: Friday: roll out to the whole team (about 60 min)
chunks.text:
- Rationale: the first interaction decides whether someone uses the tool again. It should be opening a Project where Claude already knows their work and standards, then pasting a template.
- **Pre-flight:** instructions validated (Mon), template ready (Tue), before/after receipts (Wed), one teammate who vouches (Thu).
- **Rollout message.** Prompt #5 writes a Slack announcement of under 150 words: lead with one specific result from the Wednesday test, one sentence on the shared Project, three things to do right now, ending "Try [template] on your next [task]. It takes 2 minutes." Casual, no exclamation marks, "like a teammate, not a manager," and an invitation to an onboarding call.
- **Seed it:** post in the team channel, then separately DM 2-3 people to try a specific template on a specific task today. The Thursday co-champion does the same so it's not only the manager pushing.
- **Collect feedback at end of day.** Prompt #6 takes the Slack reactions and returns: instruction adjustments, new templates to add, the biggest misconception to address, plus a Monday follow-up message with one team quick win.

chunks.heading: Why Claude, and his closing view
chunks.text:
- He argues Claude is "simply the best out there" and cites Polymarket as expecting it to stay on top for a long time; he says he is betting on it.
- Closing framing: "intelligence compounds." Teams that use AI together get smarter together, which he compares to humans hunting together.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues LLMs output the statistical average (70th percentile) in a confident tone, so people who use AI to fill skill gaps can't spot errors. His fix: extract your expertise (standards, constraints, landmines, audience) into a reusable context file, let AI draft v1, steer with follow-ups, and write the final 5% yourself.

chunks.heading: AI is an average-answer machine (the "70th percentile")
chunks.text:
- Ruben argues LLMs "don't know things, they predict." They output the most likely next word, based on everything they were trained on: "every blog post, textbook, Reddit thread, corporate memo, and Medium article ever written."
- The result is the statistical average of human writing on a topic: acceptable to the most people, offends no one, excites no one. He calls this the 70th percentile answer.
- He says this is by design, not a bug. The goal for users is the 95th percentile, which AI will not reach on its own.
- His consequence: using AI to fill a skill gap ("I don't know sales copy / financial modeling / design, AI will do it") is "exactly why you use AI wrong."

chunks.heading: The confidence trap
chunks.text:
- The more confident AI sounds, the more suspicious one should be. Real expertise is messy: a great strategist says "it depends," asks clarifying questions, flags exceptions, and tells you when it didn't work. "That mess is the expertise."
- AI gives clean, confident, structured answers (headers, bullets, authoritative tone). Non-experts mistake "legibility for quality" and confidence for competence.
- Experts spot it immediately: it feels like someone who read a lot of books but never did the work. "Too clean. Too confident. Too agreeable."
- His line: "AI has consensus. And consensus is just another word for average."

chunks.heading: What expertise actually is (four things AI lacks)
chunks.text:
Ruben says "expertise isn't knowledge," it is a set of capabilities built over years:

1. **Taste:** you feel wrongness before you can name it (a designer senses off spacing, a writer senses a clunky sentence). This is pattern recognition from thousands of reps. AI has seen more examples but has no visceral response to quality. "That feeling is the asset."
2. **Scars:** constraints learned the hard way. His examples:
   - "Never present strategy without a 'what kills this' section" (blindsided in a board meeting).
   - "Never commit to a timeline without 40% buffer" (shipped late three times, lost a client).
   - "Never use jargon in the first paragraph."
   - "Never design without knowing how it fails."
3. **Knowing where the danger is:** consultants know the real risk is internal politics, designers know it's the edge case (a 47-character name), writers know it's the wrong frame, executives know it's second-order effects. AI gives the textbook path and misses the landmines.
4. **Knowing what your audience won't say:** their unspoken fears, objections they won't raise, what they tried before and why it failed. AI knows generic "marketers" or "executives"; you know your specific ones.

His conclusion: give AI your expertise as context. You are not hoping it will "act like an expert"; you ask it to draft while you steer.

chunks.heading: Build a reusable context file (2-3 hours, once)
chunks.text:
Ruben's five-step process, run in one chat (he recommends Claude Cowork with Opus 4.5 for the extraction):

1. **Upload what you love:** 5 examples of excellent work (yours or others'): PDFs, screenshots, links, pasted text.
2. **Extract patterns:** ask the AI to analyze why each example works and write each pattern as a rule starting with "Always" or "Never."
3. **Add your scars:** have the AI interview you one question at a time: what you never/always do, where you were burned, mistakes you see others make.
4. **Add your audience:** same interview format: who they are, what they tried, what they fear, what they won't say aloud, what builds or breaks trust.
5. **Export:** compile into one file with four headings: STANDARDS, CONSTRAINTS, LANDMINES, AUDIENCE. Paste into a Google Doc, download as markdown.

chunks.heading: How to use the file on each task
chunks.text:
- Upload the markdown file at the start of a chat, then prompt simply: read it fully, list the 3 rules from the file that matter most for this task, and give an execution plan before writing anything.
- Then instruct: do the task, follow the file strictly, and "if you're about to break one of my rules, stop and tell me."
- He says the file is reusable "for months." Most people skip the follow-up steering, which he treats as the key step.

chunks.heading: The steering wheel: the 95/5 split
chunks.text:
- AI's first draft will be about 60% there, and he says that is fine: an expert can see exactly what's wrong.
- Each redirect takes ~30 seconds. His examples:
  - "Paragraph 2 is too generic. Make it specific to B2B SaaS."
  - "You missed the risks. Add a section on what could go wrong."
  - "This sounds like a textbook. Make it sound like someone who's actually done this."
  - "Wrong angle. They don't care about features. They care about not looking stupid in front of their board."
- Non-obvious steering prompts: "What did you leave out?", "Argue against this.", "Write this for someone who's seen this advice 100 times.", "What's the uncomfortable truth you're avoiding?", "What context would change this completely?", "Now give me the 20% that will yield 80% of the results."
- The formula:
  1. AI writes v1 using your context file.
  2. You name what's wrong (your taste).
  3. AI rewrites from your direction (60% to 95%).
  4. You write the final 5%, the parts only you can write (your voice).
- "AI does the prep. You do the surgery."

chunks.heading: The shift: use AI for strengths, not gaps
chunks.text:
- Flip the default from "I don't know X, so AI will figure it out" to "I know X deeply, so AI will help me move faster while I steer."
- Reason: on things you're bad at, you can't tell when the AI is wrong. On things you're great at, you catch every mistake and push it further than it would go alone.
- His TL;DR: build the context file once (standards, scars, landmines, audience), upload it before every task, steer with follow-ups, write the final 5%. He claims this puts you in the top 1% of AI users.
- To go from top 1% to top 0.1%: join a community of obsessed AI users (he mentions his Slack with 900 professionals), play with AI the way you learned through games as a kid, and use AI for your strengths.
- Closing line: "AI is a mirror. It reflects what you bring. So bring your best."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben walks his non-technical mom through Claude using a real task (planning an apartment succession). He shows a simple prompt formula, how to fix hallucinations with source rules, and how to turn an answer into a product. The second half is paywalled.

chunks.heading: How Ruben teaches Claude to a non-technical beginner
chunks.text:
Ruben taught his mother, a retired pharmacist, "how to Claude". His claim: "If my mom gets Claude, you will." He frames Claude (and any AI) as a guide that works the same across ChatGPT, Gemini or Grok, saying that soon they will be "like picking up sneakers".

- He says Claude is still small: it grew 10x in a year but is about 6x smaller than ChatGPT.
- Most non-technical people see AI as whatever is on their phone (his mom's AI is Gemini on Android).
- He ends the lesson by telling her she doesn't need to open Claude. She is retired. She will use products built on Claude without noticing.

chunks.heading: Explaining what AI is: prediction, not search
chunks.text:
Ruben's first correction for beginners is that Claude is not Google. It is closer to a phone predicting the next word.

- He uses the sentence "This is how AI finds the next [...]" and walks through four steps Claude takes to pick the missing word.
- His line: "You are also just predicting the next word very well."
- When asked how it knows which word, he explains in one sentence: it read so many books and internet discussions that it got a good feeling for how sentences are made.
- He admits the training ethics are "Meh". Anthropic trained on millions of single-unit books and then burned them, and got away with it legally. ChatGPT did similar, and new AIs now distill other AIs.
- His takeaway: "technology can't be stopped. It can be contained, regulated, safely deployed - but never stopped."

chunks.heading: Where he sees work going: frontier tech or likability
chunks.text:
He argues the world is dividing in two: people extremely good at handling frontier technology like AI, or people so likable that customers keep coming back (his mom's pharmacy).

- He warns that "likable = job" is not guaranteed.
- Example: the French porter, whose job was carrying luggage. Wheels on luggage and easier roads replaced them. "Technology replaced likable people."
- His implication: anyone relying only on likability should get better on the technology side.

chunks.heading: The beginner prompt template
chunks.text:
Ruben says a beginner needs only this structure, and promises "you won't need more than this":

- "I need [goal] that I will consider achieved once [success criteria]."
- "I am [context about me, my situation]."
- "If necessary, ask me clarifying questions first."

Worked example: his mom needed a plan to pass her apartment to her four children with minimal tax under French law, normally a costly notary question.

- Goal: a plan to pass her apartment to four children with minimal tax.
- Success criteria: she has the best options under French law.
- Context: age 61, retired, in Paris, 4 children, one apartment, wants to keep living in it after transferring it.
- The clarifying-questions line matters because she feared not saying enough. Claude replied with a form where she clicked options 1-2-3-4 or typed in "Something else".
- He used Wispr Flow, a dictation tool, because she types slowly. She simply talked as she would to her notary.
- Result: in about 10 minutes she had every answer the notary gave her, without the cost.

chunks.heading: Showing the difference from Google: Claude produces the deliverable
chunks.text:
Ruben says the moment his mom understood AI was when it produced documents, not just answers.

- Claude wrote a complete strategy document and a pre-filled contract a notary can review, in under 10 minutes and almost for free.
- His framing to her: "Imagine if you started the conversation with the notary having these documents first. Would it be the same price?"
- His principle for expanding someone's view of AI: let them feel how it widens their options. "They are now capable."
- Search and find answers is one step. Then build the strategy and write the contract.

chunks.heading: Handling hallucinations with source restriction
chunks.text:
Ruben defines a hallucination as the AI making things up ("The AI hallucinated [something]").

- He cites a paper (arXiv:2608.27167, Aug 2026) finding that AI trusts a fancy-looking chart as real without checking the numbers.
- His fix is a prompt that restricts domains and forces citations: "Answer only from [DOMAINS]. Cite the exact reference and link for every figure. If it's not there, say 'not found'. Don't fill from memory."
- For his mom, the domains were legifrance.gouv.fr and bofip.impots.gouv.fr, official French government sites, with the exact article and link cited for every figure.
- He argues most "AI is bad" takes come from one bad experience or one bad story: hallucinations exist, but you can fix them.
- Privacy: public Claude with private data carries some risk. Business Claude is SOC 2 compliant and can't leak that data, "the same way Microsoft or Google works."

chunks.heading: Turning a result into a product with a simple prompt
chunks.text:
Ruben says it is easy to build anything with Claude, so his mom will likely use a Claude-made product without noticing.

- Example: in the same chat, a simple prompt had Claude build a website so any mom in her situation could get the same strategy and contract results, with a share button.
- He then says he uses Claude less like he taught his mom and more through Claude Code.
- He says he is not technical and doesn't code, yet spins up live websites almost every day for any use case from one simple prompt (the prompt itself is behind the paywall).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben shares 27 non-obvious tips from heavy daily Claude use. Most are about keeping context clean (new chats, editing instead of correcting, fewer connectors and skills). The rest cover dictation, Artifacts, Claude Code and Cowork, and seat pricing. Several tips are product-specific and will date quickly.

chunks.heading: Where Ruben uses Claude Projects, and where he avoids them
chunks.text:
- He argues Projects are a poor fit for creative work. Loading around 40 files into a Project means "every answer is a remix of your own documents": Claude answers from the files instead of thinking, which is why a user's LinkedIn posts all sound the same.
- Projects suit repeated tasks with fixed material, such as writing a contract, standard procedures, client reports or weekly formats.
- For a new idea, he says to open a normal, empty chat every time.
- He applies the same logic to skills. Skills are the best for "do this exact task this exact way" (reports, formats, recurring workflows) and the worst for creativity. Every loaded skill bloats context and narrows what Claude explores.
- For maximum anti-clutter, he sometimes opens incognito mode inside Claude so it has zero context.

chunks.heading: Managing context, cost and conversation length
chunks.text:
- Claude re-reads everything in the conversation before every answer. Long chats get more expensive and less sharp with each message, and contradictions force Claude to reconcile too much at once.
- His rule of thumb for turns (you say something, Claude replies): around 30-50 turns is when Claude starts to get dumb. Above 100 turns, leave and start a new chat.
- Don't reply "no, that's wrong". The wrong answer stays in the conversation, Claude works around it, and you pay for it on every later message. Instead go back to the prompt right before the bad answer, edit it and click "Save".
- Turn off Connectors (Gmail, Slack, Granola and so on) unless actively used. Every active Connector is loaded into every message, used or not, so it costs extra tokens.
- Model sequencing: frame the whole problem in the first prompt, since it is the most important one, using the most powerful model (Fable-5 on High). Then switch to a cheaper model, Opus 5 (High), to continue without spending extra.
- When combining Connectors on purpose, turn them on together. His example for a big email: Slack (what was said in shared threads), Granola (what was decided in the meeting) and Gmail (what was promised in writing). The prompt: "Using Slack, Granola and Gmail, draft 3 different emails with 3 different tones about […]."

chunks.heading: Prompting: give more context, not adjectives
chunks.text:
- Dictate rather than type. Typing makes you organize thoughts and silently delete context, while talking shares everything, including the messy parts. He says it makes "prompt engineering" 100x better.
- His process:
  1. Use Wispr Flow (what he uses) or Claude's built-in dictation.
  2. Talk for 10 minutes straight: goal, constraints, what you tried, what you hate, your contradictions. Don't clean anything up.
  3. End with: "These were messy voicenotes. Ask me clarifying questions if you didn't get something as a form."
- He writes his newsletter this way.
- Add this line to any prompt: "Before answering, use the AskUserQuestion form to get more context from me if necessary." Claude then shows tappable multiple-choice questions, which he calls "the most underrated feature in the app." His summary: "AI is all about sharing enough context."
- Adjectives like "make it nicer/punchier" do almost nothing. Say what you hate instead: "Never write like this: [paste]." It draws the exact line not to cross.
- In Claude Code and Claude Design, start with a screenshot (a competitor's page, a dashboard you like, a photo of a napkin sketch) rather than a description. It also works in normal Claude for HTML designs.

chunks.heading: Claude Code, Cowork and building with Claude
chunks.text:
- He says Claude Code is better than Cowork at everything, but looks scary and built for developers. He expects the two to merge eventually.
- Everyone should try Code once, via the "Code" tab at top left: dictate and ask it to vibecode something, e.g. "Build a website to track my daily frisbee sessions." You don't need to master it; you need to know it exists. You can hire someone to use it later.
- Cowork's real feature is spawning agents: multiple Claudes working one problem in parallel. Give it big tasks, e.g. "Prepare the full client onboarding: the deck, the welcome email, and the checklist."
- To set up Cowork, run the Anthropic-made skill `/setup-cowork` with the prompt "start". It interviews you and configures preferences, styles and workflows.
- Vibecoding won't make you rich, because you need much more than code. But when you have an idea, skip the briefing document: build a rough version in one afternoon and send that to the technical team. Talking to engineers and designers with an actual half-baked site is useful.

chunks.heading: Artifacts, images and outputs
chunks.text:
- Claude can't generate images like ChatGPT, but it can generate HTML that you export as an image. Upload an example image with: "Code an HTML-like infographic like the one I attached, but about [topic]." Text in HTML is always spelled correctly, which image generators can't guarantee. Most graphics in his newsletters are made this way; he exports to Canva.
- Mini-apps: "Build me an artifact that tracks [my habits / my client pipeline / my reading list], and make it save my data between sessions." Each artifact gets its own shareable link.
- Put Claude inside the mini-app: "Make it so there is a Claude coach inside I can talk to and it has the context of this artifact." Publish and share it (a proposal analyzer for clients, a quiz for a new hire, a tone-checker for a team). Recipients don't need Claude themselves.
- Paste numbers or a CSV and ask "Make this an interactive chart" for an interactive chart inside the chat.
- He opens Claude documents in Google Drive rather than on his computer.
- Research mode is rarely used but good: it plans, reads dozens of sources and returns a structured report you'd normally pay an analyst for. Ask a decision question ("Should we price at X? What does the market do?") and wait.

chunks.heading: Team pricing, Claude vs ChatGPT, and safety
chunks.text:
- Premium seats cost $100/seat/month and come with usage limits high enough that a team stops thinking about them. Past 150+ seats you pay per usage regardless, which gets very expensive, so he advises staying under 150 seats.
- He does not tell people to switch to ChatGPT. "ChatGPT is good. Anyone selling you a 10x difference is selling something." He still prefers Claude, for narrow reasons: it writes and reasons slightly better, and the Premium company tier is a better deal.
- He would reconsider only at 5,000+ employees, where an open-source setup starts to make sense.
- On safety: if you use Google, Claude is just as safe. Business plans are SOC-2 compliant, and a team account needs at least 2 seats. He notes Fable-5 has a data retention problem, while the other models are fine.

chunks.heading: Mindset: ignore trendy techniques, AI can be creative
chunks.text:
- Ignore "loop engineering" and whatever technique comes out next month. A technique matters once it becomes invisible, like Chain-of-Thought prompting, which gave us reasoning models; you just benefit from the AI thinking before answering.
- "Focus on doing your job better, not on falling in love with the technology."
- On the claim that AI can't be creative because it is data and data is the past: he says it's both true and false. Math problems that had stayed unsolved for 80 years were solved simply because someone asked the AI with the right context, and it was not a one-off.
- He has also built a skill that audits text so it passes AI detectors, covered in his guide "Can you detect AI?" (published Jul 22).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues AI made effort and strategy worthless, leaving taste and consistency as the real edge. He breaks LinkedIn growth into three levers: reader-centric (not personal) topics, pattern-breaking hooks, and scrappy useful media, then insists on daily posting and picking a target to pursue with action.

chunks.heading: Core principle: nobody cares about you, they care about what's useful to them
chunks.text:
- Ruben grew his own LinkedIn account from 8,000 followers (pre-ChatGPT) to 770,000 in 3 years, using ChatGPT first, then Claude, Grok and Gemini. He did the same on 5 different accounts organically, for a combined 1.56 million followers.
- He gained 344,258 followers in 2025 alone, on one account, with no ads (roughly 1,000 a day).
- He says he never writes a personal post: "No one cares about me. Strangers can't relate to my achievements."
- A prompt like "this is my achievement, make a viral LinkedIn post" yielded 8,000 impressions and +46 followers. At that rate, 1 million followers would take 21,739 days (about 60 years).
- Personal posts make people around you proud (mom, kids, boss). They don't make new people want to follow.
- Readers read alone, facing a screen, with their own life problems. "Either I help YOU now, or you won't care enough to follow me."
- Bragging example: "my Substack made me hundreds of thousands of dollars" gets "why is he bragging?". "Here's how YOU can generate $1,000 with Substack" gets attention.
- People follow people who are useful to them. They praise the personal posts of people they know. His question: "Do you want to be praised or get new followers?"

chunks.heading: Why AI alone doesn't win: only taste and consistency are left
chunks.text:
- AI made the effort to start and a reasonable strategy easy, so both are now worthless as differentiators.
- What remains scarce is taste and consistency. His formula for 1M followers: AI + taste + consistency.
- AI can produce 1,000 post variations an hour and apply any public "LinkedIn growth strategy", yet that doesn't produce stars.
- If a shortcut feels tiring, that's the point: "If you can't pursue the effort, the goal isn't worth pursuing." The effort is his competitive advantage.

chunks.heading: Finding the post angle: a clarifying-questions prompt
chunks.text:
Ruben's workflow for turning expertise into a reader-centered post:
1. Open Claude (Cowork) and upload your "about me" text file.
2. Paste a prompt asking Claude to find the best angle and topic for one LinkedIn post that is useful, relatable and 100% about the reader, not bragging.
3. The prompt tells Claude to read the uploaded files first, not execute yet, and ask clarifying questions (via AskUserQuestion) about: the real problem the audience struggles with, which piece of expertise is most useful to a stranger, and how to frame it so the reader sees themselves in it and has a clear reason to follow.
4. Work only starts once aligned.

The aim is to force "useful" over "personal".

chunks.heading: Hooks: break the reader's pattern
chunks.text:
- A hook is the first two lines on LinkedIn, before "… more". Ruben defines it as exactly 2 sentences of about 55 characters each. If people click "… more", you win.
- The job of a hook: stop the scroll. Readers are bored, understimulated and doomscrolling. Example he gives: writing "Abuse me" mid-newsletter made the reader's thumb stop.
- He argues every successful thing broke a pattern: Nirvana (vs hair metal, a $20 guitar), Picasso (painted what people felt), iPhone (removed the keyboard), Google (white page and a box), Galileo.
- Hook prompt (a follow-up to the draft post): write hooks that are about the reader or a universal tension, never about Ruben; create an open loop; no achievements, no emoji openers, no hashtags; should feel like a friend's text that makes you reply "wait, explain."
- The five techniques in the prompt, with his examples:
  - Contradiction: "The worst LinkedIn posts get the most followers."
  - Specific number + unexpected context: "I mass-unfollowed 2,000 people. My engagement tripled."
  - Direct accusation: "You're writing LinkedIn posts for your mom, not your audience."
  - Stolen thought: "You know your LinkedIn posts are boring. So does everyone scrolling past them."
  - Absurd reframe: "Your LinkedIn hook has 1.2 seconds to live. Most die instantly."
- Claude generates 10 options by technique via an AskUserQuestion form. The key is the conversation with the AI.
- Claude won't write the perfect one-shot hook, but it will create 100 variations. Your taste picks one; posting 100 times sharpens your taste.

chunks.heading: Media: the image matters more than the text
chunks.text:
- Ruben claims the image takes about 80% of the screen, the hook 20%, and the rest of the text 0%. He compares media to a book cover.
- Three misconceptions he corrects:
  - "The text is what matters": only the hook and media matter.
  - "Videos are the best format": people on LinkedIn don't binge video.
  - "I need a strong recognizable brand": the more it looks like an ad, the worse it performs. Be scrappy.
- Best media: a single 1080 x 1350 image, scrappy and unbranded, useful right now, something you want to send to a colleague or bookmark. "This is the opposite of an ad."
- Reverse-prompting workflow with Gemini:
  1. Search Pinterest for your niche + "graph", "cheat sheet" or "infographic" (his example: "rare earth infographic") and download a good one.
  2. Upload it to Gemini (Thinking model) with: "Extract all of the information from this infographic so another designer could remake it. Your goal is to brief it, as if the designer was Gemini nano-banana (reverse prompting)."
  3. Find a second Pinterest image in an organic style (he searched "handwritten style infographic").
  4. Follow up: "Now remake this infographic with the information, but with this style I just uploaded (copy only the style, your content comes from what you just shared)."
- He says the result is something a designer could charge hundreds of dollars for ("I could have paid $500").

chunks.heading: Consistency: post daily, action produces information
chunks.text:
- Ruben says he never missed a day in 3 years and tracks posts in a Notion calendar.
- "Action produces information." He wrote thousands of posts and learned from each; that is the difference between him and most people.
- No AI prompt makes you consistent. The requirement: one post a day, about 30 minutes. "Someone infinitely dumber than you is getting what you want by simply being consistent and using AI smartly."
- It means sacrificing other things that don't serve the goal. His advice: go all in.
- Comparison: you can't expect a bodybuilder's body working out twice a month.

chunks.heading: Pick a target and go all in with AI
chunks.text:
- Ruben says most people don't truly want 1,000,000 followers, so they don't follow the playbook. Followers may not be what you really want, but pursuing a target generates information.
- AI made action cheap, so some people get "a godlike amount of information from a godlike amount of action."
- Advice: pick a target, pursue it with everything, and use AI to build an unfair advantage "so unfair it feels insurmountable to catch up with you."
- From planning to mastering:
  - Join a community of obsessed AI users (his Slack has 1,108 professionals).
  - Pick one tool (likely Claude for most) and master it.
  - Use AI to produce action, to get information.
- Reader behavior note: he expects about 300 of his 300,000 weekly email readers to actually apply the guide, and urges applying it immediately and sharing it with a team chat for accountability.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues AI makes intelligence a cheap commodity, so average work dies first and the market stops paying for it. Durable value shifts to judgment and taste, which you must extract into reusable context files, and to building repeatable systems rather than selling hours or answers.

chunks.heading: Cheap intelligence turns average into a commodity
chunks.text:
- Ruben's core claim: "Your salary is being compared to a subscription now." AI cost per unit of intelligence fell about 6,000x in 4 years, and the 2026 DeepSeek model is smarter than the original GPT-4.
- Tasks that once needed an expensive human (memo, market scan, spreadsheet, landing page, sales email, first draft, contract review, 20 campaign ideas) now take a prompt, about 30 seconds and about $20/month. He says the output is "fine. Sometimes good. Sometimes better than the junior person they hired last year."
- He cites crashing junior jobs as proof the market has decided AI beats juniors.
- The threat is not that AI becomes perfect. It is that AI "becomes cheap enough to replace good enough."
- The better question is not "Will AI replace me?" but "What happens when the thing you used to sell becomes almost free?"
- Knowledge work was priced around 3 hidden costs: knowing enough, thinking the work through, and producing the final thing. AI attacks all three.
- Cheap tools don't need to be perfect, just good enough that people use them 100 times more.

chunks.heading: Jevons Paradox: AI means more work attempted, not less
chunks.text:
- Ruben invokes Jevons Paradox (which he spells "Jevon's"): when a resource gets more efficient, total consumption rises because lower costs unlock new demand.
- His prediction: AI doesn't mean less work, it means more work gets attempted (more drafts, tests, research, prototypes, analysis, cold emails, content, dashboards, legal first passes, financial models).
- The lazy prediction is that AI replaces people. The better one is that AI raises the amount of work humans are expected to manage.
- Intelligence is becoming a commodity. You lose not because AI can think, but because everyone around you can think 100x more often while you work as if thinking were still expensive.
- Intelligence used to be the bottleneck: ideas waited on analysts, designers, writers, interns, consultants, developers and manager reviews.
- Now the first serious attempt is almost free (the final work is not). Before, you tested 1 headline; now 50. Before, you read 3 competitor pages; now you scan 300. Before, 1 client deck; now 4 versions for 4 buyers. Before, one question to one analyst; now 10 questions you never would have asked.
- "Impossible volume is now possible," and when volume changes, the job changes.

chunks.heading: Average dies first; effort is no longer a moat
chunks.text:
- AI is very good at average: average memo, sales email, research summary, content calendar, Python script, slide outline, support answer, job description, legal summary, market analysis, "strategy."
- Average used to look professional because it took time. Now it looks suspicious because it took 12 seconds. The worst sentence a client can say: "Did you just use ChatGPT to do this?"
- Knowledge workers used to have a moat made of effort (sitting there, typing, knowing the format, searching, assembling). AI removed most of it, and the market now asks "Why am I paying a human for this?"
- His instruction: "Stop trying to make average work. Move above it."

chunks.heading: Judgment and taste are the new scarce work
chunks.text:
- When intelligence gets cheap, judgment gets expensive. Everyone can generate options but few can pick; everyone can draft but few can decide what should exist; everyone can summarize but few know what matters; everyone can make a slide but few make the one that closes.
- The valuable person looks at 20 versions and says "This one," "This angle," "This risk," "This is wrong," "This will fail with our buyer," "This sounds good, but solves nothing," "This should never be sent."
- Taste is trained by doing the work: thousands of reps, bad calls, awkward meetings, failed launches, clients who didn't buy, bosses who killed the project, users who clicked the wrong button. "AI has read about those things. You lived them."
- He expects this gap to get more expensive over time.
- Directive: "You must find a way to extract your taste and give it to AI," because taste trapped in your head can't be used by AI.

chunks.heading: Turn expertise into markdown context files
chunks.text:
- Ruben's method: put your standards, taste, mistakes, audience, rules, constraints, likes and hates, and "the weird little things only you know" into markdown files, and give them to AI before important tasks. This feeds AI what it can't scrape from the internet and stops the average answer.
- "A prompt is a one-time request. But a file (inside a folder) is reusable memory."
- Folder structure he uses (built for Claude Cowork; works in other AI by uploading the files into a "Project", including ChatGPT):
  - ABOUT-ME/: about-me.md, anti-ai-writing-style.md, my-company.md
  - TEMPLATES/: examples-i-love.md, examples-i-hate.md, plus examples of work you love
  - OUTPUTS/: whatever AI produces
- Keep it small: "Please don't dump 400 PDFs into a folder and call it context."
- Starter prompt: "I want to [task] for [success criteria]. Start by reading my about-me folder and its files. Then, ask me questions to complete your task with my answers."
- All his AI sessions start with a Q&A so the AI is prompted better. It feels slow, and he says that's good because transferring taste takes time.
- "Most people want AI to skip thinking. You want AI to extract your thinking." Your value is your unique way of thinking, not the manual work. "Stop selling hours. Start selling taste."

chunks.heading: Stop selling hours; become a system person, not an answer person
chunks.text:
- "I spent 6 hours on this" no longer signals quality, because time spent used to signal quality only when production was expensive. What stays expensive: outcomes, taste, trust, responsibility.
- Better arguments than hours: understood the real problem, knew what to ignore, found the missing risk, made the decision easier, shipped the version that worked, saved the team from "doing the wrong thing beautifully."
- The answer person (answers questions, drafts, researches on request) gets replaced first. The system person asks "Why do we keep needing this?" and builds the repeatable way to handle it: template, checklist, context file, project folder, recurring review, workflow, trained AI setup for the team, a way for others to get 80% of the answer without asking.
- "You stop being the bottleneck. You remove bottlenecks."
- Prompt he gives: list 5 tasks people keep asking you to do, paste your exact step-by-step process with tools, then ask AI for each task to (1) identify the repeated pattern, (2) say what context files are needed, (3) turn it into a reusable checklist, (4) draft the first workflow version, (5) say what should stay human.
- He means simple recurring systems, not "monster-automation sending emails on your behalf to your loved ones."

chunks.heading: Use AI where you already have taste; take responsibility
chunks.text:
- People use AI backward ("I'm bad at this, AI will do it"). If you're bad at the thing you can't judge it and will "approve clean garbage."
- Examples: great at sales, have AI draft 20 angles and you'll spot the 19 weak ones; great at finance, have AI test your model and you'll catch the lazy assumption; great at writing, use AI for raw material and cut the fake voice; great at operations, have AI map workflows and you'll see the missing handoff. "Your skill becomes the steering wheel."
- Where humans still win: knowing what should exist, what to ignore, who needs to trust it, what will fail in the real world, when an answer sounds right but is wrong, how to fit work to your exact context, and "taking responsibility when the output matters."
- Responsibility is the big one: "I pay my lawyers to take responsibility. Be like my lawyer."

chunks.heading: Ruben's offers and positioning for his newsletter
chunks.text:
- He calls AI "a lonely experience": using it alone at work, unable to brag about it or skip it, and unable to ask touchy questions of coworkers while companies push "AI champions." That is why he started the "How to AI" newsletter, because only developers had a community around LLMs.
- Three tiers: "I do it myself" (free newsletter, twice a week, with a suggested 20-minute weekly meeting with yourself); "Do it with us" (paid Substack at $200/year, includes a private Circle channel and $219 worth of partner AI tools such as Gamma, Wispr Flow and Granola); "I do it for you" (enterprise consulting).
- Enterprise consulting: he helps US enterprises adopt AI (Claude) faster, runs workshops for teams of at least 50 people, deploys engineers where automation is needed, and says he had handled 14 businesses since January but was not yet live.
- Distribution note: he says the newsletter grows from shares, he keeps hitting 1,000+ shares, and shares are his weekly north star. The post asks readers to share it and to book 20 minutes that week to act on one section.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ruben argues AI raises demand for knowledge work (Jevons Paradox), so the goal is making 5 people do the work of 50, not cutting headcount. He shows how he duplicated himself with AI tools, trained a team via recorded demos and SOPs, and hires for openness, humility and taste over technical credentials. The list of jobs AI will kill is paywalled.

chunks.heading: How Ruben thinks about AI, jobs and scaling a team
chunks.text:
- Ruben argues AI creates more jobs than it replaces, citing Aaron Levie (CEO of Box): "We need **more** humans, so we can use AI **more**."
- He frames this with Jevons Paradox (1865): efficient steam engines led to more coal use, and more efficient cars led to more fuel consumed overall.
- Cheaper cognition means companies run more projects, experiments, personalization and long-tail ideas that were previously too expensive. Result: more white-collar work, innovation and growth.
- The mindset shift he demands: stop asking "How to replace 5 members of my team with AI?" and ask "How can 5 members of my team do the work of 50 with AI?"
- He says it starts with duplicating yourself.

chunks.heading: How Ruben duplicated himself, then hired
chunks.text:
- He has been obsessed with AI since November 2022, with the goal of doing better and faster instead of hiring.
- Limit he hit: even if AI makes him 10x more efficient, he still works about 8 true hours per day, so he can't have 10x more hours. He hired people to use AI for him.
- His stack:
  - ChatGPT to analyze his content (upload best and worst LinkedIn posts, get a diagnosis, "Winner DNA" checklist, next-post concepts and repurpose angles).
  - Grok for search; he says it is slowly replacing all his LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude).
  - Gamma for carousels and decks.
  - Wispr Flow to write as he talks.
  - Prompt Maker to create prompts quickly.
  - Gemini for images, Opus Clip to edit videos, Claude to write.
- Team: Anisha, Axelle, Zane, Rica and three different agencies, running "How to AI" (newsletter, content, support). He partnered with Pete on consulting, helping Fortune 500 businesses in the US actually use AI.
- Without AI he says he'd still be solo, or two people at most. With AI the team handles 100x more: client workshops, curated content, case studies, research. "Efficiency created massive new demand."

chunks.heading: Start with one AI win today (research example)
chunks.text:
- Wrong: wait for "perfect" AI. Right: 10x one real task now.
- His example is research, a common bottleneck:
  1. Pick research.
  2. Go to Grok (or Claude/Gemini); he prefers Grok.
  3. Paste a prompt: act as a world-class researcher in front of a [audience]; summarize the latest 2025-2026 trends on [topic] in bullets with key stats, 3 emerging tools, 2 risks, 1 opportunity for consultants; sources only from reputable sites (McKinsey, Gartner, a16z).
  4. Run it until the result matches your usual research.
  5. Teach someone to run it daily and decide what to do with it.

chunks.heading: How to teach someone to use AI for you
chunks.text:
- Example workflow for his team: pull the 300 latest cs.AI papers from the arXiv API (sorted by submission date), paste the whole list into Grok, and run a prompt that picks exactly one paper most likely to go viral with non-technical audiences.
- The prompt ranks by: catchy or provocative title, surprising or myth-busting insight about LLMs, explainable by simple analogy, timely or emotionally resonant, little technical detail. Output: title and arXiv ID, a one-sentence viral hook, and 3 bullets on why.
- His briefing process:
